text: I asked my dad about sex when I was five, and he briefly explained:: “Sex is what you do when you are older and you find a friend you want to have children with.”
It was a good tip, but it left out the whole question of romance: why that friend rather than one of the others, what problems people have in relationships, and how to prevent or handle them.

I can't expect my dad to have developed a whole guide to all that, because that wasn't his main mission. So I ended up learning most of it the hard way, and this is what I'd like to pass on to my kids, although by the time they read it, the existence of natural humans, romance, love, might be long forgotten, for all I know.

This guide isn't universally applicable for everyone even now, since it comes from my particular life experience (including influences I've had from friends & research). I’m a straight man, and I’m writing from relationships I’ve had with women, so she and her are going to show up a lot. Most of this has nothing specifically to do with being male or straight. The Primal Attraction section is the exception, because there I’m specifically talking about the man-woman dynamic I’ve actually lived.
English isn't a scientific language when it comes to love. This leads to a lot of romantic confusion because we don't have one word for one meaning.

One meaning is selfless love—what contemplative traditions call agape, metta, loving-kindness, divine love, and so forth. In Buddhist metta practice you sit there wishing, may they be well, may they be safe, may they be happy. It's not about them being yours.

Then we use the same word for romantic love (eros): I want you. I want your attention and your body. I want to be special to you, and I want our lives tangled up together. I don’t think there’s anything fake or shameful about this.
A good relationship must have both kinds of love at once. Too often, the trouble is there’s a whole lot of I want you and hardly any I want you to be happy.

Most people fail this test: what would I want if she herself thought she’d be happier with somebody else? But if they can get past the initial horror, the conflict starts to fall apart. Being wanted is part of what makes me want someone.

But the horror is unavoidable, because I can’t wait until I know I’m wanted before I let her know I want her. If we both do that, nothing gets started. And it doesn’t stop being true once we’re together. If I start feeling less wanted, I may pull back. She feels me pulling back and starts feeling less wanted herself, then she pulls back too.

Agape or divine love does two jobs at once to rescue the erotic love. First, most obviously, it keeps eros from becoming totally selfish and fickle by making the other person's happiness part of the wanting: I want you because I know you'll be happy with me. Second, it gives eros a landing pad. When two people pull away because eros seems unreciprocated for a moment, the backdrop of actual, genuine care, keeps the couple from simply abandoning each other, and then they might even rekindle the eros when they see that it's based on something deeper.
Eros can help build the agape too. It has a drive to it: it keeps pulling me toward this particular person, and over time that closeness can grow an agape that survives the drive itself.

That drive can weaken for reasons that aren't really my fault. I can get old, sick, depressed, or grieving, and I would hope the agape is deep enough that she sticks by me through some of that even if it puts strain on eros. But if I just get bored with life, stop having much of a life outside her, and make her responsible for nearly all my warmth, meaning, reassurance, and excitement, that's different. I don't get to be shocked if she wants me less.

Kim Anami calls the sexual current between encounters “the simmer”. Maybe she texts from work, “I can’t wait to touch you.” Maybe he tells her what he wants to do later. And if our sex life suddenly changes, keep some curiosity about why rather than automatically going with the flow and creating a potential “new normal.” Maybe we're pissed off at each other. Maybe one of us doesn't feel wanted. Maybe somebody's sick, stressed, on a new medication, whatever.

Looking for a partner is arguably backward, and can work against you. You can’t help looking if you want one, but once you start seeing every new person as a potential partner, you perform for them and they perform for you. Try to see people for who they are before you think of them that way. Actually it was Bee who kept drilling this into me: "You see a pretty girl, but you don't see the ugly stuff she's dealing with inside."
On the other hand, if you aren't looking for one, then you also aren't filtering & comparing potential matches, which makes you more vulnerable to someone who targets you with their love bombs.

Maybe a good compromise is to look for people that match you without directly looking for a romantic match. Join a local group that fits your interests. Go forage for wild plants, meditate, hike, study philosophy, whatever. At least you have fun, learn something, and maybe make some friends even if nobody attractive shows up.

I would never recommend dating apps based on my own experience, although I suppose it depends on the person. Maybe you don’t care much about spirituality or anything, you’re not unique and don’t care if they are, you just "like big butts and you cannot lie," and they want the same sort of thing. Then maybe the app fits what you're looking for. 😅

Case in point, OKCupid didn't tell me my first wife was going to try to kill me and my family, take my son, and then put me on child support that I can't pay and wouldn't pay on principle if I could. That was the worst choice I ever made.

On the other hand, the app did give me information that I ignored because she was cute and interested in me. Her OKCupid profile almost made her sound like a prostitute, or at least someone who liked casual sex. Both turned out to be true. But once she started chatting with me and I saw the nice photos, I thought maybe she had been joking in the profile or something.

Ok wait, Judge not, lest ye be judged... An app could be fine as an introduction if you use it as a proper gate. Assume 99.99% of the people there are a bad match for you. If you’re just going to get excited by every cute guy or girl who hits you up, forget it. That’s such an easy way to find a weirdo, a psycho, a mooch, a faker, or whatever. Those people are easy enough to find in modern society in person anyway.

I always tell young guys especially: don’t worry about not finding a girl. Worry about finding the wrong girl. Girls are usually more selective, but they still need to think twice, because they often go for guys who aren’t respectful or mature.

I recently tried Hinge again for a few days while I was in Kenya after my last breakup. I was getting something like a hundred girls interested in my profile every day, so I looked through a lot of profiles. Some were cute but none seemed deep. So the app did tell me something useful.

Sometimes when you don't go looking, others go looking for you! My dad at one point decided I needed a girlfriend. This was long before dating apps, so he suggested we put up posters around the neighborhood advertising me as eligible for girls to date. I was horrified and we dropped the idea. That gives you some idea of the mildly autistic background I’m coming from: we didn’t understand people. That's why it might seem absurd the level to which I'm trying here to help you understand what perhaps is already obvious. 😅

The advantage of meeting through your community, unlike through an app, is that you see someone over time. Other people know them. You see how they act when they aren’t on a date, what they’re like with friends, and what happens when they’re irritated, bored, jealous, or not getting what they want.
Community also supports you regardless of who your baby daddy may be, and you aren’t desperate for just any kind of closeness because hopefully the community already fulfills most of that need.

But if you don't have community, the move is to find someone who is also looking for one that would interest you both. You can visit communities together, or at least make a real plan to eventually live in one together. It’s a wide world, and traveling around looking at possible communities is a supremely good way to get to know someone.
On the other hand, you may end up having sex too fast if you’re traveling together, but I'd still rather have sex with someone who's trying to find a commune with me than someone I met at a party.

Modern life barely has an intermediate stage between being interested in somebody and getting sexually entangled. One old example is bundling, a mostly extinct practice now especially associated with the Amish even though it existed much more widely. Courting couples could spend the night together in bed, usually clothed, with the idea that they could talk and be close without having sex. It sounds a lot like the missing middle I’m talking about.

It also didn’t exactly solve the problem. In late-eighteenth-century New England, bundling coexisted with a lot of premarital pregnancy: 30–40 percent of brides were already pregnant. So it wasn't exactly a reliable way to keep courtship nonsexual. I don't think we need to bring bundling back, but we do need some socially recognized way to explore tenderness and attraction without immediately sliding toward sex, cohabitation, and a life bond.

text: That doesn’t mean I’d advise somebody to knowingly enter a dangerous relationship because it may be worth it. Going in, it helps to recognize your pattern, stop idealizing without becoming suspicious and closed, and have some idea what you’re getting into.
Idealization can be pathological, but it can also come very close to real deep love and appreciation. That’s why it’s so easy to get confused.

So far in my life the main experiences of this have been with Bee and Key. They’re also the two women I’ve actually been in love with, which is probably not a coincidence. Both of them saw me as their knight in shining armor, and that brought out this divine-feminine beauty in them that made me into a real love slave. I’m not Superman out here trying to “save a hoe.” There’s just a natural protector/muse dynamic that sometimes plays out in an exaggerated way.

Legitimately seeing someone as amazing doesn’t depend on what the seeing gives you. Once you start identifying with the way you see them—she’s perfect, this is destiny, I’m the one who finally found her—you’re already lost in the sauce.

The degree of idealization also predicts the degree of demonization for me. I don’t mean this as a clinical diagnosis, but I use it almost diagnostically in my own life. If a woman says, “He’s such a great guy. Of course he has flaws like anyone, but I love him,” that sounds healthy. If she says, “He’s perfect. I can’t find any flaw,” I’m already running.

When the splitting happens, private hatred can replace worship. Then come public accusations, rewriting the whole past and treating every flaw as proof that the person was fake all along. Sometimes the woman who thought I was perfect later accuses me of thinking I’m perfect.

I’ve learned to get nervous when somebody knows too much about me too soon. We’re twin flames. She knows my motives. I’m Lord Krishna. Okay, maybe I really am way better than the other guys she’s found. But if she hasn’t found anything about me that bothers her yet, she hasn’t found all of me.

I still love women I’ve loved before. Sometimes I talk about them because I’m thinking about them. I’m not trying to make her jealous. If she can’t handle that I still love them, she isn’t ready for me.

If she says, “Can you talk less about your exes?” Sure. Maybe I do talk about them too much sometimes. But they still matter to me. If I’m supposed to listen to everything on her mind, I don’t want to have to pretend that isn’t on mine. You can see something in a person before she fully lives it, but then you have to ask her:

If she says no, forget it. You’re in la la land. If she says yes, ask what is blocking her. Is the block more than you can handle? Or does she mostly need somebody to join her on the journey and believe in her?

Partners should help each other grow. Who else is going to do it? Your mom and dad? You’re already grown. Everybody else will usually be a smaller influence, so you’d better choose someone who helps you grow well. Like the FM Laeti song here says, “Inspire her to see the best in herself, actualize that.” If something severe is happening, sometimes a demand or boundary is necessary too.

Spiritual depth also doesn't tell me how dependable somebody is. She may meditate for two hours and still not show up for boring work, sickness, or something she promised yesterday. I may be seeing the divine archetype while ignoring the adult I would actually have to build a life with.
Ask what flaws she sees in you from time to time. Notice whether either of you is relating to a real human being or just to the divine archetypal energy the other person temporarily opened.
I’ve been through the wringer so much with idealization that now no matter who praises me I’m basically like, “Okay, thanks.” I try to do my best.

section: Two Pillars Don't Hold The Roof Up
text: Even if I found my twin flame, she'd still be one person. The polarity could be perfect and we'd still need other people around us.

section: Two Pillars Don't Hold The Roof Up
text: Let me show you how this looked for me. I’ve noticed in my own relationships that whenever a serious issue arises, both of us tend to turn to our separate circles of friends for support. Then I resent the one-sided story she’s telling, she resents the one-sided story I’m telling. Some of the friends may even be exes who want us to break up, and eventually neither of us wants to talk to the other's friends anymore. That's a pretty terrible time to be trying to run the rest of life with two people. Housing, money, children, health, emotional crises—if one person goes down, the other becomes the whole backup system. Who even has time for the relationship itself at that point?

section: Two Pillars Don't Hold The Roof Up
text: Maybe an unusually strong couple can get away without much community. I think that's rare.  But sometimes a friend who actually knows us both sees the pattern before either of us does. On the other hand, If both people are falling apart, there is only so much anyone else can do.

section: Two Pillars Don't Hold The Roof Up
text: That's not abstract to me: I'm sure B. and I would still be together if we'd had a real community around us. Most of all, she would not have been capable of demonizing me when everyone already knew both of us and knew I wasn’t a narcissistic abuser. It would have contained all the insanity. text: Commune friends could also have helped her in ways I couldn’t, because she was projecting onto me, which made me the wrong person to help her see beyond the projection. And it's actually natural to be a bit BPD when your entire survival depends on one person, because if they aren't perfect, and especially if you need a lot of support, how will you survive? One fairly normal but large flaw in them could make your life really difficult. We were left alone inside something that needed other people around it, and that's what's happening to most people these days.

text: H. taught me another part of the same dyad problem. I learned not to treat what either of us thought the relationship was as a guarantee of what it would remain, because feelings can and usually do change over time. In our case, the relationship continued to naturally deepen while our outside relationships often felt more shallow, so it was natural for the dependency to increase. She was never into monogamy, but that didn't stop her from becoming possessive once she found something really worth keeping. And then she began demonizing me when I refused to be possessed. Because we did not have a shared community capable of supporting us, her friends heard her side and affirmed her truth. The accusations couldn't have survived among people who knew us both.

section: Two Pillars Don't Hold The Roof Up
text: Separate confidants can be helpful and harmful. Sometimes you need privacy from your partner and somewhere else to say what you’re feeling. But if your confidant doesn’t have a good connection with your partner, the conversation can turn into an echo chamber very easily.

section: Two Pillars Don't Hold The Roof Up
text: Having the same confidant creates the opposite problem: now you may not have a release valve when you want privacy from your partner. There isn’t one perfect arrangement.

section: Two Pillars Don't Hold The Roof Up
text: If you do have separate confidants, you need enough emotional maturity to remember they will automatically be biased toward you. Take what they say with a grain of salt. They are hearing a partial story, usually while you’re upset, and they may be trying to protect you rather than understand the relationship fairly.

section: Two Pillars Don't Hold The Roof Up
text: Make as much community as you can wherever you are. Go to meetups together. Make deep friendships together. Find some shared purpose beyond maintaining the relationship. Introduce your old friends to your partner and try to mutualize those friendships as much as possible, so they aren’t experienced as slyly antagonistic or partial to one side. You don’t need to spend all your time together, but two completely separate social worlds will automatically start taking sides when something goes wrong.

section: What are you actually choosing together?
text: A lot of romantic pain starts with two lovey bunnies entering one of the biggest arrangements of their lives without ever discussing their ideas, dreams, and fears about it.

section: What are you actually choosing together?
text: “We’re together” ... what does that mean exactly? I can hear a whole future in those two words—sex, exclusivity, living together, money, children, caregiving. She might mean, “We really like each other; let’s see what happens.” I actually like letting a relationship flow without naming every part. The problem is when we’re using the same words for two different futures.

section: What are you actually choosing together?
text: Sometimes what two people want is much more practical. They want to share a home, raise children, support each other financially, take care of each other, maybe have sex, and not pretend all of that depends on overwhelming romantic love. I’d call that a practical partnership.

section: What are you actually choosing together?
text: That feels wrong to me because I’ve been in love, but I don’t think there’s anything inherently wrong with it if both people know that’s what they’re doing. What would scare me is one of them meeting a heartthrob at work or church one day and suddenly wondering why they settled for less.

section: What are you actually choosing together?
text: Another honest option is a romance with humility, even if romance and humility seem to clash. Two people really are in love and want to build something together. They can choose exclusivity, shack up, have children, and plan a life without pretending they can guarantee what either heart will feel ten years later.

section: What are you actually choosing together?
text: My actual ideal is to have intimacy embedded in community. Obviously most people are not going to live in a free-love community unless we really have a New Earth soon. But, as Pema Chodron says to prisoners when teaching them meditation, “Start Where You Are.” Build mutual friendships, and keep other sources of meaning and support alive.

section: What are you actually choosing together?
text: Then the questions change for me. If the romance changes, which parts are still supposed to remain? Are we promising actions, or quietly pretending to promise permanent feelings? Which needs are we still going to meet outside the relationship?

section: What are you actually choosing together?
text: And the biggie: what happens if one of us falls in love with someone else? What counts as betrayal, and what just means we need a serious conversation? If our lives change, can we revisit the agreement honestly? If we separate, what do we still owe each other, and what do we owe any children involved?

section: What are you actually choosing together?
text: These are just a few questions I could think of to start the ball rolling, but be creative and see what you come up with! You can make a card game out of this and have some fun with it. If there's real love, it will survive a bit of honest curiosity.

Conventional marriage vows are dishonest, and most people know it. You can't promise how you'll feel in the future. You can promise actions if you really believe you're capable of delivering them. So for example, you could promise to tell the truth, to keep showing up, to support the children, or whatever else you genuinely believe you can do.

We also find something like my warning in the New & Old Testaments. Ecclesiastes 5:4–6 says it is better not to make a vow than to make one and fail to keep it. If you tell the priest you didn’t mean what you promised, the passage warns that God will be angry and destroy your work.

Matthew 5:33–37 and James 5:12 are stranger still beside wedding vows: let your “Yes” be “Yes” and your “No” be “No,” and anything beyond that comes from evil. To me, the extra promise itself starts to look suspicious. If your yes is trustworthy, why does it need another layer?

Where did the idea of promising to have romantic interest in your partner come from, anyway? It turns out it never existed in any culture I'm aware of until the Victorian age, when romantic feelings were elevated in England to the status of immutable truth.
You can sign a contract about what you’ll do. You can’t sign one saying what your heart will feel ten years from now and expect the contract to produce the feeling.

Marriage itself is a sham in many ways. You could honestly say, “I’ll love you to the best of my ability, in accordance with how you love me.” But “I’ll always love you more than anyone else”—based on what? Because God wants you to?

It's hard to find sexually monogamous animals, have you ever looked? And as it turns out, we humans aren't a natural exception to the rule, either.  Plenty of tribal cultures were (and some still are) much looser about this, while still generally retaining the primary-partner "social monogamy."  Sexclusivity started gaining sway around the time we started planting carrots and peas, and owning land. That's when it made sense to keep track of how to keep our land in the family bloodline. By the Industrial Revolution, this ironically bureaucratic basis of romance became the only definition of marriage, by law.  I'm not trying to say we're just like bonobos, but the academic consensus is that humans  tend toward flexible pair-bonding, with a propensity for occasional infidelity. And now we've gone one step further, so that even the brief inkling of attraction to another person becomes almost a sure sign that sexual infidelity is next. That's why I felt I had no choice but to address the issue head on  when B. wanted to marry me. I told her, “I can't fully commit to you if I’m still attracted to other women, so before I do, let's see if I can fix that."

I meditated for a while and surprised my own self to find something like a switch in my mind. It felt like evolutionary programming around whether I had found my life mate and true love. I asked myself, “Is she the one?”

It worked about 99% of the time. I was no longer interested in other women, aside from one extremely beautiful girl who grabbed my attention once. That amazed me, although B. never quite believed the switch was real. She even started hallucinating that I was looking at or talking to other women when I wasn’t. So her jealousy was not simply tracking what I was doing in the present. More likely it was insecure attachment from childhood trying to justify its continued existence.

Jealousy is always insecurity, but sometimes that insecurity can be an important indicator that the relationship actually is not secure, rather than just a remembered script from childhood. Although, either way, it can become a self-fulfilling prophecy.
Instead of stewing in jealousy and throwing out microaggressions now and then, say the actual thing without hiding the insecurity behind anger. In a monogamous relationship, you might say:

“I notice you pay attention to this other girl more than me, and it makes me feel unloved and insecure. Can we talk about it? Do you really want to explore things with her? If so that's fine, but don't make the decision lightly because it's irreversible.”

Maybe he really is neglecting you or wanting to be with someone else. Maybe the “attention” was one glance and your baseline insecurity inflated it into a threat that it wasn't. That part should not be projected onto your partner. Every couple has to work out for themselves what actually feels healthy.
I do believe two people can choose sexual exclusivity honestly. They can admit that attraction to other people exists and decide not to act on it each day.

I would rather make every attraction possible to mention casually, including the low-stakes ones. If only the serious attractions are supposed to be disclosed, each disclosure becomes such a major event that people are less likely to say anything at all.

That's not to say that polyamory is automatically better, because it can be dishonest too. These days, I believe it is often a way to cope with an inability to connect deeply with one person, or a way to admit a lack of self-control without necessarily doing the self-development that would make the arrangement ethical. If you can't do monogamy, saying so is still more honest than pretending you can. Sometimes the pretending does more damage than an outside connection would have.
I learned most of this by screwing it up. Some of it I just thought through, and I’m still not sure about all of it.

I'm sure I'm not alone here. Everyone does this. You meet someone and you automatically start imagining how good it could be to have them as your partner. You start thinking you know this person because of how your fantasies went, but really all you know from that is what you want. Actually, that's the most useful thing about the fantasy, to figure out what you want. But I usually make the mistake of playing out just the first part of the fantasy.

I think imagination can work a lot better for starting relationships right if we use it against our tendency to idealize people. So for example, I might start with the regular lovey sexy stuff, and that's fine because that's what's drawing me in. Then after that, when I have a bit of wisdom available, I will continue onto the mundane and difficult scenes. I'm not trying to force anything or oppose anything. I just try to open my eyes when they want to close, ignore, look away. Here's my checklist:

What's it feel like after we have sex? Do we feel comfortable and happy about that, or do we feel guilty that we gave in to temptation too quickly and now there's some weird feelings? Name the feelings and explore.
How about a week into the relationship? What's starting to get annoying perhaps? What are we trying not to say and not to notice?
Get in the ring before the ring gets on you. Let's imagine we have a real fight about money, jealousy, or something else important. What do we do to handle the conflict?
Fast forward. Now we've got kids. What might be the values conflicts in how we raise them? Schools, screen time, vaxes, religion, helicoptering vs freedom, food, gender & sexual orientation issues.
Rewind. What if we disagree on having kids?
Fast forward five years. What has each of us gained or given up, and do we have any resentment about it?

This isn't to make predictions and we're not consulting the magic 8 ball nor doing Istikhara here. I mean you can do that too if you want. Distinguish between fears and what really seems likely just as you do between wishes and reality.

If every scene is beautiful, consider that you may be, and almost certainly are, still rehearsing the relationship you want. There's nothing wrong with expecting the best, but it takes work to get there in a wise way.

Before I say anything good about psychedelics in relationships, the warning has to come first. You cannot negotiate consent on MDMA. The drug is changing how safe, loving, open, and connected everything feels. Advance planning doesn't turn getting high and starting a relationship into a safe procedure. People need that warning before they take it, because once you're inside that feeling, sober caveats may sound ridiculous.

Psychedelics, especially certain types of shrooms, very pure LSD, very pure therapeutic-grade MDMA, ayahuasca, loveyhuasca haoma, and iboga, can be extremely useful when a couple is trapped in defensive stories.

With Bee and Key, there were many times when we could argue forever sober, then take something and finally understand each other. It could feel like we were telepathically synced. Instead of each person defending their version, we directly understood what the other was perceiving, feeling, misunderstanding.

But the problem is most people are lazy about integrating what they learn during this window of clarity. We enjoyed the understanding while it lasted, and then the same defensive story would resurface later. In neuroscience, this is called state-dependent learning. What you learn in altered states doesn't automatically translate into your normal sober mind state without the work to do that.

Probably one of the most important benefits we can hope to get long term from any therapy is the ability to express what we feel in a non-combative way. Otherwise, people tend to ping pong between not expressing or downplaying their feelings and expressing them combatively. MDMA can make this temporarily much easier because all the problems can look so small and silly. The question is what happens when you're sober again.

So I would say the therapy worked if a week or two later, you and your partner can comfortably say, “Honey, I'm feeling unappreciated right now. I know you're not trying to make me feel that way, and maybe you feel like I'm making you feel that way, but I'd like us to take some time soon to discuss the issue beneath this in a kinder way. What do you say?”
If you don't have a partner, you can do the same thing with whoever you tend to have trouble relating with, in a less lovey way but still with compassion.

It's not always possible in that moment to change a defensive posture into non-defensive loving communication. That's why I suggest setting a time soon with a nice intention, like a ritual. Sober is fine. You can put some rose petals around you or something to build the feeling, or play some song you both like.

Starting a relationship through psychedelics has another danger. Key and I met and then spent a few days taking iboga with friends. We got to know each other very deeply that way, and that was great. But it was especially her higher self I was getting to know. I tend to idealize people even sober, and that gets worse when I'm high. It was still beautiful to see the real higher self potential in her, I'm not denying that. But that information didn't help me understand how we would get along in normal life.

I’ve also had friends get together at MDMA parties and stuff. It’s rarely a good idea. The intimacy can be completely real without telling you whether the two of you actually work together sober. Or you might even sometimes have the opposite problem, like I had with H.D., where the connection continues to deepen while sober, and it becomes something that one person might cling to desperately, never imagining they could find that again.

The obvious advice is to wait before making large promises and spend time together sober, around other people, and in ordinary situations. Write down what each of you learned, do some peer counseling, check with friends to see if you're too pie-in-the-sky. But the problem is, you won't necessarily be interested in sober advice when you're high. You're "beyond all that." And the high can continue after sobriety because intimacy itself is like rose-colored glasses.

section: Why all of this sounds artificial
text: By now this probably sounds terribly artificial. Is anyone actually going to do scheduled check-ins, delayed cohabitation, conversations about hypothetical disasters, imagination exercises, not to mention resisting the heat-of-the-moment stuff and continuing your own reparenting practices when a warm body is available to do some of the soothing?

section: Why all of this sounds artificial
text: Well, yeah. It is painfully artificial. In a healthy communal society, the couple would have access to witnesses, elders, friends, and other emotional outlets and resources. Most of us these days don’t have that, so we’re trying to recreate consciously and clumsily some of what the wider field would have done without a checklist.
Most of this article is about what to do before jumping head first into head over shoulders. But if you’re already married with children, advice about slowing down arrives a little late.
I wish I had a special method for fixing that. Mostly I learned the obvious thing the hard way: one person can’t fix the relationship (unless they're the main problem in it).

With Bee and Key, the biggest thing sitting underneath everything was trust. They wanted to be with me and would say they trusted me, but really they didn’t trust me, themself, or anyone else. It was all or nothing: blind trust, or none. I kept saying, “It’s not possible to have a relationship without trust.” I think that rigidity came from trauma and never really growing up.

Even dishonesty was sometimes hard for me to define in these relationships. Bee once opened a door and, a second later, said she hadn’t opened it. That drove me crazy. Why would she lie like that? She was lying, but “she lied” only named the momentary behavior. There was no strategy behind it, and she was usually quite honest. Looking back, I could have understood the lie in the context of some kind of mental illness instead of treating it like ordinary dishonesty.

Some things were less mysterious. They were acting as if the trust problem wasn’t there because they still wanted the relationship. Attractions to other people sometimes went unsaid too, and sometimes got imagined from nowhere. Some people keep a relationship like this going for a long time, just sweeping everything under the rug.

On the other hand, sometimes I was more honest than my partner could handle, which was its own kind of damage. Ask whether both of you actually want to prioritize radical honesty, first. But the other person also can’t keep saying “not now” forever and think that's going to save the relationship.
This is the time for agape to shine, because the best thing for both of you may not be holding onto the relationship pattern you originally committed to or dreamt of.

When did you two last dance? And not the “we dance around our problems” joke (LOL).. if that’s where things are at, the trust is out the window. Ouch. I know that one from experience with my first 2 wives and K, too. That generally marks the point of no return, so try not to wait for that. Because once you're there, as my dad explained a thousand times whenever we had a visitor, unconscious resentment begins to snowball, and we feel colder together than alone. Pretty soon, old Romeo & Juliette might get wandering eye syndrome.

section: Outside help can sometimes break the loop fast
text: Bee and I were once desperately misunderstanding each other, so we called my friend Eshwar, the only friend of mine whom she respected. He told a related story about something that had happened with his sister. Somehow, Bee immediately understood what I had been trying to say. It was like magic.

section: Outside help can sometimes break the loop fast
text: So, don't think of outside help as a formal last resort. I think of it as a part of building community when we learn to rely on each other for this kind of intimate, real-life support. It could be calling up a mutual friend, peer counselor, couples therapist, doing Imago dialogue, Restorative Circle, and/or joining a men’s or women’s group. The key is that both people need to respect the person or process enough to hear something new.

section: Outside help can sometimes break the loop fast
text: What they say is also partly true, "The only one you can change is yourself." Restart whatever you stopped doing because the relationship was soothing you: inner-child reparenting, meditation, body practices, peer counseling.
It might repair the relationship, open it, turn the romance into friendship, preserve the family through separation, or show you that ending it is better.
Temporary separation helped Bee and me. It also became more permanent, although I’ve always thought maybe we would get back together in a few decades.
I think everyone generally agrees that parents have more responsibility to children than they do to each other, since children can't take care of themselves.

Before having or adopting children, sit down for an imagination session to figure out whether you two lovebirds can preserve some civil co-parenting capacity after a terrible breakup. That's the actual long-term commitment.

When it comes to stepchildren, even if they aren't technically your children, they still become attached. If you've been acting as their parent for years, it's not right to vanish from their life just because the marriage ended. You don't have parental rights legally, but you can stay a mentor or close friend, and hopefully your partner would agree with this. When children have parental figures come and go, it can damage their ability to have good relationships as adults.

This was particularly difficult for me because Ann was very much unfit at the time to care for our son, Bear. I did fight for custody, but, as my lawyer told me, there was no point, because men generally lose. Eventually I exhausted my options for fighting, and I was left with weekly supervised visits.

Ann was brainwashing Bear into believing that I was "breaking his bones" at these visits even though he didn't know what bones were. That's when I told him I had to stop the visits before I end up in jail. So it was for my protection, but his as well, because if he realizes one day his dad is in jail because his mom manipulated him into telling a dangerous story, that could really wreck him.
As it is now, he may miss me, but he is well cared for (I think) by his grandmother, and probably soon he'll seek me out when he gets his own phone.

It takes a village. The nuclear family, built on parents' romance, can often be the worst arrangement for children. If there's trouble in paradise, parents will try to protect the kids by hiding their tension. But the truth is, children absorb that unresolved tension and integrate it into their very being. In a community, romance is one bond among several, and adult stability for children doesn't rise and fall with it.

If leaving feels right, then just go. You don’t owe it to them to try counseling unless you also owe it to yourself. If you actually don’t want a good relationship with them anymore, go. No amount of counseling will fix something that has nothing at the base of it.

If you love them and wish it could work, ask if they feel the same, and then go to counseling. On the other hand, even when you love each other, sometimes you already know the issue is beyond what counseling could fix.

Do you have irreconcilable memories of key events? I did with both my first and second wives. I took my first wife, A., to two counselors. A very good one eventually told us, “I’ve never told anyone this, but you guys need to split up for at least six months.”

There's no way to resolve a situation where one person remembers that you ruined her life on purpose, while you remember that she was having a manic episode and had to be committed for her own safety. We also didn’t have mutual friends who could corroborate what happened—only friends on each side who were partial.

If you’ve been there for someone, don't abandon them in a crisis unless it’s unsafe for you to stay or they're creating the crisis to keep you, or they aren’t willing to help themself. You may need to arrange other care. That doesn’t mean you have to pretend the romance still has a future.

Many say it's best to save face and work things out privately, but I'd disagree. Recruiting friends into the conflict is often exactly what you SHOULD be doing. If you don’t have friends who can help with the conflict, then you’re really stuck (and you might wanna find some new friends). But do it honestly, with the goal of helping the conflict, not just getting approval for your own interpretation. Both people should have a chance to speak, and good friends shouldn’t automatically validate either side.

I can believe a friend's experience and still tell them that my ability to know what is really going on is extremely limited. If someone says, “I don’t have all the evidence,” I trust their thinking more. Living in community would help because your friends would not only hear two stories afterward. Sometimes they would actually see how the two of you treat each other when you argue.

Often times the breakup is hard, but the aftermath is worse. Public demonization should be avoided, but I don't think that means hiding the truth about the relationship to save face. Sometimes the truth is abuse, coercion, or serious deception. How much you say, to whom, and how publicly depends on what happened and why you're telling people.

A breakup can expose things you genuinely couldn't see while you were bonded. Look at what you contributed, but also try to understand whatever was true in your ex's perspective, including the conflicts they were carrying inside themselves, rather than one-dimensionalizing them.

Sometimes the easiest story is that they were fake all along. Don’t grab that story just because it makes everything easier to explain, and don’t reject it if it really is the most parsimonious explanation. Ask people who aren’t heavily invested in seeing your innocence. A therapist, pastor, or even a stranger may see the evidence more clearly than a lifelong friend. Even the curiosity itself can be therapeutic for you.

Spiritual practice during an ending is critical, but don't use it to get around the feelings. Pray for your ex's wellbeing. Remember what was real and good, and don't use your pain as permission to hate them. Avoid the New Age belief that everyone is simply a mirror of you. No, that isn’t true. We partly mirror one another, but each person was formed by plenty that had nothing to do with you. No matter how enlightened the Buddha was, Devadatta still kept trying to kill him. Looking honestly at your part doesn't erase theirs. Sometimes it helps to ask, "What would Mr. Rogers do?" (if you're old enough to remember that show).

I also learned that public demonization doesn’t always have to be the last chapter. If you avoid contact forever, they might never apologize and learn. Doormat mode would be letting them back into your life without making them lose face themselves through a public apology. Allowing an apology is not the same decision as resuming the relationship.
Going back to someone who's already gone through that cycle can be foolish. But realizing they need to apologize publicly for demonizing their ex can really help some people develop honesty.

At this point, I can say I'm better off because of what happened with B., K., and H., without pretending every part of those relationships was beneficial or destined. Loss taught me things love alone never would. And as Rumi said, "You must keep breaking your heart until it stays open."

From B., I learned what it means for me to be really in love. I learned the kind of woman I actually want: deeply spiritual, sensitive, creative, unique, somebody who inspires me and makes me question everything.

K. repeated a lot of that, which is why I fell in love with her. I learned some of the same harsh lessons from both of them: don’t take openness and curiosity to be fully good. They can also indicate that someone hasn’t developed their own sense of self or opinions, or enough inner adult.
From H., I learned that I can be extremely close to someone and feel completely understood and supported without actually falling in love. I still treasure the support we gave each other.

Too many people judge a relationship only by the result, so start measuring what you actually learned from it instead. Relationships are a process of growth in many dimensions. The result is not only whether you stayed together.

Romantic love is not easy, and the things that actually make it work are not very marketable. I can't sell you the fix with one click or one monthly subscription to my love class. (Just kidding, click here!)

Both people have to be committed to honesty, reparenting, peer counseling, community, conscious agreements, and spiritual practice. It's rare, and that's probably why romantic love has been seen with suspicion as a destabilizing force throughout history.

One of the best books that makes that point today might be the one I was reading with K: The Spirit of Intimacy, by Sobonfu Somé. Somé came from the Dagara tribe in Burkina Faso. To her people, marriage is an arranged, ritualized spiritual and communal responsibility. They're suspicious of romance. But one of her ideas fits what I’m trying to say: the relationship is bigger and more important than the egos in it. She calls it the spirit of the relationship.

That spirit is like the universe living its desire to know itself through us, which might be why we see ourselves in ways we can't imagine prior. Nobody can command the spirit to remain. At our best, we serve it. We tell the truth, keep reparenting ourselves, ask the community for help, and listen for what Spirit wants to change. When we start thinking we own it or deserve it, that presumptuousness tends to push it away.

My parents agreed with Somé that community matters and that we serve Spirit. They were also not romantic, though they were loving and poly. I actually wished they were in love with each other, I guess, although I couldn't have articulated that since I didn't even have that concept at the time. Also reminiscent of Somé, they also wore rose-colored glasses and taught me that everybody was basically good. So I learned something about love and community, but not how hard romance is without a community around it, or how much damage basically good people can do when their fears, trauma, and undeveloped parts take over.

It took me many decades to figure out what probably everyone else already knows: real private pathology exists. But pathology festers when the environment is perfect for it. The dominant culture hermetically seals two people together and calls that a luxurious privacy. It tells them that sealed room should provide all the fresh air you'd get from a lover, family, community, therapist, and so on. Then it treats the predictable failure as privately caused as well, like mold that grows out of nowhere.

The myths around romantic love become real because we co-create them. We act as though jealousy proves love, permanent feelings can be promised, conflict should stay hidden, and the relationship failed if it ended. Then we suffer inside ideas that were never natural laws, and we walk blindly into our first, second, third, fourth, and fifth marriages!

Speaking of which, I wish I’d prioritized understanding the basic fears, desires, traumas, values, strengths, and weaknesses of the women I got close to in a more conscious manner. Instead, I often went with the flow of conversation and hanging out until closeness had built itself before we had decided what it meant.

On the other hand, with H., maybe we had the opposite problem. We reached real depth quickly. That depth kept pulling us toward romantic partnership even though, instinctually, we felt more like family. Depth is powerful, but you still have to ask what kind of relationship you’re actually building.
It might be that I wrote this whole article for my son, Bear, who sadly, I last saw when he was about five, right before he was supposed to get the Rosenblum sex talk.

Bear, sex can be what you do when you’re older and find a friend you love in a super special way that makes you want to raise children together. Don’t imagine you love each other just because you want each other. Don't feel pressure to promise commitment; it comes by itself naturally & honestly as your hearts sync. Learn about each other before getting too close, and make sure to keep friends and community around who know both of you.

Trauma doesn’t only live in the story you tell about what happened. Your body learned things too. It learned to brace, collapse, freeze, disconnect, scan for danger, or flood, and it can keep doing those things long after the original danger is over.

For many people, especially people with complex or developmental trauma, lasting recovery follows a broad sequence: establish enough safety and nervous-system regulation, release some of the accumulated stress and survival responses, and then go deeper into trauma processing.

So before I go digging for the deepest memory, I want to know something much more basic: can I stay here while I’m doing it, can I stop, and can I come back to ordinary life afterward? If getting close to the trauma makes you disappear, stay highly activated, or lose the ability to function, going deeper is not automatically progress.

This is why I find it useful to put Somatic Experiencing, trauma-sensitive yoga, EFT, shaking practices, Brainspotting, EMDR, and cognitive integration on one loose map. They are not all doing the same thing, and they are not all even the same kind of thing. Some are therapies, some are adjuncts, and some are experiential practices that may be very useful for particular people without having anything like the same scientific support.

They can also overlap with deeper inner-child therapy. Sometimes the body needs to become a little easier to inhabit before you can approach the younger parts of yourself without simply getting swallowed by them.

section: Don’t be so serious, you silly willy!
text: Remember, therapy is not just work. It’s also play! We often make the most incredible discoveries when we approach things with playful curiosity. For example, here’s a bridge between somatic therapy and inner-child therapy which I recently learned from Professor Baby Sheep:

section: Don’t be so serious, you silly willy!
text: And in my personal experience, what actually works better for me than all of these therapies is shaving my head and massaging it, especially while on loveyhuasca!

section: This Is a Map, but You Are the Explorer
text: The five-job map I’m using here is meant to solve a practical problem: people can easily end up doing yoga, tapping, shaking, Brainspotting, breathwork, EMDR, maybe hypnosis too, without being clear about what they are trying to accomplish with any of it. The more useful question is: what job does my nervous system need help with right now?

section: This Is a Map, but You Are the Explorer
text: The rough order below makes the most sense to me when somebody is repeatedly overwhelmed, severely dissociative, actively unsafe, unable to settle after activation, or simply does not have enough support to tolerate deeper trauma work. But this is my synthesis from first-principles reasoning and community signal. It is not a scientifically validated five-stage protocol, and there is no evidence that everyone has to finish Somatic Experiencing, yoga, EFT, and shaking before they are “allowed” to begin EMDR.

section: This Is a Map, but You Are the Explorer
text: Even if somebody eventually ran a beautiful trial and found an average best sequence, you would still have to look at your own response. Can you stay present enough to do the practice? Can you stop? Can you get back to ordinary life afterward? Is it actually reducing symptoms and giving you more freedom, or are you becoming more activated and more obsessed with processing?

section: This Is a Map, but You Are the Explorer
text: Capacity matters, but I do not want “capacity building” to become an endless waiting room where the trauma itself never gets treated. I care more about what happens to your sleep (see my sleep guide), relationships, functioning, freedom, and symptoms than how dramatic the session felt.

section: This Is a Map, but You Are the Explorer
text: And none of these modalities permanently belongs to one box. Gentle shaking may be Job 1 for one person and Job 2 for another. Present-focused self-hypnosis is very different from immersive memory work. Resource-oriented Brainspotting is different from going straight into highly charged developmental material. You can also have several jobs at once: daily discharge, one discrete traumatic memory that keeps firing, and basic inner-child reparenting can all be real needs in the same week.

section: This Is a Map, but You Are the Explorer
text: I’m also moving between different kinds of evidence here: published research, common clinical practice, my own experience, community reports, and traditional or energetic explanations. I’ll try to keep those categories visible instead of letting them blur together. A practice can be useful without every story about why it works being true.

Job 1: Stay Present and Keep Choice. Build enough safety, orientation, stopping ability, and return capacity for whatever comes next.
Job 2: Regulate or Discharge Accumulated Activation. Keep pressure from building between deeper sessions.
Job 3: Work With Diffuse, Bodily, or Hard-to-Narrate Material. Approach sensations, impulses, emotions, images, or fragments that do not yet make a clean story.
Job 4: Work With a Discrete Memory or Trigger Network. Go after specific traumatic events, flashbacks, and stubborn residual triggers.
Job 5: Integrate, Differentiate, and Build a Life. Update beliefs, identity, relationships, values, and direction once survival mode is taking up less of the room.

section: Somatic Work and Inner-Child Reparenting Can Overlap
text: If somebody is flooded, almost completely identified with the child-state, or cannot access a Nurturer or Protector at all, I would start much smaller: look around the room, get outside help, borrow an adult perspective, find a neutral witness, or take one ordinary Protector action. Gentle self-hypnosis can fit here too when it stays in the present instead of pulling you deep into memories or child dialogue.

section: Somatic Work and Inner-Child Reparenting Can Overlap
text: In my experience, EFT, Somatic Experiencing, trauma-sensitive yoga, gentle shaking or qigong, non-forced longer exhales, and gentle Buteyko-style breathing can all help the body loosen a little. I especially notice this around the solar plexus or abdomen. When that area softens, heart-chakra love can become easier for me to access, which can make the inner-child work much easier.

section: Somatic Work and Inner-Child Reparenting Can Overlap
text: You do not have to use that opening to go straight into pain. Bring to mind a pet, a baby, a friend, a partner, or anybody you naturally love. Feel the love that is already there and see whether a little of it can move from the heart toward the younger part around the solar plexus, then back up again in a loop.

section: Somatic Work and Inner-Child Reparenting Can Overlap
text: Brainspotting can also sit on either side of this boundary. A resource-oriented or carefully titrated session can prepare you for deeper work; going into highly charged developmental material is a different dose. With diffuse relational trauma, I sometimes think EMDR fits better after at least a little inner-child reparenting, because access to a Nurturer and Protector gives you something to hold the material with. A stable person working on one discrete event may not need a long preliminary sequence at all.

section: Somatic Work and Inner-Child Reparenting Can Overlap
text: I would save deep hypnosis, immersive child dialogue, suggestive exploration, and other deep memory work for the point where you can stay present, stop voluntarily, and return to ordinary life afterward. The useful question is always what the practice is doing right now: orientation, regulation, discharge, resourcing, processing, or integration.

Somatic Experiencing makes sense to me as an early option when the main problem is that activation runs away with you. Instead of forcing a detailed trauma narrative, it pays attention to sensation, orientation, impulse, defensive response, and pacing. The basic skill is noticing activation without immediately drowning in it.

This is where the usual language about expanding your “window of tolerance” becomes practical. Titration, pendulation, and orientation are all ways of asking: can you touch something difficult in a small enough dose, notice what happens, and come back? Some people may spend three to six months mainly building those capacities, and severe developmental trauma can take longer. I would treat that as orientation, not a countdown. If you are stable and have one clear target, you may be ready for focused trauma work much sooner.

Yoga can fit early too, but I mean a very particular kind of yoga. No power yoga. No hot yoga. Nobody announcing, “Open your hips and release your trauma.” The useful version is slow, choice-based, and non-invasive, with body awareness, flexibility, enjoyment, and agency as the point.

Good options include trauma-sensitive yoga, restorative yoga, gentle somatic yoga, and very gentle yin when it is propped, short, and easy to leave. The language matters too. “You might try…” is very different from “stay there.” “You can keep your eyes open.” “You can come out whenever you want.” “Notice whether this feels useful, neutral, or too much.” A posture can have several valid versions; choose one that actually fits your body.

I would avoid intense stretching, long passive holds, forced breathwork, breath retention, hands-on adjustments without clear consent, aggressive hip openers, or anybody telling you to push through sensation. If the point is to rebuild choice, the practice should contain actual choices.

Shaking can also live in Job 1, but here I mean a small dose. Basic Trauma Release Exercises, light neurogenic tremoring, standing and gently shaking, even a short playful movement that you can stop immediately. You should finish more settled, not blasted open.

If the shaking becomes compulsive, frightening, dissociative, or hard to stop, back off. And if tremoring reaches your neck while you are lying down, do not let your head whip around unsupported. Stop or reduce the movement, support your head—or have an experienced provider help you support it—and get guidance before continuing; forceful, rapid back-and-forth neck movement can injure the neck.

section: Job 2: Keep the Pressure Low Between Deeper Sessions
text: A good therapy session can only do so much if activation keeps building again during the rest of the week. Job 2 is the ordinary-life part: what can I do between deeper sessions so the pressure does not keep accumulating faster than I can process it?

EFT fits well here because it is quick, private, repeatable, and concrete enough to use while real life is happening. Conflict. A shame spiral. Social fear. Abandonment panic. Freeze. Anger. An intrusive fragment of memory that suddenly has your whole body involved.

It can fit before a difficult conversation, after getting triggered, before or after a therapy session, or when the mind is looping and the body is obviously in the loop too. It can also bridge body-based and cognitive work. I would not make it the only treatment for severe trauma, and I would not use it to avoid deeper work that obviously still needs doing.

Shaking Qigong is basically shaking plus qigong. I’m linking to a $10-per-month Skool class my friend Louka took because he had already tried many different healing and somatic modalities, including basic TRE, without getting much help. This was the one that finally helped him.

Here the job is daily autonomic discharge and energetic decompression. For Job 1, shaking stays mild and exploratory. Here it can become a regular discharge practice—as long as you can still stop, orient, and settle afterward. A regular practice might run 10–45 minutes. I think of the use cases as chronic freeze, non-verbal emotional processing, stress that accumulates between therapy sessions, and leftover activation after a deeper session.

You do not have to accept the qigong explanation to see ordinary reasons shaking might help: rhythmic movement, less muscular armoring, more awareness of bodily sensation, a possible shift out of fight-or-flight, release of chronic tension, and perhaps completion of defensive impulses that got interrupted.

Qigong has a different explanatory language. Qi means vital energy, and from that perspective the same practice may be described as removing stagnation, increasing qi circulation, dissolving stored emotional charge, and reconnecting breath, body, and movement. These are different explanations for the same practice; one does not prove the other.

What I would not do is turn shaking into a catharsis contest, treat it as the primary trauma-processing modality for everybody, or use it as a substitute for skilled help when somebody is highly dissociative or unstable.

Shaking Qigong / TRE to discharge excess activation.
Restorative or gentle yin yoga to let the body soften, settle, and rebalance energy flow.
EFT tapping if there is still emotional activation or mental looping.

The reason for the stack is practical. I do not want to shake a lot of material loose and then walk away raw. Yin can help here, but I keep the same caveat from Job 1: prop it, keep the holds shorter when necessary, and leave the pose if it starts feeling coercive. A shorter hold your body can actually tolerate may be more useful than an ambitious five-minute shape.

section: Job 3: When the Trauma Is More Body Than Story
text: Some trauma gives you a scene you can point to. Some of it gives you a body reaction, an impulse, an emotion, an image, a fragment, or just the sense that something enormous is happening before there is a coherent story attached to it. This is often called “subcortical” processing. I use the word as shorthand for material that shows up through sensation, impulse, emotion, image, or fragments before it becomes a clear verbal story—not as a claim that one precise brain region contains it.

Brainspotting is one option I would look at for this kind of material. The method uses gaze position, focused attention, bodily awareness, and therapist attunement to stay with emotionally charged material that may be difficult to narrate.

Before going deep with it, I would want enough nervous-system safety to remain present, at least one way to regulate ordinary triggers, some way to settle or discharge afterward, and enough comfort with bodily sensation to notice when the dose is getting too high. Those are capacities, not prerequisite therapies. How you built them is secondary.

Brainspotting interests me especially for diffuse developmental trauma, pre-verbal or body-held material, trauma that has not responded well to purely cognitive approaches, and those emotional knots where the body seems to know more than the story. You do not necessarily need to explain every detail for the session to move.

I would resist the urge to turn the rest of the day into another processing marathon. If spontaneous shaking comes, let it happen gently. If the body still wants discharge, use gentle Shaking Qigong. If you feel floaty or far away, walking meditation may be better. Restorative, gentle yin, or somatic yoga can help if what you want is rest, stretching, toning, or reconnection. EFT can help if emotional activation is still high.

section: Job 4: When There Is a Memory You Can Actually Point To
text: This is the part of the map I think of as targeted memory work or reconsolidation. The problem is less “my whole body seems to carry something I cannot quite name” and more “this event, this flashback, this trigger network is still alive.”
EMDR is often a very good fit here: specific traumatic events, accidents, assault memories, military trauma, distinct flashbacks, and residual triggers that remain after other somatic work.

I still care about regulation and what happens after the session. EMDR can be highly effective, but if somebody has diffuse developmental trauma and an unstable nervous system, I do not automatically assume it should be the first thing they try. If you cannot identify any clear targets and most of the material is bodily, pre-verbal, or relational, Brainspotting may fit better. A stable person with one discrete event is a different case and may be ready for EMDR much earlier.
Sleep, substance use, medication effects, pain, nutrition, and general physiological stability can all change how much therapy you can tolerate. I have a separate sleep guide here.

This is also one place where neurological de-armoring support may matter. EMDR directly engages memory reprocessing, so anything that changes fear learning, inflammation, dissociation, glutamate/GABA balance, or autonomic tone may change what reconsolidation feels like. I go into that separately in my de-armoring supplement guide.

Afterward I would keep things almost boring: walk, eat, hydrate, sleep early if you are tired, do restorative yoga, journal only if it grounds you, maybe use a little EFT if activation is still there.

I would not casually stack Brainspotting, EMDR, intense shaking, and deep yin on the same day unless you already know your system handles that much and you have skilled support. More processing can simply be more processing. Sometimes the missing piece is integration.
Eventually there is a point where cognitive work becomes much more useful. Trying to reframe a danger while the body still experiences the threat as present often does not get very far.

Once the body is less trapped there, light CBT and narrative work can help you revisit old beliefs, build a coherent life story, separate past danger from present reality, clarify values and boundaries, reclaim agency, and deepen inner-child reparenting. This is also where identity, differentiation, forgiveness when it is actually relevant, and life direction may become easier to work with.

section: How I Judge Whether Any of This Is Helping
text: But even that line is only a map. Yoga can show up early for body awareness and agency, after shaking because you need to settle, or after deeper processing because stretching and reconnection feel good. You do not need every modality.

section: How I Judge Whether Any of This Is Helping
text: Check the dose more than once. How do you feel immediately afterward? What happened to your sleep that night? What about the next morning, and the next two or three days? A calm ending to a session does not prove the dose was right. I would watch irritability, dissociation, pain, compulsive processing, relationships, and ordinary functioning before deciding to repeat or intensify something.

section: How I Judge Whether Any of This Is Helping
text: Keep the explanation as modest as the evidence. Published research, common clinical use, my own experience, community reports, and qigong or energetic explanations can all point toward the same practice without proving one another. Some shaking, qigong, breathwork, and somatic communities make huge claims about releasing decades of trauma, awakening kundalini, clearing stored emotion, or rapidly healing the entire nervous system. Treat those claims as hypotheses and community signal, not guarantees. Judge the practice by what changes in actual life.

section: How I Judge Whether Any of This Is Helping
text: A thin research literature does not prove a method useless, and a large research literature does not tell you which therapy your own nervous system needs first. I would start from first principles, pay attention to people with patterns similar to mine, change one thing at a time when possible, and keep asking the unglamorous question: am I actually doing better? Go slowly enough to see what the practice actually did, and do not confuse intensity with healing.

section: Optional High-Intensity Practices: Sky Hypnosis and Vagal Blitz
text: Sky Hypnosis and Vagal Blitz do not have to wait until the end of the map. Stable people may find them useful before doing any of the other therapies. I treat them as optional high-intensity state-shift and release practices, not ordinary regulation exercises and definitely not prerequisites for healing.

section: Optional High-Intensity Practices: Sky Hypnosis and Vagal Blitz
text: They also deserve their own physical-safety rules. Sky Hypnosis can make you lightheaded. Vagal Blitz is a lying-down-only practice with cardiovascular and mental-health cautions. Use the complete guide, start with the least intense version that gives you a useful shift, and stop when balance, orientation, or recovery becomes unreliable. Do not chase fainting or loss of consciousness.

section: Optional High-Intensity Practices: Sky Hypnosis and Vagal Blitz
text: There is also a psychological trap here: a practice can produce so much bliss, relief, or altered-state intensity that you feel healed while the same trauma is still running your relationships and behavior. So I look at what happens afterward. Am I more able to meet pain, set boundaries, deal with conflict, and participate in life? Or did the practice become a way to avoid grief, conflict, practical problems, or deeper relational healing?

section: Optional High-Intensity Practices: Sky Hypnosis and Vagal Blitz
text: And a huge release does not automatically mean you are ready for deep memory work. I would still check orientation, ability to stop, sleep, physical recovery, and whether I am actually more willing to approach the real issue. The benefits I describe in the linked guides include my experience and community signal. The proposed physiological mechanisms are a separate question.

Céline’s title gets the problem right: we don’t change. The child remains. What can change is who leads. A lot of people stay identified as the child, meeting adult life from the position that still feels small, abandoned, helpless, impulsive, frightened, or desperate to be chosen.

My answer has been to stop asking the child to heal itself. The present-day person becomes the Nurturer, Protector, and Leader or Guide who reparents the child. That assumes the present-day person is at least willing to protect vulnerability rather than exploit it; I return to that safety gate below.

But that creates a chicken-and-egg problem. What if you’re so identified as the child that you can’t summon those adult archetypes? The method works most easily for people who already have some access to them. Somebody with very little access may sit there trying to sound loving while the inherited critic, numbness, panic, or urge to escape runs the entire session.

I think the missing first phase is borrowed adulthood. Before you can reliably become the inner parent, you may need to experience, imagine, imitate, and practice one adult function with help. You receive care, observe how it is given, participate in it, initiate a small part yourself, and gradually internalize it.

I developed this practical map from the rest of the method. Treat the complete sequence as a provisional synthesis: some components have direct research behind them, while the full arrangement is my own:

The child alone: orient to the present and establish enough outside safety to begin.
The child with a borrowed adult: experience one reliable adult function through a real, remembered, imagined, or symbolic figure.
The adult apprentice: care for the child together with support and do at least one part yourself.
The inner adult: repeat warmth, protection, and direction until those capacities become familiar enough to summon.
The adult and child in relationship: the adult leads without exiling the child, and the child no longer has to run the whole life alone.
You don’t have to stop being the child. You become larger than the child-state. A useful sentence is: “I am still this child, and I am also becoming the adult who stays.”

I used to preach Buddhist enlightenment a lot. Eventually I realized that most people chase spiritual freedom as a way to get above childhood trauma or character defects they don’t want to meet. That’s called spiritual bypassing. It produces a split personality: the spiritual identity loses awareness of the trauma while the buried material festers and runs the person from underneath. Plenty of seekers and gurus show the split too; I’ve written about the Dalai Lama as one example.

The analogy I like to use for understanding this concept is: imagine you’re broke and starving. Your baby also has nothing to eat. Understandable. Now imagine that they opened a nice food bank in your neighborhood and suddenly you’ve got lots of nutritious munchies available. But you’re just devouring them all yourself while baby you is still starving. Unforgivable.

That sounds ridiculous, and nobody would really do that. But because we don’t believe there is a baby us, we do do that. That damages the baby way more than if both of you are starving. Once you realize baby you is in there, you’ll naturally offer him/her the love and freedom you’ve hopefully found on your spiritual path.

People are spiritually bypassing not because they’re stupid or crazy, but because that’s what they figured out so far. I was doing that as well until a few years ago, because I didn’t know about the inner child. It sounded pretty silly to me at first, but through direct experience I discovered he’s really in there! And when you can really reconnect and reparent your inner child, it’s much more of a true embodied healing than an escape hatch.

On the other hand, therapy risks becoming endless processing if the whole horizon is still “how do I manage this wound better?” For me, spirituality opened a much larger horizon of what happiness and love could even mean, beyond conditions & life story.

I don’t think everybody needs the same depth of spiritual experience. Some people already have enough love, meaning, beauty, and belonging for the life they want and aren’t especially curious for more. But for somebody who feels that ordinary life and conditional love are radically insufficient, the question of whether something much deeper is possible can become central.

section: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
text: In my experience, most people do not start by becoming their own loving parent. They go looking for one. Sometimes it is a spiritual guru; sometimes a therapist, coach, partner, community, or ideology. That can be a healthy first stage. I call it borrowed adulthood. The helper lends a function you cannot yet hold alone. The trouble begins when the helper keeps it.

section: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
text: A spiritual practice can change your relationship to pain. It cannot make an abusive person safe, repair a house, treat an infection, pay a debt, or leave a coercive relationship. Sometimes the adult move is to sit and feel. Sometimes it is to lock the door, call somebody, go to a doctor, get legal advice, or leave. A teaching that turns actual danger into merely ‘your story’ has stopped protecting the child.

section: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
text: No-self teachings can also arrive out of order. If you were never allowed to discover what you like, believe, want, or refuse, you may need to build a self before you start dissolving it. Enough selfhood to stand; then enough flexibility not to become imprisoned by it. Using emptiness to erase an undeveloped self is spiritual bypass wearing very advanced clothes.

section: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
text: The same problem appears with therapist-gurus. A helper may see a blind spot, challenge you, or model a missing adult function. They do not get final authority over your memories, relationships, body, medicine, conscience, or future. Even Pema Chödrön, writing from a tradition that emphasizes devotion, says the teacher should “wean us from dependency altogether” and help us grow up. That is the test I keep. Are you becoming more able to think, disagree, protect yourself, and act without the helper?

section: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
text: Disagreement with a helper is not automatically a defense against healing. Their interpretation may be wrong, their method may not fit, or you may not share their goal. They should be able to examine that without making your objection prove their theory.

section: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
text: My own version was strange. I was well-loved as a child, but from age twelve to twenty-six I was depressed and cried every night from feeling the pain of the world. Loving-kindness (metta) meditation healed that depression almost instantly. There was already a great deal of love underneath it—from my parents, Buddhist teachings (which it turns out also include inner-child self-love!), and loveyhuasca. The meditation gave that love somewhere to land.

section: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
text: It still didn’t reach all of my inner-child material, especially my attachment to women. The self-directed inner-child therapy I tried later felt imaginary at first. San Pedro cactus, CBD tea, and sublingual mapacho cracked it open; structured sessions with an inner-child therapist deepened it.

section: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away
text: The method now has four elements: a wounded child, three adult functions, protective parts that may stand at the door, and a bootstrap phase for people who can’t yet occupy the adult role.

section: Before You Try to Go Deep
text: Reparenting needs enough adult capacity to pause, compare options, remain in the present, and act. It also needs enough protective intent that bringing the child forward will not put vulnerability in the hands of somebody who wants to exploit it. When somebody is flooded or identified almost completely with a frightened child-state, those capacities can be hard to reach. The immediate task may be outside support and regulation. Deeper dialogue can wait.

section: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
text: Most of this guide assumes that the present-day person at least wants to protect the vulnerable part. That cannot always be assumed. Somebody may enjoy frightening or humiliating people, want to exploit vulnerability, or hope therapy will make them more effective at manipulation. In that case, do not invite the child forward—not even briefly to find out how the child reacts. The child’s fear is not a diagnostic test, and the exercise must not become another source of gratification.

section: When the Present-Day Adult Is Dangerous to the Child
text: Stay with the present-day adult. What help do you actually want? Why are you here? What, if anything, are you suffering from or hoping to change?
