section: Appendix A: How to ask the subconscious a useful question
text: The subconscious isn’t an AI model, but prompt engineering offers one useful lesson: the shape of a question changes what kind of answer can appear. A prompt should make you more present, honest, loving, and able to hear the next signal—never more controlling.

section: Appendix A: How to ask the subconscious a useful question
text:
Role: who or what you are addressing.
Context: what situation you are bringing.
Intention: what kind of change is desired.
Constraint: safety, truth, kindness, no forcing, no false certainty, and capacity before content.
Output: image, phrase, body signal, memory, next action, question, symbol, silence, or rest.
Evaluation: true, kind, timely, stabilizing, specific, testable.
Iteration: revise after life gives feedback.

section: Appendix A: How to ask the subconscious a useful question
text: “And if the system needs more time to process this, or if silence is the safest answer today, let my body settle into deeper comfortable rest instead. A peaceful silence is a fully successful answer.”

section: Appendix A: How to ask the subconscious a useful question
text: Sometimes nothing answers because nothing is happening. Sometimes the answer is not yet, rest first, build capacity, or do the ordinary thing you already know to do.

“Wise subconscious, please show me what is true, kind, and timely. If the full truth of this situation is too intense for my body to integrate today, pass it to my conscious mind only as a gentle symbol, a body signal, or a single next step. Show me my capacity to hold peace before you show me the content of the wound.”

“Wise subconscious, please help me look at this impulse clearly. If part of this signal belongs to family programming, religious fear, marketing, erotic imprinting, political tribe, trauma response, or a childhood bargain for belonging, let that part become visible as conditioning. Let it soften or step back only as much as is safe. Leave behind whatever belongs to true guidance, the universal heart, and a better ordinary life. Let my body feel the difference.”
“If this daydream is useful, reveal the guidance inside it. If it is avoidance, bring me gently into the present and help me deal with what I need to deal with.”
The prompt defines the search. NLP language affects how gently the question enters. Used together, they can create a safer field for an answer without pretending the answer is automatically true.

section: Appendix B: NLP without turning yourself into a sales seminar
text: You can practice the core method without learning one term of Neuro-Linguistic Programming. Read this appendix when you want more precision about imagery, bodily states, rehearsal, and sentence design. NLP is useful when it helps the system listen; it becomes a bag of tricks when technique replaces love, truth, contact, or consent.

Language NLP shapes the sentence: pace what is already true, open awareness, presume only safe capacity, link cause and effect carefully, embed invitations, and use de-hypnotic questions when language becomes vague, absolute, manipulative, or grandiose.

section: The Milton Model, minus the covert sales seminar
text: The Milton Model concerns the architecture of the sentence. Commands such as “Relax now,” “Stop being anxious,” or “Trust me” often make a part brace.

section: The Milton Model, minus the covert sales seminar
text: Part of the point of indirect language is to get past that reflexive skeptical argument without having to overpower it. The destination can still be deliberate even when the route is subtle.

section: The Milton Model, minus the covert sales seminar
text: “As the body notices the bed beneath it, it may become a little easier to stop holding the whole day alone.”Pace reality. Open awareness. Validate function. Presuppose capacity. Bridge gently. Invite one small movement. Test with the body.

section: Pattern 1: Pacing and leading — truth before suggestion
text: “Anxiety is here. The body is activated. A protector is trying to help. And one breath at a time, the adult can start to listen.”

section: Pattern 1: Pacing and leading — truth before suggestion
text: “It is completely true that [current sensation or emotion] is here. It makes sense that my system is reacting by [current protective behavior or thought]. And right alongside that truth, my adult self is here, breathing in this room, ready to listen to whatever comes up next.”
A presupposition hides an assumption inside a sentence. Use that power only to presume choice, timing, capacity, safety, love, and adult leadership. Don’t smuggle in obedience.
Words such as as, while, because, when, after, before, and which means connect one event to another. Use them carefully. A gentle voice doesn’t make a false causal claim true.
Too strong: “Because I breathe, the trauma leaves.”Better: “As I breathe, the adult self may become present enough to hear one small piece of what the wound needs.”

“And somewhere inside this breath, I can let the adult self listen.”“As I sit here, I may allow one small truth to become clear.”“The child does not have to trust me all at once; it can simply notice I am still here.”

Nominalizations turn processes into nouns: healing, safety, trust, integration, communion, clarity, rest. Their vagueness can sometimes help because the subconscious supplies its own concrete meaning.

section: Pattern 10: Meta Model questions — the de-hypnosis tool
text: “How specifically?”“According to whom?”“Compared to what?”“Always?”“Never?”“What exactly would happen?”“How do I know?”“What evidence would change my mind?”Use Milton Model to soften into the body. Use Meta Model to return to truth.

section: Submodalities — editing the form, not denying the truth
text: Fear, craving, fantasy, belief, and memory usually arrive with sensory qualities: near or far, bright or dim, loud or quiet, moving or still, heavy or light, inside or outside the body.

section: Submodalities — editing the form, not denying the truth
text: Ask how the experience is represented. What changes when the image moves two feet back, the voice gets quieter, or the edge becomes less sharp?

section: Submodalities — editing the form, not denying the truth
text: “Would it be okay if we moved this image back just a little, or lowered the volume slightly, purely so my adult self can stay present enough to hear what you need to tell me?”

section: Anchoring — giving the body a doorway back
text: An anchor is a cue connected to a state: a hand on the heart, two fingers touching, a breath, a word, a posture, scent, or song. Find a real state you want easier access to, feel it, and pair the cue while it is clearly present with the phrase, “This is available.” For hypnotic re-entry, choose a usable receptive state rather than peak emotional intensity; follow “A shortcut back into hypnosis” in the main induction section. Keep alert calming and the synchronicity wake-up cue separate.

section: Using synchronicity as your own wake-up bell
text: People notice a synchronicity and immediately ask what it means. Sometimes that opens insight; sometimes it starts compulsive pattern-hunting. I prefer using the moment of noticing as a wake-up bell. The coincidence doesn’t have to contain a message. It has already captured attention, which is enough.

section: Using synchronicity as your own wake-up bell
text: “Whenever I notice something that feels like a synchronicity, I wake up inside the state I am in. I feel my body and the room. I remember that the coincidence is not proof of an interpretation. I let attention widen beyond the story my current mood is telling. I ask what is fact, what is interpretation, what needs warmth, what needs protection, and what needs action. I return to the highest perspective I can access without leaving the body, the facts, or ordinary human reality.”I make room for whatever is genuinely available: objectivity, clarity, ease, peace, freedom, joy, and gratitude. I do not have to manufacture any of them.Synchronicity noticed → pause → orient → widen → reality-test → listen → choose one loving action.

section: Using synchronicity as your own wake-up bell
text: The cue interrupts identification without erasing the state’s message. A negative state may still contain an inner-child need, a Protector warning, grief, a bodily problem, or a real demand for action.

Imagine noticing an ordinary, harmless synchronicity.
Feel the moment when attention says, “Whoa.”
Use that opening to feel the feet, body, breath, and room.
Repeat: “The noticing is my wake-up bell, not proof of a message.”
Ask the Nurturer, Protector, and Leader what each sees.
Rehearse returning to a grounded, wider perspective.
End with one small action and the complete waking exit.
The cue remains self-authored, visible, reversible, and limited to orientation. It can’t authorize a decision, prove an intuition, suppress a warning, or let another person control the response.

Psychologically, this resembles an implementation intention: an advance “if X, then Y” plan that links a recognizable cue with a chosen response. Gollwitzer’s foundational paper supports the general mechanism. This particular use of synchronicity hasn’t been studied directly.

The same mechanism creates the risk: rehearsing synchronicity as a cue may make you scan for it. Pattern perception can drift toward false-positive meaning, especially during absorption or destabilization. Research links stronger apophenic pattern detection with false-positive judgments and psychosis-spectrum traits, although ordinary pattern noticing is not itself pathological. See Blain and colleagues and Grant and colleagues.

To retire it, stop rehearsing it and say while fully awake: “Synchronicity is no longer a cue. I release this association and return coincidence to ordinary uncertainty.” Remove it from the written cue list and stop rehearsing it. The statement expresses your decision; it does not prove the association has vanished immediately.

section: Reframing — changing the meaning without lying
text: “What else might be true?”“What is this part trying to do for me?”“What would the Nurturer, the Protector, and the Leader each say about this?”

section: Perceptual positions — self, other, witness, universal heart
text: First: what do I feel from inside myself?Second: if I sit inside the other person, what might they be feeling or protecting?Third: if I watched this from across the room, what would I notice?Fourth: from the universal heart, what serves truth, love, boundaries, and the good of everyone involved?

Classic NLP uses the Swish to replace an old self-image with a new one. Done mechanically, it can feel like an inner eviction. Here, the old pattern stays visible, the new possibility stands beside it, and the body compares which future protects the child more honestly.

section: Parts integration, without pretending the conflict is solved
text: “What does one side want?”“What does the other side fear?”“What need sits under both?”“What third option honors both without letting either run the whole life?”

section: What I will not use NLP for
text:
To talk myself out of a real signal.
To override fear before asking what the fear protects.
To recover memories.
To manipulate anyone else.
To convince myself an intuition is true.
To erase pain, hunger, grief, anger, or a medical symptom.
While panicking, destabilized, manic, psychosis-like, chemically overwhelmed, or too dissociated to reality-test.
To make another person’s no feel like resistance.
To make someone feel spiritually inferior for disagreeing.
To hide a command inside soft language.
To create urgency where time is needed.
To bypass consent by calling something “subconscious agreement.”
To use trance, fatigue, attraction, shame, grief, or altered states to get compliance.

Induce or contain. Gather attention, or stabilize first if you are already wide open.
Ask permission. Is it useful to work with this image, feeling, or pattern today?
Represent the pattern. How does this show up — image, voice, sensation, posture, distance, size, color, movement?
Ask what it protects. What is this trying to do for me?
Adjust the form, gently. Move it back, lower the volume, add space, change posture, slow the scene.
Bring in the three adults. Nurturer warms, Protector makes it safe, Leader points a direction.
Anchor the useful state. Heart, fingers, breath, posture.
Future pace. If the old cue shows up, what is the smallest new action?
Test with the body. Does this feel true, kind, steadying, and doable?
Exit and act. Come back to the room. Do one ordinary thing.

section: Appendix C: The extended de-hypnosis checklist
text: “I notice influence is happening.I do not need to obey it or attack it.I can slow down.I can ask what is being presupposed.I can ask who benefits.I can ask what my body knows.I can ask what love, truth, humility, and ordinary life would require.If this is true, it will survive questions.If this is love, it will survive boundaries.If this is guidance, it will survive sleep.If this is for me, it will not require me to abandon my adult self.”

section: Appendix C: The extended de-hypnosis checklist
text:
Is there urgency?
Is there secrecy?
Is there shame?
Is there a threat of exclusion?
Is there a promise of specialness?
Is there sexual charge?
Is there spiritual superiority?
Is there a demand for money, sex, loyalty, silence, or obedience?
Is there a narrowing of choices?
Is questioning treated as betrayal?
Is resistance pathologized?
Is ordinary life being downgraded?
Is the child part being seduced, scared, or rescued?
Is the adult self still allowed to say no?

section: Appendix C: The extended de-hypnosis checklist
text: A good guide increases your adult self. A bad guide replaces it. A good guide can tolerate your no. A bad guide calls your no resistance, ego, fear, low vibration, trauma, sin, or proof that you need more of their guidance.

Was I plainly told that induction mechanics are being used?
Can at least one answer lead to pause, modification, full alertness, or stopping?
Does the speaker treat not noticing as secret proof that the process worked?
Are roles, ownership, obedience, age, identity, or belonging being used to lower adult judgment?
Are fractionation, cues, later behavior, or memory effects disclosed before they are used?
Are ordinary body sensations being turned into evidence for a hidden claim?
Does the exit restore ordinary identity, movement, orientation, and critical judgment—and plainly say that the session has ended?

Anxiety is often a Protector trying to prevent danger, shame, abandonment, failure, exposure, illness, rejection, loss of control, or a feeling it believes would be unbearable. Don’t begin by cross-examining it. Help the body first.
Don’t recite the words like an incantation you’re hoping the subconscious will grade. Say them the way you’d speak to a frightened child you actually love.
Use this gently. Buteyko-style reduced breathing can help some people who overbreathe or panic, but don’t force breath holds. Air hunger can briefly increase anxiety before it settles, so go slowly.
Breathe through the nose. Let the inhale be small. Let the exhale be quiet. Pause only if comfortable. Let the breath become less dramatic. Stop if dizzy, strained, panicky, or medically concerned.

EFT can be a simple bodily ritual: name the fear, tap gently, and stay in contact with what you feel. The evidence is still developing. A 2025 systematic review found seven randomized controlled trials involving EFT for anxiety disorders; EFT beat no intervention in several of them, although the evidence should still be treated cautiously beside first-line therapies.

Sometimes the mind is too activated to meditate usefully. Then help through the body: foot, scalp, temple, neck, or shoulder massage; warmth; pressure; a weighted blanket; darkness; familiar calming music; or a massage gun used carefully. Avoid the front of the neck, injuries, numb areas, bruises, inflamed tissue, recent surgery sites, varicose veins, and anything that produces pain, dizziness, tingling, or a symptom that feels wrong.

Other people settle with warmth, darkness, music, massage, weighted blankets, breathwork, familiar objects, or personal relaxation technology. Use the support that actually helps rather than assembling a tiny wellness trade show around the anxiety.

Personal relaxation-tech note: On my ZHoly3O page, I discuss ozonated charcoal “holy water” as one relaxation support, and I also mention Blushield. These remain optional supports. They don’t prove that any inner signal is true. Stabilize the body, listen gently, reality-test, and return to one grounded action.

First, body.Feet, chair, breath, room.Little one, I am here.Protector, thank you for warning me.You do not have to scream for me to listen.If there is real action needed, show me one step.If there is no action needed, help the body stand down gently.I will not abandon the signal.I will not worship the signal.I will listen, test, and act.

section: Appendix E: Is the daydream helping or replacing your life?
text: Daydreaming can be intuition, simulation, grief digestion, creative rehearsal, symbolic teaching, or the subconscious showing a possible future, fear, or desire. It can also become avoidance, fantasy addiction, dissociation, romantic obsession, or an escape hatch from adult life.

section: Appendix E: Is the daydream helping or replacing your life?
text: Does the daydream return me to life with more clarity, love, and action? Or does it pull me away from life into repetition, craving, and avoidance?

section: Appendix E: Is the daydream helping or replacing your life?
text: When it seems to be pulling you away, change the body before debating the story. Sit upright. Open the eyes a little. Feel the feet.

section: Appendix E: Is the daydream helping or replacing your life?
text: “Subconscious, thank you for showing me images. If this daydream is useful, please reveal the guidance inside it. If it is avoidance, please bring me gently into the present and help me deal with what I need to deal with in a gentle but structured way.”

section: Appendix E: Is the daydream helping or replacing your life?
text: The answer may be: send the message, stop sending the message, clean the room, eat, sleep, grieve, create, apologize, leave, tell the truth, make the plan, ask for help, return to the task, or stop chasing unavailable love.

section: Appendix F: Self-trust, outside guidance, and oracle-like states
text: Suggestibility varies wildly. Some people open more with an external hypnotist, some with themselves, some only in particular states, and some barely respond to commands while responding deeply to imagery, music, metaphor, or spiritual feeling. A professional can bring pacing, containment, and another set of eyes. Self-hypnosis gives you instant follow-up, real-time correction, and a private line to your own protectors.

section: Appendix F: Self-trust, outside guidance, and oracle-like states
text: Self-hypnosis may be best for daily intimacy with the subconscious.Skilled outside support may be best for trauma complexity, blind spots, dissociation, destabilization, and relational wounds that need another nervous system.

section: Finding a hypnotist who can work with you
text: Ask what they are trained to treat, how they use hypnosis, and how they respond when a suggestion doesn’t fit. For trauma work, ask about actual trauma and dissociation training, not only a hypnosis certificate. Credentials matter without guaranteeing competent care.

section: Finding a hypnotist who can work with you
text: Describe what has helped, what hasn’t, your preferred directness, acceptable touch and imagery, and how you’ll stop. Ask about unexpected reactions, uncertain memories, and the full return. Firm encouragement can fit; refusal still ends it.

section: Finding a hypnotist who can work with you
text: Evaluate what actually happened, not the method’s name. Was its purpose explained? Did you agree? How did the practitioner respond to you? Discomfort alone doesn’t settle the question; treating every objection as proof you need more of the same deserves scrutiny. Ask the app or another informed person for explanation, without expecting a practitioner to be certified from a brief account. Self-hypnosis, combined work, or another practitioner remain your choices.

section: When the subconscious speaks like an oracle
text: The subconscious can notice things the conscious mind misses: anticipations, pattern reads, and sometimes something uncanny. Respect the signal without turning a vivid image or directive into an order.

section: When the subconscious speaks like an oracle
text: When the message has large or irreversible consequences, slow the action to the scale of those consequences, ask the adult questions, and bring the message to a council.

section: The council — internal first, then outward
text: The first council is internal: child and adult, conscious and subconscious, intuition and analysis. Reach outside when the message is bigger than those parts can hold alone. The larger and less reversible the move, the more seriously you seek other minds.

section: The council — internal first, then outward
text: Ask people who love you, like-minded people, or somebody who has walked the path. Going alone can be legitimate, but I’d make it the last step after counsel was genuinely sought.

section: The council — internal first, then outward
text: The opposite danger is giving away your power. “Seek counsel” can quietly become “find an authority and obey.” Another person deserves neither automatic trust nor automatic dismissal.

section: The council — internal first, then outward
text: Peer support can lend a different kind of help. In Hearthwork, equal time, warmth, confidentiality, and respect for “no” let each person lend Nurturer and Protector without taking over the other’s Guide. Then you switch roles. A carefully timed question can help your own direction become audible; the peer doesn’t decide what the experience means.

Forgiveness can’t be forced. It grows from understanding, and pushing it too early creates bypass. Staying angry forever can also let the injury keep governing the present. All of these can remain true together: the harm happened, the boundary still matters, the person remains accountable, and forgiveness may come later when your relationship to the event changes on its own.

The understanding that helps me is seeing how conditioning, history, pain, and capacity shaped the harmful move. Given the total person they had become by that moment, the harmful move was the only one their accumulated nature had available. The harm remains real, and so do accountability, consequences, and the work of making a different response possible now. Understanding someone’s limitations should make expectations more realistic, not make the limitations less consequential.
“You do not have to forgive before you are ready. I will not use spirituality to silence your pain. I will also not build our whole life around this wound forever.”

“What happened?”“What was the impact?”“What boundaries are still needed?”“What shaped this person into someone capable of that harm?”“What belongs to them?”“What belongs to me?”“What does accountability require?”“What would release look like without denial?”

For self-forgiveness, name what you did without taking responsibility for what wasn’t yours. Let remorse register the harm or violation of your values without making the person who acted a permanent criminal. Then move through responsibility, remorse, rectify, release: name the action and impact; allow the remorse; repair or prevent repetition where possible; and stop holding yourself hostage after responsibility has been faced.
This guide doesn’t tell anyone to use substances. It does acknowledge that many people first encounter self-hypnosis, inner-child contact, or Higher Self dialogue while altered.

A past opening can be a resource without becoming a state you must reproduce. Having experienced love once, being able to access it only in a particular state, and contacting it reliably in daily life are different things. Let the experience widen what seems possible while you build usable access. If the child cannot receive it, meet the difficulty rather than escalating the intensity.
“Help me stay grounded.”“Help me receive only what I can integrate.”“Help me remember love.”“Help me return when it is time.”“Help me translate this into one ordinary-life change.”
Don’t use self-hypnosis to prolong an altered state indefinitely, recover memories, intensify fear, bypass sleep, override medical needs, or make yourself less able to communicate.
If the state makes you less loving, less grounded, less honest, less able to sleep, less able to communicate, or less able to meet ordinary responsibilities, stop deepening and start integrating.

Self-hypnosis can become very powerful during loveyhuasca, meditation, lucid dreaming, grief, sexual energy, prayer, sleep loss, or other plant-medicine-adjacent states. Sometimes the mind opens faster than the adult self can organize what is arriving.

Intensity then gets mistaken for meaning. Sometimes the inner child is finally speaking. Sometimes a Protector is showing fear, or shame, grief, anger, longing, and other buried material are asking for care. But an intense state can also be bodily overload, environmental chaos, sleep deprivation, or plain confusion. A frightening image isn’t automatically truth, a bad feeling isn’t automatically a lesson, and a “download” doesn’t deserve belief merely because it came with excellent lighting.

section: Appendix H: Demons, jinn, hostile presences, and “Unattached Burdens”
text: During self-hypnosis, meditation, lucid dreaming, loveyhuasca, grief, prayer, plant-medicine-adjacent practice, or other altered states, people sometimes meet something that doesn’t feel like an ordinary emotion or younger part. It may appear as a demon, jinn, parasitic energy, dark intelligence, or terrifying archetype—a voice or image that feels intrusive, hateful, seductive, mocking, or simply alien.

section: Appendix H: Demons, jinn, hostile presences, and “Unattached Burdens”
text: I don’t need this guide to settle the metaphysics. Perhaps these are literal beings. Perhaps they are symbolic mind-forms, trauma in a frightening costume, dissociated energy, or ancestral and relational burdens. The practical question is:

section: Start with the room, the body, and basic safety
text: When a demonic, jinn-like, hostile, or intrusive presence appears, don’t reward it with instant metaphysical certainty. Run the triage first: medical danger, environment, body, overload, and how open the mind has become. Open the eyes, feel the feet, name the room, lower stimulation, leave hostile company, and stop adding prompts. Don’t deepen, hunt for hidden truth, or debate ontology while destabilized.

section: Start with the room, the body, and basic safety
text: Danger to self or others, psychosis-like fear, inability to sleep, extreme paranoia, chest pain, seizures, serious overheating, overdose concern, or loss of basic functioning means the self-hypnosis session is over. Get real-world help.

section: A response check, not a verdict about what it is
text: Once you’re stable enough to stay present, notice what helps without turning the response into a metaphysical test. Put a hand on the heart if that feels welcome, take a comfortable breath, and keep the room available.

section: A response check, not a verdict about what it is
text: I don’t have to decide what this is right now. I can notice whether warmth or distance helps, and keep my boundary either way. Nothing here requires my obedience.

section: A response check, not a verdict about what it is
text: If vulnerability appears—a knot in the throat, sadness, fear, or a sense of trying to protect something—you can bring in the Nurturer. If the experience remains hostile or becomes more frightening, stop engaging with it and return to the body and room.

section: A response check, not a verdict about what it is
text: Neither response establishes its origin. A protective part needn’t reveal its fear quickly; a comforting response doesn’t prove an interpretation either. The useful question is whether this way of responding helps you become clearer, steadier, and less hooked. Love and boundaries don’t require a verdict first.

The first impulse may be to fight, banish, hate, prove power, argue, panic, or identify completely with the threatened self. Some traditions use prayers, mantras, protections, banishing rituals, or exorcism forms, and some people find them useful. But fighting from fear can fasten attention more tightly to the thing you want gone.

Fear gives it center stage. Hatred gives it a hook. Pride gives it an opponent. Panic gives it the nervous system.“I do not need to hate this. I do not need to merge with this. I do not need to obey this. I do not need to defeat this from fear. I return to loving awareness.”

section: A bodily boundary: compassion present, door closed
text: When the presence feels hostile, cold, alien, parasitic, or boundary-violating, don’t offer soft sentimental love as though inviting it in for tea. Use love with a boundary.

section: A bodily boundary: compassion present, door closed
text: Sit upright. Press your feet into the floor. Let the spine rise. Gently draw the shoulder blades back so the chest is open but not exposed. Feel the skin boundary of the torso. Feel that this body has a perimeter.“I recognize that suffering may be here, and I wish all suffering to return to the space where it belongs. But the boundary of this skin belongs to my adult life. You do not have permission to enter this house.”“Compassion is present. The door is closed.”

section: If it might be psychosis or destabilization
text: A symbolic hostile-presence experience that settles with grounding and love is very different from a state that becomes persistent, paranoid, sleepless, dangerous, or impossible to reality-test.

section: If it might be psychosis or destabilization
text: If somebody believes they’re under attack for days, can’t sleep or function, hears commands, feels compelled to hurt themselves or anyone else, becomes manic, can’t communicate normally, or can’t distinguish symbolic experience from ordinary reality, stop treating the problem as hypnosis material. Get help.

section: If it might be psychosis or destabilization
text: If the practice makes you more loving, grounded, relational, honest, and functional, continue gently. If it makes you more paranoid, sleepless, grandiose, isolated, frightened, or unreal, stop deepening and get support.

Hostile presences, shadow forces, grandiose parts, and altered-state imagery don’t always attack through fear. Sometimes they seduce through importance: a cosmic secret, a special mission, a vast download, a feeling of being uniquely chosen, or a revelation that makes washing dishes seem beneath your new rank.

“Thank you for the imagery. I do not require a grand performance. If this information cannot become a simple, honest act of care tomorrow morning — washing the dishes, cleaning my room, keeping a promise, apologizing, resting, eating, or helping someone I love — it is not useful to my path.”

Demons, jinn, hostile presences, and “Unattached Burdens” all lead to the same practical training: can love remain present without surrendering the boundary, and can the mind become harder to hook? I’m not trying to turn anyone into an entity hobbyist.

section: Appendix J: A practical induction library
text: Preview the sequence, choose one purpose, and decide whether you want to begin. Each family can be light, eyes-open, or replaced by no-trance contact. Notice the actual response—including no change—and let it determine the next move. Move, imagine, change the sensory channel, remain still, or stop. Use the complete waking return after every induction.

section: Appendix J: A practical induction library
text: If vivid images don’t come, translate the metaphor into words, rhythm, spatial sense, touch, movement, or simple knowing. The mind doesn’t owe anybody a movie.

Feel the support beneath you and the position of one hand or foot. Press gently, stretch slightly, and release—or imagine it. Notice ease, tension, warmth, breath, or no change. Repeat with no more than three areas, letting “release” guide the sequence. Which area or inner voice wants attention? What support is needed? Restore ordinary movement and return.

Notice where your weight is carried. Let support carry 1% more effort, as if floating without losing contact, or keep ordinary weight and pressure. Notice the response. You may deliberately alternate attention toward ordinary awareness on the inhale and support on the exhale; name this fractionation beforehand. What becomes easier to hear? Keep the support, regain chosen weight and firm contact, then return.

Accompany a natural rhythm: breath, a comfortable hum, a finger tap, outside sound, or silent counting. No rhythm is also an option. Repeat “here, and here again,” noticing where attention lands between repetitions. Stop the deliberate rhythm and notice the first quiet beat, without trying to become blank. Is a word, feeling, need, or action clearer? Let ordinary rhythm resume and return.

Notice a concern with several strands. Imagine yarn unwinding, bubbles settling, or knots placed visibly beside you. Leave the object unchanged or label it in words when that fits better. Count only strands you actually set down; nothing is erased. Which needs warmth, protection, or action? Keep one useful strand, give the others a visible holding place, and return.

Hear the actual room and feel the body before imagining a step toward a chosen destination. Use footsteps, textures, or landmarks to gather attention. Change scenery or skip directly to dialogue when useful. Notice a detail without assigning hidden meaning; the mystery is how the scene develops, not what will be done to you. Who or what needs to speak? Return by the same route and close the imagined space.

Start with a small neutral area and what is already there. Imagine warmth, steadiness, or attention spreading to the next comfortable area, or keep it localized. Pause at each step and notice what changes without claiming medical repair. Does the body want contact, space, words, or ordinary care? Let the image recede, feel the whole body and real contact points, and return.

Prepare time, a place, tools, and boundaries for patient care. Let a signal, feeling, or younger state approach only as closely as welcome; choose language that doesn’t make you feel fragmented. Ask before responding, wait, reconnect only where welcome, rest, and reassess. An available inner adult or one borrowed function can help; you choose words, pace, and action. Aim for “good as you,” not erased history. Close the workspace, affirm wholeness and adult presence, and return.

Choose qualities you understand: warmth, boundary, steadiness, curiosity, or dignity. Imagine posture, voice, or attention with 1% more access to one quality. Observe rather than embody it when preferred. Notice a movement, word, image, or no response. Repeat to strengthen access, not replace identity. How would that quality meet today’s situation? Keep the quality and one useful action, release the role, affirm “I am myself,” and return.

Observable pacing: Keep the eyes open, name the room and day, feel the feet, and read or write in ordinary awareness.Invitation: Ask one clear question and wait without narrowing attention further.Genuine choice: Answer, write “unsure,” rest, change the question, seek another person’s view, or stop.Autonomous signal: Record a word, sensation, impulse, objection, or silence without interpreting it as proof.Deepener: None. Full alertness is not an inferior version of the practice.Handoff: Let the internal adult respond in writing or through one practical choice.Integration and exit: Reality-test the signal and do one small action. Because no altered state was cultivated, simply close the exercise and continue the day.

section: Appendix K: Sources and further reading
text: The personal accounts and the way I arrange this practice are mine. The revised teaching brings them together with body-oriented and hypnotic approaches described below. That combination is an adaptation, not a treatment validated as a whole. These notes are for readers who want to follow an idea further; you don’t need them open while practicing.

Maggie Phillips and Claire Frederick, Healing the Divided Self (1995), especially pp.24–27, 45–50, and 83–90, discusses interactive hypnosis, sensory learning, self-hypnosis, and a definite return. It is a professional clinical book, not a self-help manual; its case procedures and historical claims shouldn’t be imported wholesale into solo practice. Adam Eason and Benjamin Parris’s ISH article on self-hypnosis discusses self-directed learning and its relationship to another hypnotist and recordings.

Phillips and Frederick, pp.53–57 and 96–100, explain pacing, utilization, metaphor, and associational cues. Nimja’s hypnotic-language tutorial and trigger tutorial describe language and cueing techniques. They are technique sources, not evidence that every NLP claim is established or every example suits trauma work. The original wording and deliberately chosen re-entry sequence here are adaptations; Nimja did not write or endorse this guide.

section: Body awareness and changing the amount of contact
text: Peter Levine, In an Unspoken Voice (2010), chapters 5 and 7; Levine and Maggie Phillips, Freedom from Pain (2012), chapters 3–4; and Levine, Healing Trauma, chapter 4, inform bodily tracking, resources, titration, pendulation, and attention across sensation, imagery, behavior, emotion, and meaning. The invitation to try a movement or image is not a claim that a particular physiological repair has occurred.

The companion Inner Child Self-Love Reparenting Guide gives the fuller treatment of borrowed adulthood, love without compulsory trust, practical and relational repair, spiritual struggle, differentiation, and mutual peer support. The corresponding practices here follow that account while retaining the self-hypnosis entry, responsive language, and complete return.

Healing the Divided Self, pp.148–153 and 171–174, discusses renurturing, somatic work, and developing nurturing capacities. Levine and Maggie Kline’s Trauma Through a Child’s Eyes, especially chapters 4–5 and 10, discusses attunement and individual responses in actual children and caregiving. Applying those ideas to an adult’s younger feeling-states is an adaptation. My three-adult arrangement and borrowed-adulthood sequence are not presented as those authors’ tested protocol.

section: Memory, support, and choosing a practitioner
text: Levine’s Trauma and Memory (2015), chapter 7, is useful on the difference between compelling experience and historical verification. The VA’s hypnosis overview includes cautions about strong reactions and false memories. ASCH’s explanation of certification distinguishes professional preparation from a guarantee of someone’s competence. The existing links in the evidence and specialist sections point to their particular claims rather than validating every use of hypnosis.

Hi! Did you know that because the Buddha & I both suck at search engine optimization, finding this article is about as hard as it is for a one-eyed turtle to pop his head up through a hoop on the surface of the vast ocean? I know, that’s what every YouTube video seems to say these days (“You’ve been guided here by the universe”), but I really feel blessed to write this and I hope you feel blessed to read, comment, share, & ❤️ it also!

Buckle in, this is a long article. The first part will be my own life experiences. The Enlightenment Manual then turns those experiences into practical guidance, along with the sutta and science case for what I think nibbāna is. If you prefer to jump directly there, use the Table of Contents on the left side of the window. And if you really just want the evidence and claims without the cute wrapper, here’s my research report, including why this analysis is unique yet still mostly grounded in the Buddhist suttas (discourses) and science.

Well, it’s not because I was bored or I like to write! I’ve been infinitely blessed in this lifetime to find the liberation that the Buddha pointed to (Nirvāṇa in Sanskrit, or Nibbāna in Pāli) in a very roundabout and crazy way. I want to share my experience and understandings because if it weren’t for others who shared theirs with me, I would never have gotten to this point. There’s so much confusion about the Buddha’s teaching, but many people have part of the answer. As the saying goes, we stand on the shoulders of giants.

Speaking of shoulders, I was lucky to grow up in a very special family. My parents ran a nonprofit called The Aquarian Research Foundation, whose mission was to find out how the planet could have a positive future. You can see my dad’s film Where’s Utopia. You can understand my early life from this pic:

Our house was situated right in the middle of a ghetto area in Philadelphia, PA, USA. Our street was between the ultra ghetto behind us and a literal mansion with its own forest on the other side. Every night, there were police helicopters, gunshots, screaming, sirens, murder & mayhem. We had kids throw cherry bombs into our living room every night for like a year until we caught them on camera and showed their parents. Some neighbor kids threw a rock at my head when I was two years old. My mom said she saw the rock swerve away from me at the last second, miraculously. I definitely feel I’ve been protected by angels.
On the other hand, we also had a lot of ghosts in that house and they kept daring me to jump out the windows. My parents had to put bars on the windows to block me from accepting the dare!

Around that same age, I told my mom (as she later told me), “I think this is one of my last lifetimes.” She didn’t understand. I also had a recurring dream as a child, in which there was only “vastness” with nothing else in it. It now reminds me of the immaterial meditative absorption the Buddha taught as the Infinity of Space. But my dad, though he was a meditator, never taught me to meditate. So I became more of a materialist as I got older, not interested in spirituality or religion.

section: Realizing the world we live in
text: Like my family, I felt the weight of the world on my shoulders, beginning at the age of 12 when I really started to understand that life is brutal for most people (especially in our ghetto). There was nothing to complain about in my life, but I became convinced that being happy myself, while others weren’t, was selfish. I had this poster in my room that really resonated with me, by the famous socialist, Eugene V. Debs. I cried myself to sleep every night. I told this to a therapist in college and she actually agreed it was a good reason to be depressed!

section: Realizing the world we live in
text: I got into political activism in my later teenage years, and volunteered full-time for the African People’s Socialist Party. That did give me some sense of purpose, but eventually I dropped out of that after visiting Cuba and seeing that socialism, while it did have benefits, was not the full solution to the problems of humanity. Later, I visited the Zapatistas in Chiapas, Mexico, which did actually give me more hope about how humans could live happily (explained in my Community article). But how could we copy their spiritual anarcho-communism without having their culture to start with? It seemed like the first step was to change the education system if I wanted to create a new culture of love.

section: Realizing the world we live in
text: So I then studied Education & History at Temple University, with the goal of helping children in public schools to feel more empowered as agents of change in the world, and teaching them about other possible ways of life for humanity. But when I finally finished my M.Ed. program and started student-teaching at Olney High School, my students threw me a curveball. They said, “Why are you trying to make us think? We don’t want to learn.” Then they slashed my bike tire. Boy was I dumb to waste all those years preparing for an imaginary career!

section: Time for A Radical Change of Mind
text: That’s also when I first tried a drug, at age 26. My friend Emile gave me a puff of weed. It was normal for him, but as it was my first, it gave a mind-blowing synesthesia experience. Colors had texture, numbers had smell, and my life story was being enacted by a cartoon mouse in the center of a stage!

section: Time for A Radical Change of Mind
text: What I learned from that crazy trip was that the limits of reality I had thought were fundamental weren’t. He suggested I try magic mushrooms next. So I got some Tampanensis truffles (“philosopher’s stones”) from the Netherlands by mail. That trip started off with uncontrollable laughter, and then, as I sat outside in a hammock in nature, suddenly “everything made sense.” I understood that everyone’s mind is operating just due to conditions. I was able to go into the mind of anyone in history and understand how it worked. Everyone is always making the best decision they know how to make in that moment (which is also something I learned in Re-evaluation Counseling prior, but didn’t grasp at a deep level).

section: Time for A Radical Change of Mind
text: That doesn’t mean you should stop trying to do your best and holding yourself accountable, just because you are doing your best. 😜 I wrote a comment on a post by Fabrizio on this question of “where are the fairy tale villains?”

section: Time for A Radical Change of Mind
text: I agree that logically, everyone always does the best they know how to do. If they don't know love, then they will not act out of love, pure and simple. It's true that everything is just conditions, at the ultimate level. From that perspective, there's nobody here, so of course there's nobody who's good or evil.

section: Time for A Radical Change of Mind
text: Anyway back to shroom trip: I called up my best friend, Michael, who was chronically depressed: “Michael! Everything is already perfect! It’s just happening automatically!” He said, “Are you on drugs?” … “Yeah, you should try shrooms!”… “No thanks.”

section: Time for A Radical Change of Mind
text: Oh well, everything may not be perfect for Michael, I guess. Anyway, that taught me once again that the limits of reality were completely unknown to me. I wanted to go deeper, so I googled “most powerful psychedelic.” It came up with “ayahuasca.” I read a trip report on Erowid where a guy drank a huge amount and became the entire universe, with infinite love & vision. I thought, “no.. you can’t be the whole universe. I gotta see that.” So I followed his ridiculously overdosed recipe (my Haoma protocol gives a much nicer trip) and within about 15 minutes of drinking a pot of this tea, I was lying on my bed, realizing some rando on the interwebz tricked me into poisoning myself and I was dying.

section: Time for A Radical Change of Mind
text: I saw my life flash before my eyes like a story flipbook and my head felt like it was about to explode. I was OK with dying at this point, just didn’t want everyone to think I wasted my life’s potential due to stupidity. But I eventually just gave up on life, and that’s when my mind exploded. 🤯🤯🤯

section: Time for A Radical Change of Mind
text: There was no more little me, and no more body. I became the entire universe, seeing everything, being everything, knowing and loving everything! Each universe would expand for billions of years, contract to a point, and then explode. Those explosions were insane!

section: Time for A Radical Change of Mind
text: MN 36 says that on his awakening night the Buddha remembered lives across “many eons of cosmic contraction” and expansion. I hadn’t read it yet, so it didn’t prime me, but the coinkydink was cool.

section: Time for A Radical Change of Mind
text: These unity experiences could be insanely euphoric. Heck, unification is arguably the main motivating factor for humanity, if ya know what I mean. Expand that urge across the universe and it can resemble making sweet beautiful love multiplied by infinity. I have spent hours yelling “OH MY GOD” after experiences like that. And it became impossible for me to even kill bugs to this day.

section: Time for A Radical Change of Mind
text: But the afterglow only lasted 1-2 weeks, and then it almost felt like a reverse realization would set in: “Oh, all that sense of perfection I had was just because I took a drug. I’m not one with the universe. How dumb.” And then ironically, that lack of belief in the experience would cause me to want to experience it again. So I got stuck on the aya treadmill for some months. It was only after I finally decided “OK, this experience must point to something real regardless of what initiated it,” that I was freed from that loop.

section: Time for A Radical Change of Mind
text: But taking the experience seriously also had its price. If you seriously believe you’ve been the All & Everything, then you can’t be satisfied anymore with a normal life. I ended up breaking up with my otherwise wonderful girlfriend, as I didn’t feel we had anything in common anymore.

section: Time for A Radical Change of Mind
text: I had to struggle with a bit of a Messiah complex. I felt it was my mission to spread this experience to everyone on Earth. The ayahuasca told me to go down to Cuba, do aya with Fidel Castro, and then he could get everyone on the island doing it, and then it would spread from there because people would visit Cuba and do aya. I was really gonna execute that plan, but I’m glad I stalled long enough to give up, even though I felt like a failure. Now looking back on it, it seems so absurd. As if everyone would have my experience, and as if there was not already a huge ayahuasca religious tradition in the Amazon jungle area. But that’s what happens when you experience apotheosis I guess.

section: Time for A Radical Change of Mind
text: At some point I decided to do a further test: if this experience was really real, I shouldn’t need to take a drug to have it. So I meditated very determinedly while sober, and indeed, I was able to have the same experience that way. So it was decided then…

section: Time for A Radical Change of Mind
text: And yet, despite having access to incredible peak states “at will” (with enough effort & time), I still felt a basic void in my heart. I remember one time, while an ayahuasca trip was coming on strongly, I thought, “I really just want a girlfriend.” Surprisingly, the aya said, “OK, fine, then go find one.” And with that, the trip completely aborted, instantly. It seems like my crown chakra was open, but my heart chakra was only open after an ego death. Could a better girlfriend be the answer for this? Or was I missing something fundamental in my “enlightenment”?

Almost everything I found in the modern seeker marketplace confirmed my experience was basically the ultimate one. Browse through the teachers on Buddha at the Gas Pump, and universal consciousness is like the default spiritual answer. Advaita, the Hindu nondual tradition, and its modern neo-Advaita offshoot supplied a complete philosophy for what I’d already experienced. It was beautiful, intoxicating, and comparatively easy: we are all one universal, happy awareness.

Many people get stuck at that stage, because it’s a nice one. But I’m a curious cat with less than 9 lives left, and I wanted to know about this guy called Buddha who was strangely absent from Buddha at the Gas Pump interviews!

So, I started branching off into Buddhist books to see if I could challenge myself & go further. The Buddha’s habit of breaking experience into aggregates – the five changing components of a person – form, sensation, perception, mind, and consciousness, seemed almost perversely backward. I had found the One. Why was this man taking everything apart?

section: 🫶🏿 May All Beings Be Loving, Peaceful & Free 🫶🏿
text: But one actually useful thing I got from reading all those Buddhist books was the idea that I could actually be of benefit to all beings by radiating love in all directions. So that’s when I started practicing loving-kindness (mettā) meditation. I was astounded at how it cured my depression instantly, and it worked every time. I started connecting it to mantra practice and it was incredible how I could walk down the ghetto streets and even violent crazy people would realize there was no point in fighting me after they felt my vibes! (note: didn’t work for the thugs in Kenya)

section: 🫶🏿 May All Beings Be Loving, Peaceful & Free 🫶🏿
text: So then I started preaching that loving kindness meditation + mantra, but a lot of people couldn’t get it to work, because the Buddha’s advice was too old-fashioned.

section: 🫶🏿 May All Beings Be Loving, Peaceful & Free 🫶🏿
text: Having gone around in all directions with the mind,There is surely no one found who is loved more than oneself.In the same way others each love themselves,Therefore one who cares for himself should not harm another.

section: 🫶🏿 May All Beings Be Loving, Peaceful & Free 🫶🏿
text: It took me many years to finally learn that these folks need to build a loving inner adult before dissolving the cosmic witness. And the Buddha actually hints at this in a new translation of the Mettā Sutta. Interestingly, my first wife was the one who told me she couldn’t let go of ego until she built it up first, although neither of us really understood what that entailed.

section: A Peak State Can Be Useless Or Worse
text: A peak experience (or satori when it shows your true nature) can truly change someone’s life if they are ready for that. It can even change the history of the whole world.

section: A Peak State Can Be Useless Or Worse
text: I’m sure you know how modern Christianity started. It was a peak Christ experience that the apostle Paul had (possibly during a seizure or heat stroke) while on the road to Damascus to persecute disciples of Jesus. Paul literally changed his name after that (it was Saul) and did a 180, becoming the most important spreader of the Christian faith, to the point that scholars even joke that Christianity should be called Paulianity due to the oversize influence he had on it.

section: A Peak State Can Be Useless Or Worse
text: But on the other hand, strangely, peak experiences do not reliably transform people. I’m sure you already have a bunch of examples in your own life that you can think of which should have impacted you more than they did. Or at least, you can think of those times in others’ lives. State-dependent learning is likely at play. It makes sense if your experience was due to taking a drug to deliberately alter your mind (especially a dissociating one like ketamine, THC, 5-MeO-DMT), or if it was a psychotic episode.

section: A Peak State Can Be Useless Or Worse
text: But we like to think that we are capable of being changed by momentous events, at least if they happen while sober. Because if a peak experience can’t change our life, then what can?

section: A Peak State Can Be Useless Or Worse
text:
After months of hearing me like a broken record saying, “Everything is just conditions, all your problems are imaginary!” my first wife entered some kind of satori for about a week. She became the loveliest presence – peaceful, gentle, and seemingly free of mental illness and personality disorders. Then she started slowly coming back to her old self. I asked, “Don’t you want to go back to being enlightened?” She said, “No, that’s done now.” Her answer still blows my mind. Some people are content with less. Is that like, reverse enlightenment crazy wisdom? I’d have to ask Trungpa Rinpoche . 😅
My mom did something equally strange while sick with cancer , roughly ten years before she died. Her hip was in terrible pain, so she had a loving, two-way conversation with it. She told me her whole body then dissolved into infinite cosmic orgasms for hours. I thought, wow, maybe she could cure her cancer if she keeps doing this practice! But strangely, she never tried it again. Later, she forgot the experience altogether. I suspect it was so alien to her ordinary reality that it kind of just didn’t register as something to incorporate into her regular life. People who take psychedelics know what I’m talking about, because you can visit all kinds of incredible realities and then leave it at that. But to me, if you experience some true magic stone cold sober, that should be life-changing.
My BFF, Emile, used to be an atheist. Then one day, while shopping at the supermarket, a Christian evangelical lady came up to him and asked: “Do you know Jesus?” Emile said, “Uh.. I guess?” She said, “Will you hold my hands and pray with me to feel him?” He said “Sure, why not?” And so they did. What he experienced then was some kind of infinite love that he’d never experienced before. Suddenly, he told me, he understood what people mean when they say they’re Born Again in Jesus. But would you believe that years later, he forgot that happened entirely? He does now identify as a Christian, although he doesn’t seem to remember what led him there!

section: A Peak State Can Be Useless Or Worse
text: I’m reminded of that Jack Kornfield book I read at the time, After the Ecstasy, the Laundry. Kornfield’s right that a real satori can still leave the moldy sheets in the closet. Less selfishness, less grasping, and a greater capacity to love your inner child & ordinary people lack the glamour of that peak, but they are ultimately what we should be after.

section: What Else Could the Buddha Give Me?
text: The loving kindness key was super awesome, but I knew that the Buddha still had something deeper to offer, since after all, pretty much every religion has some teaching about loving kindness. What about life, death, and rebirth?

section: What Else Could the Buddha Give Me?
text: Most Buddhist books I read challenged my oneness, but they still gave me lists (4 noble truths, 5 precepts, 3 refuges, 8-fold path… and a partridge and a pear tree!) rather than one useful paragraph about what the absence of unified awareness actually felt like. That seemed ironically opaque for a religion that’s supposedly uniquely open to investigation and debate, as in the Kalama Sutta, AN 3.65.

section: What Else Could the Buddha Give Me?
text: Later I found that some of the uselessness was built-in due to the monastic rules. The Vinaya, the code of conduct for Theravāda Buddhist monastics – in the oldest surviving Buddhist sect – includes Pācittiya 8, requiring confession if a monastic tells anyone not fully ordained about a genuine “superior human state,” including meditative absorption, psychic knowledge, or a path or fruit of awakening. A false attainment claim brings Pārājika 4, permanent expulsion from the order. So CYA applies to anyone with status to protect: monastic authors have an excellent reason to repeat lists and techniques while staying maddeningly vague about their own experience. It’s like asking a doctor whether they ever tried the medicine they prescribe and being told, “I studied medicine. I’m a doctor.” I needed to find someone with direct experience.

section: Then I Found The Map Past Oneness
text: Then I found Awakening to Reality (AtR) and Soh Wei Yu. Soh described his ordinary 24/7 experience as fully disjoint “mind-body drop”: each appearance self-aware without a knower. Hearing that made life without a hidden observer imaginable enough to practice toward. He called my nibbāna experience mind-body drop too, because he didn’t categorize nibbāna as an experience. But AtR’s own accounts retain the ordinary body, world, intention, and function within a transparent or boundless “one suchness.” I now think that is closer to what I’ll explain as partial untying than the full unweaving I experienced.

section: Then I Found The Map Past Oneness
text: I use “unification” for the functional coordination through which a person speaks, crosses a road, recognizes a friend, and answers a message, even with no separate knower. Most of my daily life includes that ordinary unification and feels almost like everybody else’s day (well, if they’re happy).

section: Then I Found The Map Past Oneness
text: I owe Soh a great deal, but one key difference remains: he says sensory unification isn’t required for functioning, which makes no sense to me. I long suspected AtR practitioners were overclaiming, especially because John Tan often scolded Soh for it. I proved one claim false when I met Soh in Singapore. He had said he was in bliss 24/7, but wasn’t smiling. “So you’re in bliss 24/7?” “Yes.” “Even now?” “Well, no, not now.” 😜

section: Then I Found The Map Past Oneness
text: John Tan’s stage map was another major help. His public stages post says it is “nothing authoritative, merely for sharing purposes,” and John does not present the stages as universal nor prescriptive.

section: Then I Found The Map Past Oneness
text: I used to think John’s experience was mostly modern, though I already knew from DN 1, MN 26, and MN 36 that the Buddha learned mind-unification meditations (jhānas) from pre-Buddhist teachers. They mistook those states for enlightenment; he saw that they weren’t liberating by themselves, but were useful for stabilizing and purifying the mind before penetrative insight (vipassanā). And no, vipassanā doesn’t mean Goenka-style body-scanning as many now believe.

section: Then I Found The Map Past Oneness
text: MN 137 tells practitioners to use unification to relinquish diversity, then non-identification to relinquish unity. In MN 121, at every depth of unification the meditator audits the remaining disturbance and finds “just this much – that which depends on oneness.” Unity itself is the last stress.

section: Then I Found The Map Past Oneness
text: My own journey included the four material jhānas and four immaterial attainments (the commentarial 5th–8th jhānas), via the excellent instructions in Ajahn Brahm’s Mindfulness, Bliss, and Beyond. They were amazing, psychedelic-like states I probably needed before I could stop thinking psychedelics were required. In first jhāna, my body dissolved into a cloud of euphoric atoms in love with each other 😶‍🌫️💗🥰 for idk how long! But I wouldn’t make those “hard/powerful” jhānas a prerequisite for insight; the suttas don’t.

section: Then I Found The Map Past Oneness
text: The general recommendation is collectedness: gather the mind before trying to untie its unity. You have to collect the trash before you can toss it. In AN 4.170, Ānanda, the Buddha’s main attendant, says everyone who reached full liberation did so with some cultivation of serenity or mental unification, though not necessarily before insight.

section: Then I Found The Map Past Oneness
text: Most seekers, now as before the Buddha, don’t get beyond unification. Advanced claimants at BatGap or Liberation Unleashed generally settle into oneness, a luminous witness, or cosmic consciousness, and almost never discuss the suttas – though the suttas can also be read with bias. The map and suttas gave me a direction beyond oneness, but they didn’t open me by themselves.

section: AtR pointed me to the Bāhiya Sutta
text: The main sutta AtR recommends for liberation is the Bāhiya Sutta, Udāna 1.10. Not only is it the only sutta giving direct instructions for immediate liberation through the senses, but it’s also such a beautiful sutta that I’ve read and repeated it hundreds of times. It has multiple lessons layered in. I’d advise you to check it out to see if you also connect with it deeply.

section: AtR pointed me to the Bāhiya Sutta
text: Basically, Bāhiya was an ascetic, not a Buddhist, who thought he was enlightened, or on the path to enlightenment. A spirit came to him and told him he was nowhere near enlightenment. Bāhiya humbly asked, “Then who is enlightened?” The spirit told him, “The Buddha is enlightened, go find him.”

section: AtR pointed me to the Bāhiya Sutta
text: So, Bāhiya asked ChatGPT where to find the Buddha and used Google Maps for the three-day walk there (just kidding, idk how people did anything back then!). When he finally found the Buddha, it was bad timing. The Buddha was on almsround begging for food and didn’t want to answer any questions. Bāhiya pressed him three times (3 being the magic number back then), saying “life is uncertain, you never know when it may end, please teach me the Dhamma briefly.” Dhamma means the Buddha’s teaching and the reality it points to (although it could also be used to refer to anything generically).

section: AtR pointed me to the Bāhiya Sutta
text: This is how the Buddha finally advised Bāhiya to practice, in the pithiest instructions ever (Ajahn Amaro’s interpretive translation, also published in Small Boat, Great Mountain):

section: AtR pointed me to the Bāhiya Sutta
text: In the seen, there is only the seen,in the heard, there is only the heard,in the sensed, there is only the sensed,in the cognized, there is only the cognized.Thus you should see thatindeed there is no thing here;this, Bāhiya, is how you should train yourself.Since, Bāhiya, there is for youin the seen, only the seen,in the heard, only the heard,in the sensed, only the sensed,in the cognized, only the cognized,and you see that there is no thing here,you will therefore see thatindeed there is no thing there.As you see that there is no thing there,you will see thatyou are therefore located neither in the world of this,nor in the world of that,nor in any placebetwixt the two.This alone is the end of suffering.

section: AtR pointed me to the Bāhiya Sutta
text: For about 15 years I read this as the Buddha literally saying there is no self between the sensory streams. He didn’t explicitly say that. Amaro’s rendering is contemplative and interpretive; literal translations are narrower and actually clearer, targeting the deconstruction of “things,” though still without my parallel-flows understanding. The full comparison is in the research report. So when I say “sounds hear themselves,” I’m giving a direct-experience pointer inspired by “in the heard, only the heard,” while extrapolating beyond the original Pāli.
The other super valuable description of awakening that AtR gave me was from Dōgen, the 13th century Japanese founder of Sōtō Zen. In the Tanahashi/Aitken translation of his Genjōkōan, he says:

section: Desperation Did The Trick For Me & Bāhiya
text: Interestingly, both of us were really desperate for an end to suffering right now. That seems to have been key for us, although we did have a bunch of preparation as well.

section: Desperation Did The Trick For Me & Bāhiya
text: Some people go to retreats hoping to experience what happened to me. I couldn’t afford that, but luckily being broke helped more (as it did for the Buddha). So did a severely unstable marriage that made me feel I had completely failed at life!

section: Desperation Did The Trick For Me & Bāhiya
text: My first wife had become unexpectedly pregnant with our son about a month before I had to commit her to a psych ward when I found out how serious her mental issues were. Imagining my life as a poor guy trying to raise a kid (or more) with a woman like this was too much. My friends & family were all starting to abandon me because they couldn’t even bear the burden of her insanity. Some even had to leave the country to escape her wrathful episodes, while others offered to help me “solve the problem” in a way that I wouldn’t even talk about.

section: Desperation Did The Trick For Me & Bāhiya
text: I would have killed myself if I had not believed that suicide would simply lead to a worse rebirth. I suppose this is what Buddha meant when he said you should “practice like your head is on fire” in SN 56.34, SN 2.16, AN 6.20…

section: Desperation Did The Trick For Me & Bāhiya
text: Speaking of avoiding a worse rebirth, I had just watched a beautiful documentary called For the Benefit of All Beings which affected me deeply. It was the biographical documentary of a Tibetan Buddhist master named Garchen Rinpoche, who spent roughly twenty years in a Chinese prison labor camp after fighting the Chinese invasion of Tibet with CIA weapons & training. He knew he was going to hell for killing people, but he felt he had no choice. And in fact, he already was in hell in his own mind of hatred.

section: Desperation Did The Trick For Me & Bāhiya
text: Ironically, it was in that brutal Chinese prison camp where he found his true master. His master taught him to love the Chinese and be happy that he was growing rice for them, since the people were not their government. That’s where his practice of loving-kindness blossomed, and he became a light of love upon the world. I thought: if he could find love there, perhaps I could stop treating my own hell as an excuse.

section: Desperation Did The Trick For Me & Bāhiya
text: So, back to desperate little me in bed beside the then-wife I feared. Inspired by the documentary, Soh’s description, and his explanation that everything is conditions, I chanted Om Mane Pemme Hum while meditating with the intent of experiencing what he was pointing at. I fell asleep, woke, sat up, and my awareness coalesced around my navel, then seemed to leave my body – a familiar prelude that usually produced oneness with the room, world, or universe.

section: Desperation Did The Trick For Me & Bāhiya
text: Awareness as one thing was gone. I was gone. What remained were the room’s flows of colored light, all experiencing themselves in indescribable perfection. They were disjoint, but not isolated: the flows ran into and through one another, connected everywhere without becoming one experience or one witnessed scene. Nothing observed them from behind. There was no cosmic knower celebrating its achievement. There was also no black void. The flows were infinitely more intimate, beautiful, and alive than ordinary perception, while possessing no owner at all.

section: Desperation Did The Trick For Me & Bāhiya
text: I now call this body-uncontained nibbāna. It was a full unweaving because unified consciousness and the functioning body-world were gone, but its scope was no longer limited to sensations inside the body as with the fingers nibbāna event. I was not seeing the room from everywhere. There was no “I” or single place from which it was seen.

section: Desperation Did The Trick For Me & Bāhiya
text: The light flows were each presenting every other flow from every corner and angle, with no overall background experience containing them. The content may still have been conditioned by the room the body had perceived before the event, so I am not claiming that it displayed all reality everywhere, but it didn’t need to.

section: Desperation Did The Trick For Me & Bāhiya
text: The closest comparison that’s worth mentioning is the out-of-body perception in some near-death experiences. People sometimes report seeing things from impossible angles, and a controversial subset of those reports were verified by others in the room. Those cases had an externally verifiable target, which was not part of my room experience, since I was not floating around to notice any specific details. They aren’t proof of my own event, but they could help explain what I mean by an experience that was no longer limited by the body’s vantage point. See this systematic analysis of near-death reports, the AWARE-II cardiac-arrest study, and a recent veridical-NDE evidence scale.

section: Desperation Did The Trick For Me & Bāhiya
text: I had already gone thru the formless absorption of nothingness before the room event, and I had also experienced being everything as cosmic consciousness. Neither was the liberation nibbāna was. Both are imaginable: one is an absence, while the other is ordinary unified experience expanded until it contains everything.

A fish could hear a precise description of air – how it moves and what breathing there is like – and still have no way to imagine being outside water. If nibbāna were imaginable, many people would have already imagined and written this account, and the Buddha would be one more person who imagined something and talked about it. Many psychedelic trips would be nibbāna instead of just unity.

It felt entirely different from the ayahuasca ego deaths: no cosmic orgasms and no screaming. The bliss was deeper, subtler, and vastly more peaceful. I believe the Dhammapada is right to call unbinding the foremost ease – the traditional line often rendered “nibbāna is the highest happiness.”
I have no idea how long this lasted. Time belonged to the unified world that was absent. Eventually, the ordinary body, room, witness, and biography formed again.

section: Your fingers are already enlightened, but your hand is deluded.
text: Some months after that first full nibbāna room experience, I fell asleep in my car while meditating. It was parked, don’t worry! Although I later found out it wasn’t my car.

section: Your fingers are already enlightened, but your hand is deluded.
text: Before “I” woke up to notice them, my fingers came online all by themselves. Each finger was its own complete experiential flow. I mean it, there were literally 10 distinct, self-presenting, indescribably blissful, and absolutely perfect, finger flows happening at the same time. (These were light flows in finger form—not my anatomical fingers each running a little mind of their own.)

section: Your fingers are already enlightened, but your hand is deluded.
text: Then “my” mind came back, the perfection vanished, and “I” realized how silly those perfections were. I literally said: “Oh, those are just my fingers!” 😂

section: Your fingers are already enlightened, but your hand is deluded.
text: The finger episode was a small flashback of my full first nibbāna experience of the room itself unweaving, which I analyze further down. Nibbāna is the word the Buddha used to refer to the deathless, perfect reality that’s misapprehended as saṃsāra.

section: Your fingers are already enlightened, but your hand is deluded.
text: I call the fingers event body-limited nibbāna and the room event body-uncontained nibbāna. Both were full unweavings of unified consciousness; the difference was scope. Nibbāna matters so much to me because the room event became the fruition that I believe launched me into stream entry—the first irreversible stage of Buddhist awakening, where rebirth is now on its way out. I’ll define those terms more carefully below.

Since that first nibbāna room experience, life has never felt like a Chinese finger trap the way it did before. The self and “my story” lost most of their authority; the Dhamma stopped being a mystery, and I began looking for a book that explained it as well as I could so I wouldn’t have to write this article. Selfishness and suffering dropped dramatically. I never wanted to kill myself again, felt angry and sad less often – even after my first wife tried to kill my family and stole my son – felt less trapped, behaved somewhat less foolishly, and became less inclined to hide things or leave them unsaid.

Paradoxically, seeing that the self I had taken as real did not exist gave me confidence, like realizing inside a dream that it is a dream. It didn’t free me immediately from the marriage or prevent later bad relationship decisions, but I never again felt the infinite desperation of owning an irreparable life.

To me, this was doubtlessly the first stage of enlightenment that the suttas called “Stream Entry.” And I was also convinced that anyone who experienced this must be a stream-enterer. However, I now suspect a full unweaving nibbāna can be had without causing stream entry.

section: Spiritual realization isn’t enough these days
text: Because personal suffering had lost so much credibility for me, I preached nibbāna to people whom I later understood often needed inner-child reparenting. Partly because I knew nothing about reparenting nor spiritual bypassing, I treated trauma as an imaginary dream problem. Interestingly, around the same time, I also had a relevant dream, in which I became lucid and realized there was no point even talking to the dream character I was with. She retorted, “I may be just a dream character, but you’re still mean!”🥲 So, I apologize to the folks that I wasn’t such a good spiritual friend to, although I did my best, as we all do.

section: Spiritual realization isn’t enough these days
text: If you don’t bring the light of awareness and love to your darkness (“shadow work”) and heal your inner child traumas, any other spiritual transcendence you do will become a form of spiritual bypassing, which will turn you into an egotistical asshole like Sadhguru, Teja Anand, or Artem Boytsov.

section: Spiritual realization isn’t enough these days
text: You can tell when you are listening to fake gurus because their answers to questions are flippantly self-righteous, due to their own avoidance of their feelings. They continually talk from the perspective of some ultimate reality and then denigrate anyone who “doesn’t get it.” Sadhguru even mentioned in one video that anyone who follows him is an idiot, and his followers lapped that up!

section: Spiritual realization isn’t enough these days
text: We humans love to deceive ourselves, and we almost beg others to deceive us with praise and flattery, while at the same time we decry the fakeness of society.

section: Spiritual realization isn’t enough these days
text: On the other hand, more genuine “non-gurus” like my friend Eshwar, will explain their own tortuous personal path to awakening, in which shadow work was 99% of the journey.

If you’re not supported by a community, your chances of a good life are slim. The Buddha taught this also when he said that “Good friends, companions, and associates are the whole of the spiritual life” (SN 45.2, SN 3.18, SN 45.3).
Peer counseling based on my hearthwork guide can help a lot. Beyond that, I’m promoting a plan to help the development of effective spiritual healing communities.

A good spiritual friend can act as a mirror for you to see what the dust in your eyes might make you blind to. They can help you realize that everything is already perfect, while still being there for you when things are hard, and give you an opportunity to be there for someone as well. 🤗🫂And just for fun, another PoV from Africa:

Life has its ups and downs. The ups feel great, but the downs are the diamonds in the rough! I’ve always had my deepest realizations and releases when I was fed up with life. What about you? I started thinking about how the average life goes: You have a few birthdays, try to satisfy desires as they arise, watch your health decline, and then die.

Maybe, if you had a good life, you leave the world a better place as well, and those who survive you continue through the same cycle. Then the question becomes: what’s next? A lot of people are afraid that nothing is next – that there is no next. But what if they’re afraid of the wrong thing?

I didn’t believe in rebirth in my last lifetime, and I still don’t. 😛 But if Buddhism is right about rebirth – I return to that evidence later on – life is a beginningless cycle of birth, death, joy & suffering, called saṃsāra.
