A lot of people might be delighted to learn they don’t need to spend $2m per year to live forever like Bryan Johnson, who btw has questioned whether he might be wasting his time with the “Live Forever” campaign.

This question of rebirth became personal after my father died. In the video below, I tell the story of an experience in which I met him in his mid-life transition, and helped him understand why he was headed for rebirth on Earth. He definitely thought everything was already perfect in his heavenly realm, and really didn’t want to come back here!

By “already perfect,” I mean that everything – including our efforts to improve it – is happening according to natural laws. You’ve already tasted a bit of the already-perfect nature if you’ve ever been in a flow state, where you’re no longer consciously directing your efforts but are having more fun & performing better than you otherwise would.

Because we don’t now “exist” as the natural laws themselves, but rather as a fabricated abstraction from them, pain, unsatisfactoriness, and injustice still hurt and still call for a response. But once we can experientially touch ultimate reality and realize the path out of the illusory cycle, those problems don’t hold the same ultimate psychological power over us. Similar to Plato’s cave, but more imminent.

I originally stole the title of this essay about 15 years ago from a question asked by a man dying of cancer, on the now defunct FB group of AwakeningToReality.com. As he was in the long process of dying, he thought to himself, “What if everything is already perfect (without me)?” For him, it was a final liberating insight, while for someone at a different stage of life, I’d suggest trying to see how, as the Buddha taught in MN 129, this lifetime is the “perfect human rebirth” because it gives you an opportunity to finally end rebirth!

Because everything is just conditions, things work and kinda make sense; otherwise, it would be a bunch of random chaos. Even if we don’t fully understand anything, electrons keep orbiting according to quantum rules which eventually collapse unknowable superpositions into predictable paths around atomic nuclei, the toaster predictably toasts, children hopefully grow up (maybe a bad example), and the sun keeps rising and setting. There was never an electron that felt like she was in the wrong orbital and wished she had ended up around a more handsome nucleus (I assume)! So, if everything is so perfect, why do we want things to be different? Maybe it’s just a hilarious misunderstanding!

How would your life be different if, instead of having to drink some whack Amazon jungle plants to get interested in meditation & Buddhism, then marry a psycho and go on a Hero’s Quest to figure this out, you learned in kindergarten that nothing happens apart from conditions?

Actually, if you ask a kindergartner, you might realize they already basically understand conditions before it gets stamped out of them. I’ve seen a number of kids, when parents tell them that “God created the universe,” respond: “Then who created God?”

Libertarian free will is defined as a chooser standing outside all conditions and causing a choice from nowhere. Well, that’s logically impossible. Of course, choices are choicing. And those choices do matter, because they become conditions for what happens next. But there’s ultimately no puppeteer self outside the web of conditions (Indra’s Net) pulling its strings. Meditative training is the web of the universe itself learning to pull more wisely.

Even after the little king or queen fantasy disappears, the mind scurries into a subtler place: “Fine, then I must be the awareness that makes everything real.” But awareness here means something that awares apart from what it awares. Every time someone claims to experience pure awareness (sat chit ananda – being, consciousness, bliss), they can still describe how it feels. So that non-duality is false. What I find instead, and what I believe the Buddha was pointing to, are aware energy flows and the processes that gather them into a self & world.

This article itself is version 2.0 of my old one-page Already Perfect essay. That was already perfect, so why on Earth did I spend weeks rewriting it? Not because of “free will,” but because my boss, Oliver, told me to! 🤪 Put another way, “already perfect without you” means experience is complete before anyone owns it. A tree falls in the woods and makes a sound with nobody there to hear it. A color colors the coloring book with nobody holding the crayon. It sounds abstract, but the next sections explain what I think the experience was showing.

The word nibbāna originally described a fire going out. My old nibbāna book wrongly treated “unweaving” as its direct etymology. “Extinguishment” is more common, though it sounds like the nihilism pole the Buddha avoided in his soteriology.

In the fifth-century Visuddhimagga, Buddhaghosa instead derives nibbāna from vāna, “binding” or “fastening”: craving laces one becoming to the next. Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu considers that less academically strict but more illuminating and thus translates nibbāna as “unbinding.” A fire depends on fuel (upādāna, also clinging or sustenance) and is freed when its binding to fuel ends. Like them, I find the interpretive meaning more useful here than strict etymology.

The suttas already speak in tangles, knots, and nets. SN 1.23 describes a “tangle within” and “tangle without,” then says the arahants’ (fully enlightened ones’) tangle is disentangled. Dhammapada 90 says the liberated person abandoned every gantha (knot, tie, or bond), while Dhammapada 180 calls craving jālinī (net-like, ensnaring). Unbinding and disentangling are native ways to describe liberation from the binding of the sense streams.

What came apart in my room experience was the fastening of sensory flows into one established consciousness, self, world, and renewed existence. The room looked like it was unweaving, and the suttas’ tangles, knots, and nets make that metaphor feel less accidental.

This distinction isn’t laid out explicitly in the suttas. AN 11.12 says a noble disciple can reach ease and joy through recollecting the Buddha, Dhamma, & Saṅgha – the community of realized disciples – or recollecting ethical conduct, generosity, or qualities shared with heavenly beings. In my experience there can also be physical loosening of unification. My percentages are playful shorthand for how much binding has dissolved: around 1%, a person remains fully functional; by roughly 5%, function is barely possible. Partial untying isn’t limited to that range.

There’s also a strange middle ground where I can have several parallel experiences, each internally bound and therefore not nibbāna, but hinting at it – for example, becoming two different solid birds flying. Ud 5.10 similarly has monastics split into a thousand bodies to clean rooms faster until someone touches one and they merge back into one.

The percentage language applies only to partial nibbāna. The fingers and room events were both full (100%) unweavings; body-limited versus body-uncontained describes their scope, not their depth or authenticity.

At something I would jokingly call 5% nibbāna, I become so peaceful and blissful that doing anything feels ridiculous. Once, at a Workaway farm in Malaysia, I remained around that level for four days. I had no interest in tasks, plans, or becoming an impressive person on a farm. Talking and interacting with people gradually brought the ordinary unification back toward 0-1%, just like in Ud 5.10.

Most of the time, I function through a mostly unified body, one present scene, and some degree of witnessing – just like other people, mostly. Independently perfect finger-flows and a cloud of independent colors aren’t so useful for using a shovel. But what’s always different from before is I no longer take this unified sense of self to be more than a bad approximation of reality. Nature assembled this unified self for survival purposes, so life could reproduce, and so forth. I get it now.

Partial nibbāna / partial untying: some unification loosens while enough of the body-world remains for recognition, desire, memory, meaning… basically, life in the normal sense is still possible, but not as tight.
Full unweaving nibbāna: the unification that creates one functioning and suffering-capable body-world disappears completely.
Body-limited nibbāna: a full unweaving limited by what the living body has made available, as in the fingers experience.
Body-uncontained nibbāna: a full unweaving no longer organized around the body’s viewpoint or sensory aperture, as in the room experience.
Reassembly: the ordinary body, scene, memory, and ability to function return.
Parinibbāna: the same full unweaving without reassembly, i.e. without rebirth, because the body is dead. The living breakthrough to nibbāna is what makes the final direction knowable. Iti 44 agrees on the difference between nibbāna & parinibbāna. It also shows the limit: a living arahant still has preferences and experiences pleasure and pain, but won’t be reborn again. Thus, in this article, saṃsāric means this constructed, dukkha -(suffering/unsatisfactoriness)-capable functioning itself, not only the craving that produces another birth.

section: Nibbāna is a meditative state and attainment
text: Many Buddhists love to tell me nibbāna isn’t an experience, just an achievement or attainment – the loss of the fetters (Buddhist deadly sins). The suttas disagree, tho.

section: Nibbāna is a meditative state and attainment
text: AN 9.47 is literally titled the Sandiṭṭhikanibbāna Sutta, “Directly Visible Nibbāna.” It answers “How is nibbāna directly visible?” with a step-by-step meditative progression: when perception and feeling cease and the taints are destroyed by wisdom, that is directly visible nibbāna “in the definitive sense.”

section: Nibbāna is a meditative state and attainment
text: Arahants also described nibbāna samādhis. In AN 10.7, Sāriputta perceives no earth, water, or normal object – only “the cessation of becoming is nibbāna.” AN 10.6 describes the same state as perceiving “this is peaceful, this is sublime… nibbāna” and nothing else, with parallels in AN 11.7 and AN 3.32. (Bhikkhu Brahmāli reads these as an idea about nibbāna; his paper is here, and I address it in the research report.)

section: Nibbāna is a meditative state and attainment
text: Contact language reinforces that these are experiences. In AN 6.46, monastics touch the “deathless element” with the body. AN 9.43-45 has the “body-witness” touch formless liberations and defines one “liberated both ways” by cessation-contact plus destroyed taints. In AN 9.34, Sāriputta treats the absence of feeling in cessation as pleasure. Ud 8.1 calls nibbāna tadāyatanaṃ (“that sphere”), using the same word as the meditative spheres. You don’t “touch” and “enter” a sphere that’s merely a philosophical abstraction.

My model of a coherent “world” starts with the finger and room experiences. Blissful light flows were present on their own, with no witness behind them. These appearances or awareness flows meet locally like a MeetUp group – although MeetUp banned me for trying to organize a study group about this, which may be why I’m a Substack author instead of the next Jim Jones.

SN 12.44 gives the canonical sequence: eye and forms condition eye-consciousness; their meeting is contact. Contact begets feeling, then craving and clinging; clinging to experiences becomes clinging to life, leading to becoming and birth. There is “the whole mass of suffering,” which the sutta calls “the origination of the world” – sutta-speak for saṃsāra.

I use awareness to mean bare, non-reflective appearance: blue is just blue. Consciousness is awareness reflecting back on itself: “I’m blue!” Pāli doesn’t give me separate nouns for this distinction, but DN 11 and MN 49 describe viññāṇaṃ anidassanaṃ anantaṃ sabbato pabhaṃ – non-manifesting awareness, without end and luminous all around – where the elements and mind-and-body (nāmarūpa, often mistranslated as name-and-form) find no footing. The texts distinguish that from ordinary sense-consciousness (viññāṇaṃ) established when one thing perceives another.

I think this non-manifesting awareness should have been “nonmanifesting awarenesses,” strange as that sounds. Without the plural, Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu can begin correctly in The Mind Like Fire Unbound and The Wings to Awakening by saying the mind fabricates the experienced cosmos, including time and the present, then leave behind one copy-pasted singular line: “consciousness without feature, without end, luminous all around.” He can’t imagine parallel flows as nibbāna because the suttas say nibbāna lacks “differentiation.”

I agree that nobody separates or counts anything in nibbāna. But the light flows weren’t one featureless consciousness either; they were nonidentical by nature, not because a mind was there distinguishing them. The fuller comparison is in the research report. This one-versus-many question ultimately separates Buddhism from prior teachings and new-age spirituality, and it matters because unification gives suffering somewhere to land.

So why would already-perfect flows ever stay tied up in an ever-expanding ball of suffering yarn? I used to think multisensory binding was the root of saṃsāra, based on the Amaro translation of the Bāhiya Sutta, even though that wasn’t my actual experiential insight. Now I realize there’s nothing wrong with the natural random tangling & untangling of stringy energy flows as long as they don’t keep tangling. “Wise” (or lucky) flows tangle and release freely, the way fields, or energy strings in String Theory, bind into quantum particles which then annihilate each other back into stringy energy flows.

And the level of suffering seems to run on the same dial as the tangling. My first-jhāna atoms were a lot more blissful than ordinary life, so calling first jhāna blissful isn’t wrong. But compared with nibbāna, it was euphoria: energized, ecstatic happiness from unification, not the peaceful bliss of release. People usually use bliss for both, and English sutta translations often do too. The Pāli is more precise: the first two jhānas have both pīti—rapture—and sukha—bliss, pleasure, or ease; in the third, the rapture fades while the quieter pleasure remains; in the fourth, even pleasure and pain are gone, leaving equanimity.

If flows forget the beauty of peaceful release, they keep tangling for more euphoric binding. DN 27 says that at some point we emerge as rapture-fed, self-luminous beings, but craving for more leads us to start munching on that yummy dark earth and become solid ourselves. Then we start hoarding food and having sex and eventually develop existentialist philosophy, and now you have anti-natalists blaming their parents for bringing them into the world!

The Buddha names ignorance (avijjā) as the root of the nonstop tangling, the first link of dependent origination. SN 12.2 and MN 9 define it as not knowing dukkha, its origin in craving, its ending, or the path to its ending. My plain-language addition: ignorance is not knowing that the euphoria of merging isn’t happiness compared with the bliss and peace of release.

Money works the same way. Children are happy with none, then get a little power in their pocket and like it. When it runs out, they don’t return to happiness; they want more. They become adults working like hell for more money while growing less happy. The happiness never came from money, but they didn’t know its source, so they chase the wrong condition harder. Nobody chooses that ignorance; we all logically start from it.

My dad once told me he was hitchhiking, and had only a nickel left in his pocket, which was causing him terrible anxiety. Someone asked for money and he gave away his last nickel, and then he suddenly felt immensely free!

The Buddha said sensual pleasure itself works this way. In MN 75 he compares it to a leper finding relief by scorching his itchy lesions over hot coals, and feeling as pleasure what a healed man would feel as burning.

The Buddha splits the accounting cleanly in SN 22.22: the five aggregates are the burden; craving is picking it up. The tangle is heavy by nature – even an arahant feels the first dart – and craving keeps us carrying it. Physics agrees that binding is literally heavy: quarks supply less than 1% of a proton’s mass; roughly 99% comes from gluon-binding energy. Matter weighs what its binding weighs. Light weighs nothing.

Skipping down to the bottom of the sequence, we see that once enough of the scene has been gathered together, it can remember itself, compare moments, anticipate, plan, and report. Then that unified mind at the end imagines it must have been the primordial witness existing before the flows that constitute it. The newly formed field extends itself through time, building the “origin of the world” from SN 12.44 toward becoming and birth.

Up till now I’ve been a bit imprecise about how a bunch of flows can add up to one me: they don’t melt into a new little soul. It works like the nun Vajirā’s chariot analogy in SN 5.10. When we assemble the parts, we call them a “chariot.” In the same way, where nature heaps together the aggregates, we call them “a being.” The sense of oneness is experientially real because you really do experience one world, but it’s the oneness of an assembly. The “me” it seems to happen to is just an overpaid and underly humble assembly spokesperson.

The main question for me and for the Buddha is whether the capacity for suffering (dukkha) remains. Taking a look at studies on automatic action and split-brain patients, it’s clear that people can function without feeling an inner controller, yet they still feel pain. Anguish requires more reflective consciousness than pain. SN 36.6 describes two darts, where the ordinary person struck by pain also sorrows, grieves, etc, while the fully liberated person (arahant) feels the bodily dart alone when not in nibbāna.

But don’t get it twisted: zombie-like functioning on autopilot, split-brain dissociation, and even a true no-self realization can all occur without making anyone an arahant. Pain without anguish is a symptom of enlightenment, not the definition. An arahant is defined by the complete release of even the subtlest unconscious belief in or craving for unified existence – the full loss of the fetters – which is what ends rebirth.

And it doesn’t take multiple sense streams together to suffer: one stream is enough. Even if all that remained were a single channel of pleasure/pain, that still leaves pain in there. The pain, like a plane, is able to land because there’s somewhere solid to land. During full unweaving, no assembled system remains that could suffer, lack, desire, gain, lose, recognize, or do anything. Supreme bliss is what seems to be left when the capacity for suffering is released (even though you might assume neutrality would be left): as Sāriputta put it in AN 9.34, “nibbāna is pleasant precisely where nothing is felt.”

section: The Theory of Light Flows As Nibbāna
text: In my experience, per the Bāhiya instructions, any sensation can be a gateway into nibbāna: one apparent sound can break apart into the many waves composing it before hearing disappears entirely. As the room unweaving experience deepened, all senses disappeared, except for luminous bliss flows.

section: The Theory of Light Flows As Nibbāna
text: The order of disappearance of the other sensations makes sense to me. Thought goes first, since nothing is referencing anything to anything anymore. Sound, touch, taste and smell all require solid molecular interactions, but all the solidity had been unwoven. Maybe this is why they call it “enlightenment” instead of “in smelly mint”? 😄

section: The Theory of Light Flows As Nibbāna
text: Ultimately, in Physics 101 we learned that nothing is really solid when you look close enough, all matter is actually just electromagnetic interactions. But even before modern physics, in SN 22.95, the Buddha was already deconstructing the idea of “solid matter” (rūpa):

section: The Theory of Light Flows As Nibbāna
text: Suppose a person saw a great lump of foam floating down the Ganges… If they inspected it and examined it carefully, it would appear empty, hollow, and insubstantial.In the same way, whatever physical form there is… a monk inspects it and examines it carefully. To them, it appears empty, hollow, and insubstantial.

section: The Theory of Light Flows As Nibbāna
text: This also explains the famous quote by the founding philosopher of Mahāyāna Buddhism, Nāgārjuna. He states in MMK 25.19-20 “there is not the slightest difference between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa,” and “the limit of the one is the limit of the other.” Exactly. It’s saṃsāra when the uncompounded light flows are established as one temporal, material body-world. It’s nibbāna when that establishment fully unweaves.

section: Light Language Like Chantress Seba Never Seen Before!
text: Light language is all over the suttas. AN 1.49-52 calls the purified mind radiant or luminous (not to say the mind is nibbāna, but a purified mind is needed to dissolve into nibbāna). As the “defilements” of the mind are washed away, and as the “dust” is washed from the eyes, the light flows start to shine through, and when unification fully unweaves, no mind remains to be luminous. Only the luminous flows. DN 27 gives the same sequence in cosmic-story form: self-luminous beings crave the dark earth and become increasingly material. Light first, matter later.

section: Light Language Like Chantress Seba Never Seen Before!
text: The DN 11/MN 49 passage is also the closest suttic description I know of nibbāna as light flows, provided you read its “awareness” in the plural.

section: Light Language Like Chantress Seba Never Seen Before!
text: And the last verse of Ud 1.10, the Bāhiya Sutta, repeats the same “no footing” image, then adds that stars don’t shine, the sun and moon give no light, and yet there is no darkness. Well, if nibbāna is light flows, of course there’d be no darkness. No sun or moon needed, because this light isn’t produced by luminous objects. Nothing finds footing because no compounded body-world has been established—the same structural reason there is nowhere for suffering to land. Light can be perceived as the material world, but it isn’t an object in the world.

Near-death experiences made “go into the light” a familiar death-transition theme. Some Christian gnostic traditions and the Tibetan Book of the Dead even tell you which light to enter and what to say to avoid rebirth.

Tibetan Dzogchen Buddhism comes at ultimate reality from a more unified lens than me, but it agrees that the essence of the elements is light, and that matter is just that light condensed. They even claim their masters’ bodies actually dissolve into rainbow lights at death. There are a few 20th-century accounts of this; one was looked into on the ground by a Catholic priest, another was written down by the dying master’s own nephew (Namkhai Norbu Rinpoche). (The full comparison with Dzogchen is in the research report.)

Ud 8.3 defines nibbāna as asaṅkhata. Bhikkhus Sujato and Bodhi usually translate that as “unconditioned/independent,” which would trash my theory of light flows because light is conditioned. Lucky for us, I think that’s an obvious mistranslation – one Ṭhānissaro Bhikkhu avoids. Here’s why:

Across AN 3.47, where saṅkhata things arise, disappear, and decay while remaining; SN 22.79, on the manufacturing of experience; and the decay and assembly metaphors in DN 16 and SN 5.10, saṅkhata means “compounded,” “assembled,” or “fabricated,” not abstractly “conditioned.” The etymology agrees: saṁ- (together, completely) + kṛ (make, do, build) gives saṅkhata: something put together from parts.

section: If nibbāna is “unfabricated,” is light also?
text: Light is energy in the electromagnetic field spectrum, and energy can’t be created or destroyed. Individual photons are emitted and absorbed, but a photon has no parts to decay or disassemble. So light isn’t fabricated, even if a factory made your light bulbs. Even “empty” space measurably seethes with fluctuations, while light converts into matter pairs and matter annihilates back into light.

section: If nibbāna is “unfabricated,” is light also?
text: If nibbāna is uncompounded, you don’t get blank nothingness. You get radiant, blissful, unestablished processes with no body-world, no observer, no timeline, and no assembled objects. Which was my experience.

section: Light is unestablished, with no time, no reference point, like nibbāna
text: Einstein’s Special Theory of Relativity hands me a serendipitous parallel: at light speed, for a photon, there’s no time or space. Light is the invariant everything else measures space and time against. My full unweaving likewise had no observer, viewpoint, time, or common background space.

section: Light is unestablished, with no time, no reference point, like nibbāna
text: The suttas repeatedly call nibbāna unestablished or unsupported. Ud 8.1 gives it no coming, going, standing, passing, or arising. SN 12.38 and SN 22.53 tie unestablished consciousness to ending renewed existence. SN 12.64, of all images, uses a beam of light with nowhere to land. Quantum physics likewise says a photon’s state isn’t established as one definite outcome until measured. Saṃsāra is the unestablished becoming established as a definite relational world.

section: Light is unestablished, with no time, no reference point, like nibbāna
text: Physics can’t demonstrate from outside what meditation can disclose within: light sees itself. Give light a mirror through which to see its own beauty, and reflective consciousness begins establishing a mind, which leads us to the Greek myth of Narcissus, who died from starvation due to unceasingly staring at his beautiful reflection in a pond.

section: How the Experiential Key Can Fade
text: After 15 years of reading popular & obscure Buddhist books, plus countless hours on forums like SuttaCentral.net, I never once found a positive definition of what nibbāna actually is. Everyone says what nibbāna does (liberates), what it ends (rebirth, consciousness, defilements), what it isn’t (anything), and then gives me the aggregates, sense bases, dependent origination, and no-self again. But what was the experience all those lists were pointing to? Why is it that no Theravāda monk ever seems to be clear despite devoting a life to this? In the Buddha’s time, it was common even for laypeople to become stream-enterers and beyond (DN 16).

section: How the Experiential Key Can Fade
text: Part of the problem is that the Buddha, or those who recorded him, left the pieces in different drawers. Ud 1.10 points to direct sensations as the gateway; SN 12.44 gives the contact chain building “the world”; SN 12.67 has consciousness and mind-and-body leaning together like two bundles of reeds – pull either away and the other falls, like Jenga. DN 15 gives the fuller dependent-origination account, and MN 140 moves through the formless unity states and beyond unity. Consciousness-first Advaita and matter-first materialism both fail because the two keep each other standing. I put the puzzle pieces back in the box in the research report. 😛

section: How the Experiential Key Can Fade
text: Those books did at least teach me that everything arises from conditions. AN 3.61 says conditioned choices still matter because they become conditions for what follows. What still bothered me was who or what was supposedly choosing; most Buddhists I spoke with didn’t even understand the question.

section: How the Experiential Key Can Fade
text: Regarding the self, the Buddha is famous for teaching anattā, or non-self. But many people remain confused about whether he denied a self or merely denied that conditioned experience is the true self. In one of the most quoted suttas, SN 44.10, he refuses to answer the question directly because either answer would confuse an already confused person further. But in many other suttas he specifically states that self-view itself is the problem, and the self is just composed of changing aggregates.

section: How the Experiential Key Can Fade
text: The suttas clearly show that the Buddha succeeded in liberating thousands of people, and the Vinaya says 500 fully enlightened monks took part in the first council after his death. The problem is that as the people who directly understood nibbāna, no-self, and dependent origination became rarer, the words kept getting interpreted by people who were still experiencing one unified consciousness and one world, and the hints stopped landing. I’m reminded of Ud 6.4, when the Buddha talks about how sectarian teachers quarrel over incomplete understandings of reality, much like blind men who each touch a different part of an elephant and argue over its true nature.

section: How the Experiential Key Can Fade
text: And the degeneration is even visible in that first council of 500 arahants, because they excluded the female arahants and shamed Ananda for asking the Buddha to admit women to the sangha.

section: How the Experiential Key Can Fade
text: The canon says this degradation had begun in the Buddha’s lifetime. In SN 16.13, Mahā Kassapa asks why training rules are multiplying while fewer monks reach final knowledge. The Buddha says counterfeit Dhamma gradually makes the true Dhamma disappear.

section: How the Experiential Key Can Fade
text: The funny part is that the words may have survived surprisingly well. They were transmitted communally for centuries, and separately preserved early collections agree on a great deal despite variants, rearrangements, and later additions. But preserving the puzzle pieces doesn’t preserve the picture on the box.

section: A Map Can Save Years – and Create Counterfeits
text: That creates a practical problem. In DN 3 and MN 56, the Buddha waits until a student’s mind is “ready, pliable, rid of hindrances, elated, and confident” before giving the teaching that opens the Dhamma-eye. What happens when a stage map lets anyone skip to the answer?

section: A Map Can Save Years – and Create Counterfeits
text: Today someone perusing Dharma Overground can pull the trigger as I did through AtR, but merely out of curiosity, competition, or hope of claiming an attainment.

section: A Map Can Save Years – and Create Counterfeits
text: Nibbāna is genuinely needed as the trigger for stream entry: otherwise, what was recognized, and where did intuitive certainty about the Dhamma come from? MN 56  says the “stainless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma” arises at stream entry. But without the ammunition of desire, prior practice, and readiness to end rebirth and attachment to self-view, pulling the trigger (experiencing Nibbana) only makes a cool sound. It gets filed away as an awesome experience without immutably overwriting the old view. That’s why the Buddha also taught loving-kindness and the Noble Eightfold Path: ethics, meditation, and wisdom are the prereqs for practice.

section: A Map Can Save Years – and Create Counterfeits
text: Dhammapada 276 says awakened teachers point out the path while practitioners make the effort  (wash the dust from their eyes & climb the mountain). MN 38 says the Dhamma must be known, seen, and realized personally. DN 16 pairs reliance on oneself with reliance on Dhamma; and MN 22 calls the teachings a raft for crossing onto “the safe shore” of nibbana, not something to identify with.

section: A Map Can Save Years – and Create Counterfeits
text: The more detailed the map, the more honesty and empirical self-scrutiny it requires. An unprepared reader can use the answer key to exalt a psychedelic rupture, depersonalization, derealization, trauma, or temporary no-self state into stream entry.

section: A Map Can Save Years – and Create Counterfeits
text: AtR’s map saved me, but I still can’t recommend its authentication culture. It seems largely Soh’s semi-authorized editorial creation from John’s journals: John supplied much of the insight, while Soh turned years of journals and chats into a searchable, teachable, generalized system. From the chats Soh sent me, John seemed ambivalent about teaching, yet allowed Soh to act as his mouthpiece. It was a smart arrangement: the student promoted the teacher while the teacher kept calling his posts “a simple sharing” or “nothing authoritative.”

section: A Map Can Save Years – and Create Counterfeits
text: I don’t want to caricature AtR as Buddhist Google Maps. Its blog discusses ethics and the Noble Eightfold Path, and John repeatedly corrected Soh on experience versus insight, view, and stabilization.

section: A Map Can Save Years – and Create Counterfeits
text: Still, Soh seemed to fancy himself the map king and became the person who “authenticated” others’ stages, even though John called awakening “self-authenticated by doubtless realization” and presented the map as only his experience.

section: A Map Can Save Years – and Create Counterfeits
text: I stayed six days with one person Soh authenticated as a stream-enterer, Frank Yang. He didn’t understand basic Buddhist teaching, including “conditions” – which Soh was also confused about while trying to refute determinism – and Frank got angry when I questioned him.

section: A Map Can Save Years – and Create Counterfeits
text: But the problem isn’t as surprising with a YouTube star as it was for me when I met with Āyasmā Ariyadhammika around that time, head teacher at the Sasanarakkha Buddhist Sanctuary, a Theravāda center offering “advanced training” to monastics. He didn’t understand conditions either. He thanked me when I explained that literally everything is conditions, and that seemed to give him a real lightbulb moment, although I never heard from him again.

section: A Map Can Save Years – and Create Counterfeits
text: Frank did suffer much less after softening his identity, which matters, but that isn’t stream entry. He was a good, if shallow, AtR parrot becoming an exalted guru through his charisma & beautiful, crazy YouTube channel:

section: Entering The Stream To End Rebirth
text: Stream entry is the first of Theravāda’s four stages of awakening. Once-returning, non-returning, and arahantship come after it. For this article, the first stage is the one that matters. Craving, aversion, and ill will can weaken a lot at stream entry because the self-view behind them has been seen through, but most fetters remain.

section: Entering The Stream To End Rebirth
text: Nibbāna, when it’s the experiential fruition of practicing the Eightfold Path, opens the irreversible “Dhamma-eye:” identity view seen through, the Dhamma intuitively understood, and as a result, fundamental doubt about the path is forever gone. Based on the suttas, it is clear that one fruition event is what establishes stream entry. If a later event is needed before that realization happens, the earlier event was, by definition, not stream-entry fruition. It may be possible for someone to investigate an earlier experience until its meaning finally becomes irreversible without a second event, but that is not the normal preparation-then-seeing sequence I find in the suttas. The detailed sutta case is in the research report.

section: Entering The Stream To End Rebirth
text: Aside from having the nibbāna fruition experience, AN 10.92 defines stream-enterers as having confidence in Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, ethical restraint, and direct understanding of causality. AN 3.87 ties the stage to ending identity view, uncertainty about the path, and grasping at habits or practices as sufficient by themselves. It calls the stream-enterer certain, headed for awakening, and safe from states of woe. Later stages keep weakening passion, aversion, and delusion until the remaining fetters end.

section: Practice can carry into a future life
text: AN 4.191 says that a monk who has theoretical understanding of the teachings may be reborn among heavenly beings even if he dies unmindfully. The Dhamma can then return to mind slowly, and after that he can quickly reach stream entry (“the destination”).

section: Practice can carry into a future life
text: And we find a stronger guarantee in SN 25.1. Someone who has fully accepted the Dhamma through faith or reflective deliberation is said to be irreversibly approaching stream entry by the time of death, and incapable of doing evil deeds that would lead to a rebirth in a lower realm.

section: Stream-entry requires more than a 2-factor authentication key
text: I know a few people who appear to have had several genuine nibbāna openings. Afterward, their interpretation kept moving between Advaita-style Unity and Buddhist Untying, then back again. One of them, Jackson Peterson, posted publicly like a ridiculous daily pendulum on the AtR Facebook, and he’s something of a guru.

section: Stream-entry requires more than a 2-factor authentication key
text: The AtR debacle taught me that both self-authentication and someone else’s authentication are problematic. In the Buddha’s time, self-authentication was possible, per DN 16, but possible doesn’t mean fully reliable, since people can make mistakes or lack self-awareness, especially in these times when the teachings are less well-expounded. We need a rubric something like this, though after-effects alone can’t settle it:

section: Stream-entry requires more than a 2-factor authentication key
text:
Do you no longer have enough obsessive greed or ill will to cause you to kill, steal, lie, take mind-numbing intoxicants, or engage in sexual misconduct ( SN 55.28 )?
Do other people notice a durable reduction in your selfishness?
Can you be content with less? The Buddha advised monastics to wear corpse-collected robes ( Kd 8.11 ) and use their own fermented urine ( Kd 1.64 ) and feces ( Kd 6.2 ) as medicine.
Are you more joyful and enjoyable to be around without becoming a people-pleaser, as in MN 89 ? Soh’s false 24/7-bliss claim isn’t the standard: AN 11.12 says a noble disciple can reach ease through recollection, while in MN 75 the Buddha says he felt pain at what ordinary people perceived as sensual pleasure. Enlightenment isn’t a simple bliss switch.
Does the Dhamma now feel intuitively coherent rather than merely conceptual?
Do you know rebirth is on the way out with the same certainty that everyone knows they will die?
Can you still recognize trauma without floating above it?

section: Stream-entry requires more than a 2-factor authentication key
text: That last test matters because a stream-enterer still has most fetters. They still need to do reparenting like other folks, and even a genuine breakthrough does not turn somebody into a therapist, let alone a saint.

Stream entry’s greatest prize is a “release date”: AN 3.88  allows at most seven more lives before final awakening. There is actually quite a lot of modern academic evidence for rebirth. But who’s going around getting reborn if no permanent self exists? Buddhists don’t imagine any permanent self-essence/soul moving between bodies. Rebirth is causal continuity without a traveler, often called a mind-stream: craving and clinging condition becoming, and becoming becomes birth. More like a driverless car. The later Buddhist philosopher Milindapañha compared rebirth to one lamp being used to lighting another.

The lucid-dream comparison from earlier also shapes how I understand the seven-life limit said to be had by the stream-enterer. Once the dream is known as a dream, it becomes naturally difficult to remain stuck in it, similar to how hard it is to be absorbed in a movie when the lights go on and you remember you’re in a theater. If you’ve ever had a lucid dream, you know what I’m talking about.

I used to attribute “life is like a dream” directly to the historical Buddha. The famous stanza I loved actually comes from the later Mahāyāna Diamond Sutra, which puts some words in his mouth, although the early Pāli texts offer closely related images. SN 22.95 compares form to foam, feeling to a bubble, perception to a mirage, and consciousness to a magic trick. Dhammapada 170 asks us to see the world as a bubble and mirage.
So should one view all of the fleeting world:A star at dawn, a bubble in a stream,A flash of lightning in a summer cloud,A flickering lamp, a phantom, and a dream.
For me, nibbāna was really like waking up from a dream, except that nobody woke up. Reasoning can make the dream doubtful. The event made doubt about the dream impossible to reverse.

section: Science Can’t Settle This, but You Can Test It
text: Science circles consciousness’s edges: people can function with no felt controller, several things can be cognized at once, split-brain patients can resemble two knowers sharing a skull, and one recent theory models minds as nested parallel observers. The full nerdy tour is in the research report. Science gives my argument a third wheel, making it safer to ride, but it will never show nibbāna itself – self and sense organs unweaving into self-presenting light flows of bliss. That requires meditation.

section: Try a Tiny Bit of Nibbāna
text: Start by feeling your head and feet at the same time without letting the middle get in the way. See whether they can become independent experiences instead of automatically combining into “my body, my choice.”

section: Try a Tiny Bit of Nibbāna
text: A similar version may work even better while walking: I let my limbs do their own thing while my already-faint torso disappears. You can give your fingers some autonomy and see whether they automatic-write the next Pulitzer Prize novel. Sounds & colors have worked less well for me than bodily sensations, but maybe I’m just kinesthetic. Either way, see whether the self loosens.

section: What Counts as Success, Confusion, or Danger
text:
My happy head and happy feet both feel vivid as simultaneous yet independent experience-flows. If my attention is bouncing back and forth, that’s still reg mode, meaning I might need to keep trying the untying, but maybe a bit less trying and more relaxx-maxxing.
Several sensations can remain present without becoming “my body.”
The witness gets hard to locate, and an unusually deep relief or bliss shows up.
I might get just a taste of that or it might feel like more.

section: What Counts as Success, Confusion, or Danger
text: If it still feels like one body watched by the Watcher, nothing has loosened. Numb, dull, or foggy may just mean you’re sleepy and it’s nap time.

section: What Counts as Success, Confusion, or Danger
text: The farther unification loosens, the less useful you become for normal tasks. That’s why I’d suggest starting this practice while lying down… certainly not while driving, cycling, swimming, cooking over fire, crossing traffic, working near heights, operating machinery, skydiving, or flying your pet dragon.

section: What Counts as Success, Confusion, or Danger
text: If it becomes frightening or chaotic, come back: open your eyes, wiggle your toes, name things in the room, and talk to your cat or pet elephant.

section: What Counts as Success, Confusion, or Danger
text: The afterglow can last for hours or days, sometimes longer, depending partly on where I am and who is yelling at me to feed the sheep.

section: What Counts as Success, Confusion, or Danger
text: In a calm moment, I can still get maybe a 1% taste – a release valve I didn’t have before. Going deeper takes more time. When the body and world come back together, they still don’t feel primordial.

section: What Counts as Success, Confusion, or Danger
text: Try it somewhere safe. Was it only an experience, or did it bring insight or realization? Did anything remain: less selfishness, fewer delusions, more love?

section: Bāhiya Got Enlightened and Then a Cow Killed Him
text: I told you about the lovely Bāhiya Sutta. Bāhiya hears one short instruction, becomes fully liberated, and instead of going on a book tour with Oprah, he gets killed by a runaway cow. The Buddha declares him totally unbound, never to be born again, and the fastest person ever to grasp the Dhamma.

section: Bāhiya Got Enlightened and Then a Cow Killed Him
text: Some people might think Buddhism didn’t work very well for poor ol’ Bāhiya. But the goal is to end existence itself, and because he wouldn’t be reborn, he reached it: he untied and was released into parinibbāna.

section: Bāhiya Got Enlightened and Then a Cow Killed Him
text: It’s worth noting that Bāhiya was not just lucky to get enlightened so fast. Ud 1.10 shows his urgency and immediate understanding, while the later Bāhiya Apadāna says he had aspired and practiced toward that quick comprehension for a hundred thousand eons. Most people are not as ready as Bāhiya was, so don’t be surprised if you can’t leap from complex PTSD, self-hatred, or a chaotic life directly into complete liberation just because I told you a sound heard itself. The Buddha’s Noble Eightfold Path still needs to be followed, and I would mainly highlight the importance of ethical practice, loving-kindness, inner-child reparenting, healthy relationships, and a supportive practice community.

I don’t want Bāhiya’s cow to get the last word. In AN 3.55, the Buddha says abandoning greed, hatred, and delusion ends plans to harm oneself or others and brings mental peace and bliss. The following formula calls nibbāna directly visible, not bounded by time, inviting one to come and see, leading inward, and personally realized by the wise.

Here’s something to ponder. SN 12.61 says mind arises as one thing and ceases as another day and night; AN 1.48 says nothing turns over faster than the mind, and won’t even offer a simile. If so, untangled reality isn’t a faraway Garden of Eden requiring an arm & a leg’s worth of past-life hypnotherapy. As Roaring Silence says, it appears in blessed moments as “the sparkling-through of our beginningless enlightenment.”

Physics shows the same shape: permanence is a pattern made from nature’s impermanence, reminiscent of a mind arising as one thing and ceasing as another, and of flows tangling, getting heavy, and releasing.

section: Are disappearing flashbacks dangerous or cool?
text: For roughly fifteen years I have also had semi-random micro-disappearances in which the felt “I” vanishes. Each instance includes, in varying proportions, a high-pitched nāda-like inner sound, bliss, and a dissolution of the felt self. Still not unweaving, but a potential gate into it, as with any sensation that goes direct. Nāda is a Sanskrit word for sound; some Hindu contemplative traditions use it for an inwardly perceived sound. Sometimes the sound dominates. Sometimes the dissolution & bliss do. This is the closest traditional comparison I know.

section: Are disappearing flashbacks dangerous or cool?
text: The effect often begins on one side of my head. By relaxing & tuning attention, I can sometimes bring the other side into it. As it deepens, the bodily sense of the head or brain area can also dissolve along with “me.” I’ve never been able to scrounge up enough money for an MRI to check if my brain is really still there, and some would argue it’s completely gone! 😂

section: Are disappearing flashbacks dangerous or cool?
text: Dzogchen, a branch of Tibetan Buddhism, also has practice advice that fits these episodes: short moments, many times. No need to try to keep the moment going if it’s effortful, since the whole point is to relax the sense of owner/doer.

section: Are disappearing flashbacks dangerous or cool?
text: At first I wondered if I should stop riding my bike to work. What if “I” vanished in the midst of a left turn and the bicycle didn’t know what to do? But so far, everything’s turned out fine, Alhamdulillah! And better than fine, I feel infinitely blessed each time, and I really do thank the universe each time. It’s become a huge gratitude practice.

section: Are disappearing flashbacks dangerous or cool?
text: My buddy E. told me he had much stronger episodes while driving: for long stretches, his own car and the traffic seemed to disappear. He never had an accident either. Luck is one possibility; so is a misunderstanding of what was happening, some feature of how these states operate, a combination, or God only knows.

section: Are disappearing flashbacks dangerous or cool?
text: Whatever the explanation, to be safe, I wouldn’t keep driving through that. Anyone having comparable episodes should stop operating machinery until they understand them better. That’s my own CYA showing. 😇

Its panels: why now (loneliness), the two deaths of community (secular and spiritual), the escuelita mission (come in, live in, learn to hold, go out and start the next one), what’s missing (inner work and healthy structure), and six core design principles.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!OKIC!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F5bc9c45d-5a42-47a4-8880-e9981386f886_1536x1024.png)

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: I just put a movie my father made in 1988 up on the Internet for the first time: Where’s Utopia? It was the result of years of work, traveling to all kinds of communes and communal experiments around the country, trying to answer a question that for him was primary: How do we live together without recreating the same loneliness, domination, and stupidity we were supposedly escaping?

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: He had already spent 17 years in the Bruderhof, a Christian community that doesn’t use money internally. They also accepted my dad as a Jewish atheist, making him a remarkably long-running doctrinal exception. In meditation there, he came to his own understanding that “God is the Universe, and the Universe is Love.”

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: ![A painted banner reading “Suddenly it’s gonna dawn on you: The New Age”, with a sun rising over hills, on the wall above a couch in a cozy living room.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!k_WM!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Febd8f0ea-e412-4f04-9ec4-d8c000529786_1536x1024.png)

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: He might have stayed, but the U.S. antiwar movement during Vietnam needed somebody who knew how to set up printing presses. He eventually founded the Aquarian Research Foundation—not a commune, but a nonprofit devoted to researching how the planet could have a positive future and publishing what it found. His conclusion was simple and enormous: human beings need small tribal communities again, because Civilization Is A Hoax, as I blogged about at the beginning of the Covid plandemic.

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: That’s where the escuelita in my title comes in. Escuelita means “little school.” I’m borrowing the word from the Zapatistas in Mexico, whose Escuelita had outsiders stay with Zapatista families for a while and learn self-government by taking part in everyday life. In the same way, people would live in the healing communities I’m proposing, to heal and to learn the relational and practical methods, so that some of them could eventually leave and set up another one somewhere else. Otherwise, we might have a lovely refuge for a few lucky souls, but we’re doing even less than a retreat center to heal the planet.

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: I spent much of my childhood being carried through Twin Oaks, Acorn, East Wind, Padanaram, Zendik, and many other communities. I was usually just a visitor’s kid. I could see how people lived, but I was never really part of the tribe. At the time it was mostly boring, with some adventures mixed in, but it means I’ve seen a lot of communities to compare against.

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: From 1999 to 2001, my family actually lived with the Love Israel family in Washington while escaping Y2K. In case you aren’t familiar with Y2K, it was the Year 2000 (represented as year 00) computer bug which some folks, like my dad especially, felt might be the end of civilization. We lived in a yurt. At Love Israel, I had my dream of picking all kinds of wild berries in nature come true. I was also lonely, bored, irritated by the cult programming, and missing my friends in Philadelphia.

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: I wanted to befriend the children there, but they treated me as an outsider. My mom never liked the place. The leader was also named Love Israel, and to me he seemed like the fakest person I’d ever met, complete with the expected God complex.

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: We spent a lot of time on our knees in the community garden growing food they could sell in town. The money was opaque and seemed to travel mostly upward toward Love. Meanwhile everybody sang, “Here in the garden, there’s nothing left to do-ooo-oo, but eat, sleep, and keep clean!” Again and again. 🌱

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: My father eventually gave the community his airplane. They sold it instead of using it. He felt tricked, began exposing what was happening, and then we were asked to leave.

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: The East Wind commune was almost the opposite way. There were maybe eighty people when I was there, enough to have a variety of personalities, small enough to actually make friends. I was happy there. I especially liked showering in a communal shower with both sexes present. I wonder if that still goes on at East Wind? That’s the sort of thing that doesn’t make it into the history books, and which takes some balls (no pun intended), considering how the wider society counts this as potentially damaging to children’s psyches, despite it being the way we’ve lived for thousands of years prior.

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: Even at East Wind, though, there was some political power usurpation under the surface. They had a nut butter factory that brought in a lot of their income, which seemed to make the woman running it very hard to question. Otherwise, I thought the community had a great social life, a nice way of distributing labor, and no obvious guru.

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: There were like eight people at Acorn when I was there, and no kids. I couldn’t tell whether it was a commune I might join or a group of people who were already friends, and who happened to live on some really beautiful land and be good at building cool stuff.

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: Twin Oaks was much bigger, like two or three hundred people at the time, and almost institutional. It was friendly and interesting, but I didn’t feel like I was in a tribe there. It was more like a tiny hippie town, but with a highly structured political system that didn’t seem intuitive for hippies.

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: Looking back, almost none of these communities had a communal therapy practice. People brought the usual human pain and suffering with them, and it all got translated into politics.

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: Which meant weekly meetings, run according to Robert’s Rules of Order, with enormous agendas, where most of the things you needed to talk about couldn’t be talked about, and you generally felt like you’d rather be sleeping. (Some people, including me, solved this problem by just going to sleep in the meeting and openly snoring.)

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: Zendik went in the other direction. They held a brutal community meeting that I’m still recovering from 35 years later. 🤣 Five-year-old me was put in the center and told I was bad because I hadn’t volunteered to help adults with whatever jobs they were doing. Apparently kindergarten had already failed to teach me labor consciousness.

section: The New Age May Dawn Suddenly
text: But what I gathered from a bird’s eye view is that the secular communities often thought they could make everyone feel loved and respected by adopting optimal democratic procedures. The spiritual communities went deeper in search of real purpose, belonging, and divine connection, but often put one person in charge of everybody’s inner life. Most of my big little article here is me attempting to describe the missing bridge between those.

Suddenly, the longing to escape loneliness, which inspired my father’s movie, is everywhere again. Back in 2023, ironically, just the year after Covid lockdowns ended, the U.S. Surgeon General even put out an advisory, saying roughly half of American adults experience loneliness, and it treated social connection as a public-health issue.

It’s obvious that a lot of people can’t tolerate modern life in isolation anymore (the UN’s rules for prisoners literally ban more than 15 days of it). Folks may disagree about politics, food, God, sex, or whether shoes are oppressive, but they agree that something about the current arrangement is starving them.

What’s starving them is anomie. We evolved to live in small groups where everybody knows, loves, and trusts everybody. In a large society, nobody knows anybody well enough or for long enough to tell who can be trusted—even your next-door neighbor is often a total stranger. That’s how large societies end up run by psychopaths. (Yes, I’m always going on about this.)

![Google Trends chart of worldwide search interest from 2004 to now: highest in 2004, sinking to a low, flat line through the 2010s, then shooting back up in 2025.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!y0li!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fae1e4fd0-563f-4c2a-8228-7a549a4fc4d7_1211x373.png)

Apart from the Covid lockdowns just prior, AI became serious around this time, and it started changing people’s jobs and relationships, and how they see the future. Suddenly, forming a village sounded like a good backup plan, not just a hippie utopian whim.

It’s poppin’ on Instagram too! 🔥 Chantress Seba—my favorite light-language love influencer—posted an application for people interested in starting a commune. I applied, although I don’t think she’s coming to Africa, where I’m at. When I saw the post, many thousands of people appeared to be interested. That was encouraging, but imagine Chantress Seba the next morning opening her inbox to a zillion excited applications to co-found her dream village. 😅

Later, when another influencer with a big following floated the commune idea, the comment section started to become a recruitment board, where people were apparently forming joint operations together right in there.

Some of the commenters were skeptics tho. The oldest objection showed up immediately, restating the collective action problem: anarcho-communalism sounds great on paper, but when property becomes “owned by everyone, cared for by nobody,” the practicality comes into question.

![Instagram comments debating whether most people will accept the responsibility required by anarchist communities, and whether communal ownership leads to theft, neglect, and nobody maintaining shared property.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!0l9H!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F966a39ab-153b-4d8f-852d-e96421f21f26_714x1228.jpeg)

I’d say the comment above is more true of the big socialism experiments than small communes, but I still take it seriously, because some people really would rather let somebody else take responsibility. Sometimes you see the same three people who end up doing all the maintenance, while everybody else talks about freedom while lounging around in their hammocks. And then unofficial leaders start gaining power just based on their indispensability.

Any attempt at communal ownership needs to take this into account by having folks take on visible and named stewardship duties, and by having a plan to deal with leeches. The How-To Manual after this essay deals with these issues. No, taking away the idea of a boss does not make everyone less passive, selfish or thieving, or suddenly unlearn their learned helplessness.

![Infographic, “Building Healing Community – How It Could Work: a lived village, a training ground, and a path toward deeper common life”. Its panels: my journey, daily life in a healing community, why children need community, the couple problem, a path toward less money, shared inner purpose, practices that keep community alive, and the invitation.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!PpTf!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0b760a8e-4a67-45e0-bb1f-6e07406abf3a_1536x1024.png)

section: Why Communities Keep Dying in the Same Two Ways
text: Most communes of my acquaintance traded inner freedom of the heart (spirituality) for outer freedom (secular, nondogmatic, political), or the other way around. The two pendulum ends of this trade-off mirror each other. I believe we can combine the best of both, but first, let’s see how each fails individually.

The secular communes (and all the manuals I’ve seen on building them) had a solution for how to distribute property or labor in a way folks could agree on, but when the deep waters of jealousy or childhood hurt or humiliation or attraction or resentment or grief came up, the group was without a common method for dealing with it.

Eventually, when people are together long enough, politics will become a way of carrying emotional material that people can’t name. There will be a fight about a schedule or committee or noise or food or some policy or other, but it won’t be about that. There’s no shared way to talk about the hurt itself, but the meeting agenda is the one place the group lets you push for something and win, so the angry communard goes there, trying to get some justice.

section: Spiritual dogma models attempting inner freedom
text: Many people have already realized that they are more interested in spiritual (or emotional) liberation than political liberation, so they tend to congregate in communities built for that. But because these communes focus so much on the inner work that the founder believes in, it can often look like some kind of prison-monastery cult, where you feel free inside as long as you don’t question anything.

section: Spiritual dogma models attempting inner freedom
text: The Farm, in Tennessee, at its largest about 1,500 people, had many beautiful values. But in the early days, the community’s spirituality and social life followed the founder, Stephen Gaskin. From what former members have shared, the community’s doctrine ran deep into members’ intimate decisions. This is how it often goes: folks talk about oneness with the universe, while one man defines what the universe is.

Let’s face it: food, housing, and logistics are not enough reason to bind whole lives together. That’s more like a situationship. A community needs a shared sacred inner practice that gives the difficulty of our life together a deeper meaning. We help each other heal and choose love over fear. And we turn outward with a purpose, using the escuelita model to bring our healing to the world.

I dream of a way to work in depth that isn’t run by a guru, and a way of being in a community with distributed authority. A place where people who’ve done the healing first can join without pretending they’re fully finished, and that also has peer practice and enough play that it doesn’t become a permanent repair shop.

The motto would be: “Nothing suppressed, everything processed.” Each of us guides our own compatible practice, and our practices weave the community into the quilt that keeps us all warm and safe. Whatever answers we find stay fluid and organic, and don’t freeze into doctrine.

Speaking of dynamically weaving ourselves together, though, a community does need some stable agreements that they’re not tweaking and revising every time somebody has a revelation in breathwork. But these agreements need to stay open to lived experience.
When agreements get frozen, religious communities tend to call the frozen version doctrine. Secular communities, on the other hand, often call it “the process,” which can become just as sacred.

To give an example of striking the balance: My contemplative practice is grounded in the early Buddhist suttas, with a critical reading. Most are treasure, while some are obviously late additions (sometimes to the point of real absurdity). A living community should relate to its own teachings in that same critical manner while staying devoted to following what they’ve decided on so far.

I realize that for most people reading this there are a lot of reasons why they can’t just head off and go join or build community on some land. Jobs, kids, pets, debt, a mortgage, a sick parent, or several of these arranged in a circle... That’s fine! The most important pl/ork (play + work) doesn’t need land anyway.

The How-To Manual which follows this essay covers the whole model: inner, relational, and medicine pl/ork, the container that holds them, tech, jealousy, kids, money, land, founder power, how the communities spread, leaving, etc.

People sometimes buy forty acres and then bring all their unprocessed stuff with them to a more scenic location. It’s a more beautiful view for sure, but now you have the conflict PLUS goats. A group that practices together weekly for two years may never own land. So what? It’s already a real piece of community, and it can still make a difference when people are going through a divorce, an illness or grief. Parenting too, and plain old loneliness.

section: Choose Values Before Falling in Love With the View
text: Have you noticed people often choose their community in the same way they would choose a vacation rental? “Wow! Look at this beautiful land! And a pond, with the sunset in it!! Who needs a beach?! And the people seem really nice, let’s get in here!” Fast forward two years. “Wait, there’s a vaccination policy?? And you need paperwork for it?!?!”

section: Choose Values Before Falling in Love With the View
text: Bring your values with you when you go to visit a community. Make a list of what you really believe about children, money, property ownership, romance, medicine, food, spiritual practice, technology, privacy, dealing with conflict, leaving the community, etc. It’s a long list, I know. Some of them will just get a question mark, if you’re not sure yet.

section: Choose Values Before Falling in Love With the View
text: Sexuality and gender belong on there too. Would LGBTQ+ people be able to live openly in your community, date, be in relationships, and stay fully protected by the community? Should children be taught to question their sexual identities from a young age, and what happens if one of the community’s children comes out as gay or transgender? Until you answer these, your community’s values on freedom and on raising children aren’t complete. Yep. Both of them.

section: Choose Values Before Falling in Love With the View
text: Are you willing to experiment? That’s a real value too. Put it on your list, because the people you live next to might think the experiment ended in 1978, and everything that came out of it is doctrine now.

Uh, but wait, where do you find people for a practice group? Try an unprogrammed Quaker or Unitarian meeting, a restorative-practice group, any open-hearted congregation, a mature recovery group, a meditation group, or find some people who have gone on long retreats and come back kinder, rather than more impressed with themselves.

And if you can get away from “civilization” for a bit, that can be really valuable to get some perspective on how others have already figured things out. Go visit some real intentional communities. Lots of ecovillages are open to visitors too. Check their current visitor requirements first.

Through visits, you’ll also get a better idea of how much togetherness you enjoy and what kind of privacy you need, and what kind of labor system irritates you. And whether communal showers feel liberating, or make you start looking at studio apartments! 😛 No manifesto is going to tell you any of that.

So, build the part of community you actually can. Call it a practice group, for now, not a commune. Do the fun and nice things first, to give people an incentive. Have a weekly meal with two households. Set up a counseling exchange with one friend, in person or by video call. Share tools or childcare. Transport or food prep work too. Or a sauna. And if you’re hippie enough, add acro-yoga, dance improv, a mothers’ circle or a cuddle puddle.

And then the hard stuff comes as a test before any talk of a shared future together. Keep your commitments, or renegotiate when they feel wrong, rather than just avoiding. Get through at least one big disagreement. Dealing with it for real includes the relational pl/ork of each of you naming what really went on, giving each of you time, figuring out what came up for each of you (jealousy, humiliation, fear, old material, whatever), and dealing with it until the emotional pressure changes enough that whatever agreement you come up with means something.

Until all of those phases are passed thru, you’re all still promising strangers, and you don’t want to take out a mortgage together yet. And once you’re past those phases, if you still want to live together, you can all live together in a rented or borrowed space first, long before anyone needs a land surveyor.

Many perfectly intelligent grownups would rather sit around for six hours talking about solar panels than talk about jealousy, God, death, childhood, money, sex, psychedelics, or somebody wanting to leave, which is what I ask people to do in this article.

This doesn’t surprise me, since we’re taught to put on a show of competence in modern society. We’re given a lot of incentives to hide ourselves and disappear behind our screens the second things get uncomfortable. Emotional intelligence doesn’t pay the bills. Instead we optimize to fit the career market with all the little energy we’ve got.

So then a lot of people end up thinking they aren’t “good enough” for community, or getting labeled by others that way. And there’s a real issue there, but it’s more about what fits where & when than good or bad.

Some people have engaged in long practices of contemplation or therapy, or have had very good luck in childhood; other people are just trying to survive some emergency in their life and need care more than responsibility. Most of us are all of these at different times in our lives.

![Diagram, “The Math of Absorption”: a community can absorb only as much need as its members have free resource to meet. With 8 people and 2 in crisis (1 in 4), everything goes to triage; with 80 people and 5 in crisis (1 in 16), they’re carried and barely felt. Small communities need new members most and can absorb them least.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!3uG-!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7daf9ea4-807c-49c1-99b3-6993e837a010_800x540.svg)

I’m going to use the phrase “free resource,” which comes from Re-evaluation Counseling, to refer to the attention, steadiness, skill and practical capacity people have left over for others once they’ve dealt with enough of their own immediate stuff, and “need” to refer to the amount of help people need at a given time.

My own need has exceeded my free resource at many points. Good Lord. During one stretch, my first wife tried to kill me while psychotic because she believed I was her sociopathic father. Then she took my son. Later she tried to kill my mother, while her pimp stalked my sister’s family until they moved to Canada.

I could go on and on, but the math is pretty clear by now. My free resource for others was approaching zero. So when I say someone might need to stabilize and do inner pl/ork before doing community (or whatever relationship), I’m not saying it just from a theory.
The ability to welcome somebody is partly a problem of resources, then, not compassion -- how many people can a group take in without hurting the existing members or the people they are taking in?

And that also brings us to a difficult catch-22 for fledgling groups. The need for new members in a small community is greater, but the ability of that community to absorb disruption is less. With only eight people in the community, someone still has to grow the food and fix whatever breaks. Somebody has to balance the books and watch the kids. And the water system has to keep working. The water well doesn’t care how beautiful the new member’s heart is.

So early on, members usually need to have more available resource than acute need, and some practical skills to contribute. They usually need to be willing to learn, too. Once there are 80 members, though, there’s usually a lot more free resource to draw on.

I still don’t know how to keep this language of capacity from becoming a respectable way to exclude people who are disabled, poor, less articulate, maybe simply uncomfortable or unfamiliar with therapeutic language, or for whatever reason deemed inconvenient. Pretending capacity is unlimited won’t solve that. Any real process would need concrete criteria, review by someone who wasn’t part of the decision, and a way to revisit a “not now” decision on membership. Even then, the power to veto membership applications based on capacity remains dangerously tilted towards elitism.
But before you submit your application to the community, submit it to yourself. This community may not be a good fit for you right now if:

You have a need that far outstrips your free resource right now. You need to take a first step of finding support where you are and building up your resources. If you don’t have a free resource calculator on hand, an easy way to tell is if you’re running from some crisis right now and mainly need a place to land, get treatment, housing, legal aid, etc. A founding group shouldn’t pretend it can give you those.
You want the feeling of village life but don’t want to take on governance, maintenance, conflict, care, etc.
You’re not willing to look at yourself when jealousy or conflict comes up.

When The Farm grew fast, a lot of the people who came were in need, and there weren’t many filters being applied. Being open to everybody was part of the spiritual “we are all one” new age philosophy. But practical burden piled up. A membership process is there to protect both the people who are already there and the newcomers.

First, correspond with the visitor. Did they read the materials? (Not everyone does.) Do they get the basic idea of why this community is here? Are they at least starting to do the relevant practices? It’s a lot cheaper to find out through a thoughtful exchange than after six months of misunderstanding, right?
The short visit: If they come for a week or two and just participate in normal life, well, most people can be charming for two weeks. Not exactly a high bar. 😅 So that’s about all you’ll find out.
The long visit: If you’re not around long enough to actually experience inconvenience and conflict with the person in question, then you’re not going to learn very much about them. Watch how they react when working and making decisions in the group. When tired, corrected, attracted, disappointed, bored, etc. (Hopefully not all at once!) Even a professional faker may be able to pull off an act for months.
Taking on responsibilities: If someone will have a role in your group that has serious consequences, involving kids, shared resources, medicine, vehicles or private records, you want to know how they handle that specific area of competence. Great skill with kids doesn’t mean they can drive the van down the windy roads safely. You can find out by checking whether you’ve seen them do this thing before, and asking for references if appropriate. Give people access to these things in stages and ensure there’s always some way to appeal decisions about these roles to a separate authority if needed.

Write down your answers: How long is a provisional membership, and what are a provisional member’s rights and responsibilities? How is it reviewed, and how does someone leave it? Who decides on full membership? (Hint: not the person who recruited them! 😜) And what rights does a full member have to the land, the shared resources and a voice in the group, and what do they owe over the long term? (Those go in your founding agreements.)

Then there are the people who aren’t fully “in” the commune politically. Visitors, volunteers, workers, renters and interns at the commune (yes, even interns) are entitled to some rights when decisions really affect their pay or access to common resources. All of them should have clear terms, and the chance to be heard and to have such decisions reviewed. The same is true for decisions really affecting their schedule, safety, housing, records or discipline. Equality that stops at the membership line can end up recreating a servant class that moves from commune to commune.

And when communal therapy processes are pre-reqs for people to get medicine or to be respected members, it can feel like the community is gatekeeping. Well, it is gatekeeping. Some people simply should not be let in the gate, at least not yet. And some people will resent that, and choose to leave, and that’s fine. Some communities will be stricter gatekeepers, and others will be more lax.

It should go without saying that nobody has to take medicine to have equal respect in the community. But medicine is an optional part of the overall therapy process, and if a member is avoiding the therapy process and becoming hard to deal with, they will naturally not belong at a certain point. If it gets to the point of being impossible to live with, they will be kicked out. But nearly always, people who don’t fit in leave way before that.

They should not be demonized for not trying to fit in. They should be offered compassion, but ultimately it’s up to them if they want to fit in and follow the communal processes. And in some cases, the community may make exceptions. If someone is actually sick and needs care, kicking them out could be like a death sentence.

Before making long-term commitments, it really makes sense to go through the choices explained in my below sections about technology, relationships, children, money, and founder power. The exit terms in the “Leaving, Removal, and Dissolution” section after that would also help with thinking about those agreements.

section: The Best Model I’ve Seen: Zapatistas
text: ![A mural across the front of a Zapatista schoolhouse: a row of men, women and children, some with bandanas or ski masks over their faces, standing among corn plants under an orange sky, with “Digna Rabia” painted at the top.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1QJp!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F745198f3-56e4-42d3-aa6b-1a608ea4b0ef_860x513.jpeg)

section: The Best Model I’ve Seen: Zapatistas
text: In 2005, a few college buddies (Emile & Dolores) and I went down to Oventik, one of the Zapatista caracoles (“snails”), the regional centers that tie their villages together in Chiapas. We almost died, literally, a few times on the way there. The muddy mountain road was super windy and going up & down cliffs, usually without guardrails, and our rental car was huffin and puffin on its last legs.

section: The Best Model I’ve Seen: Zapatistas
