text: San Cristóbal de las Casas is where the only white man we met sat us down in a café and grilled us so directly that he seemed like a CIA agent. Why were we there? Who were we working with? What were our plans? When were we leaving?

section: The Best Model I’ve Seen: Zapatistas
text: It made us feel important for a minute. We were just college kids in a dying rental car, but apparently the empire had questions for us. 😂

section: The Best Model I’ve Seen: Zapatistas
text: Oventik itself was like something out of a dream. We played basketball outside with the Zapatista youth, and people gave us talks about their history and philosophy, which I translated for my friends because my Spanish was better. Visitors were coming from all around the world to learn, and to make the communities less easy to attack in silence.

I felt a deep spirituality from the Zapatistas. The Mayan language, as they explained, doesn’t even have subject/object structure. Instead of “I put the glass there” it’s something like “With me, the glass moved there.” I also suspect there may be a private relationship they have with ayahuasca, since Mimosa hostilis (a potent DMT ayahuasca plant) mainly comes from that region, and the Mexican government vaguely accuses them of narcotrafficking. That’s another reason to look at them as an example of much of my model, since if they are using ayahuasca, it could explain some things about their political struggles and spiritual successes, including the fact that they have the most beautiful poetic rhetoric I’ve ever seen published.

What impressed me the most was how they do authority. It’s mandar obedeciendo, to lead by obeying: the representatives carry the decisions people made in the assemblies, and they have to answer to the people who gave them the mandate.

The Zapatistas are also the closest thing to a whole political-economic example that I found, because their autonomy goes beyond how they vote. They’ve set up their own education and health care, and their own justice, and they run their own collective production.

The Fire and the Word describes the movement growing from family to village, village to region, and region to larger structures. It also gives one of the most useful Zapatista principles for community design: build the practice first and develop the theory afterward. The autonomous municipalities came first; an association of them became a rehearsal for the Good Government Juntas (Boards). When different municipalities encountered different problems and uneven progress, that experience generated another structure rather than being forced to fit the original plan.

section: Real democracy is a continual struggle
text: After a long internal review, in 2023, the Zapatistas announced they were dissolving their previous federated governmental structure, which was split into Rebel Zapatista Autonomous Municipalities and the Good Government Juntas. The original idea was to have power vested in the local communities, but it had crept up and consolidated itself at higher levels over time for practical reasons. Their new arrangement moved authority downward toward a Local Autonomous Government in each community.

section: Real democracy is a continual struggle
text: Institutions get more and more layers and offices as they age. We see this same pattern happen repeatedly, everywhere in history, except usually it goes one way without reversal, unless there’s a revolution.

section: Real democracy is a continual struggle
text: But there is a special reason the Zapatistas were successfully able to reverse this degeneration. Zapatista autonomy grew out of Indigenous communities with long histories. They share language and family ties. They’ve fought land struggles together, and defended themselves together for decades.

For the 10th anniversary of their autonomous governments, the Zapatistas opened up the Escuelita. The goal of the escuelita was to expand their anarcho-communal, spiritual-humanist revolution worldwide. Outsiders came from all over the world, lived with host families there and learned autonomy by taking part in day to day life. Around 1,500 students came to the first sessions, and thousands more came to later ones.

But despite actually trying to train people in their model, the Zapatistas themselves have been clear that people shouldn’t expect to directly or easily import/export their philosophy (Zapatismo) as something ready-made, shake & bake. A new ecovillage can’t copy the diagram everyone can see and get the trust underneath it right away.

Now, the Zapatistas also don’t prove my whole money-free economy goal. They still use money internally in some cases, not others, and they still use it externally for trade. They’ve also benefitted from outside economic help, while at the same time making efforts to remain politically independent from donors and more self-sustaining.

One way an escuelita could fail is if it becomes a business, where residents spend their lives performing community for paying outsiders, and success gets measured by how many people come instead of how many daughter communities there are. A week of feeling transformed isn’t what it’s for.

As part of my research I have also looked for evidence of what happened after the Escuelita. While I found information on alumni networks, people bringing practices back with them, and organizing later, I couldn’t find a clear chain of somebody having been to the Escuelita, then a new communal institution being set up, and then evidence about how its members and their children actually did over time. Zapatista influence was already spreading abroad before the Escuelita, so if some institution resembles a Zapatista one later, that alone doesn’t prove the Escuelita was responsible.

Sociocracy has a very different history, yet some similar features have emerged there as well: circles, decision-making by consent, distributed authority, and linking between the levels. That means people building institutions of this sort have another serious system to study, instead of inventing their governance during their first dispute.

section: What Community Looks Like From Sénégal
text: ![The African Renaissance Monument in Dakar: a giant bronze statue of a man holding a child up high, with a woman at his side, overlooking the city and the ocean.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!Uv0z!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7db4e048-c31e-445c-9d1d-5c4f48de86ab_340x339.jpeg)

section: What Community Looks Like From Sénégal
text: Westerners often start out isolated and try to rebuild a tribe. A lot of Africans start out with a communal life they inherited, and watch parts of it fall apart. Kind of the opposite problem. And urban Africans who get interested in intentional community might come to it feeling alienated from both the city and the tradition they left. So the issue is global now, not just a “first world problem.”

section: What Community Looks Like From Sénégal
text: There’s still knowledge in the living villages which can help us in learning to live together once more. But visiting to learn from them should be done respectfully. Would you like people coming to your house to stare at you and your family? So come and share as part of the human family.

section: What Community Looks Like From Sénégal
text: In the villages and families I’ve spent time around, so much is taken care of by the extended family and the local memory, alongside the formal systems. Whether it’s land, childcare, housing, food, obligations, etc, etc. I’d probably not sell any tickets if I held a workshop called, “Rebuilding Intergenerational Belonging.” 😅

section: What Community Looks Like From Sénégal
text: Oh, and a practical note: getting my residency in Sénégal was pretty cheap and straightforward. French and Wolof matter a lot more than English. And the country’s famous ideal of Teranga (hospitality) is real in my life. I’m staying in a friend’s family’s house, and they won’t let me pay rent! Of course that Teranga is part and parcel of the whole culture of watchfulness, witchcraft, social conservatism, bureaucracy and all the usual complications of a real society and country.

section: What Community Looks Like From Sénégal
text: ![Screenshot of a text chat with a friend about living in Dakar, buying farmland in the south, and how almost nobody in Sénégal took the Covid vaccine.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!BmI8!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd33aef69-9a43-44f1-885f-777d53769f46_967x617.png)

section: What Community Looks Like From Sénégal
text: Sénégal is unlike anywhere else I’ve lived. It’s the only Sufi Muslim country (aside from Gambia, a tiny nation inside Sénégal). Sufi muslims are the ones who value a deep, personal connection with God, rather than just following the religious rules. Five times a day the prayers pour out into the streets. I find them so soothing. And Sufism doesn’t stay inside designated “spiritual” places here. It’s in the music, in the pictures everywhere, in the murals, in the names, in the conversations. Prostitution is also legal here.

section: What Community Looks Like From Sénégal
text: And the humor! People are outside laughing for hours at a time. This is the most joking culture I’ve ever been in, and I keep wondering if I’ll ever understand the really complicated jokes in Wolof.

section: What Community Looks Like From Sénégal
text: Even in Dakar, the overpopulated capital, I found this graffiti on a wall: “Tolerance! Openness! Union! Happiness! Love!” And elsewhere there are murals of Sufi leaders. Spiritual graffiti still surprises me. Where I grew up, a city wall was either selling you a product or showing off somebody’s inability to draw a penis. But the “tolerance” part is funny…

section: What Community Looks Like From Sénégal
text: ![A pink wall in Dakar with hand-painted words down one side, “Tolérance! Ouvert! Union! Bonheur! Amour!”, their first letters spelling TOUBA, next to a swirling drawing.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!1Hvp!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F98df3b3c-7b43-40df-80d7-112f1bc91d75_849x1037.png)

section: All is not well in paradise
text: Sénégal passed a law in March 2026 that increased the penalty for “consensual same-sex intimacy” to 5 to 10 years in prison, and it also made public advocacy for homosexuality a crime. Homosexuals were already facing arrests, family rejection, harassment, assault and mob violence, so ironically, some say they’re actually safer once they’re arrested, because then at least the mob can’t get at them. And also ironically, LGBTQ+ people are using this prejudice in their favor to get refugee status and live in rich countries.

section: All is not well in paradise
text: One other shadow side of the otherwise forgiving social culture here is that people may go to great lengths to avoid confrontation. Who stole the sheep? We all know, but nobody wants to cause a stink by bringing it up. 🙉

section: All is not well in paradise
text: Where I live, neighbors steal our moringa pods every morning. Every morning! They could plant a moringa tree in their own yard. Apparently maintaining this relationship with ours is more entertaining. 😂

section: All is not well in paradise
text: Everybody here has sheep (even me), and they are super cute. It can feel like you’re living in another world, with the music, the animals, the joking, the praying, and just being around people all the time.

section: All is not well in paradise
text: Of course, the old communal ways here are changing. Young people move to the city, get a job, get a phone, eat imported food, become part of the wider world, etc. (some of the men even make the dangerous journey by sea to Europe). So what about the families? The ones that used to share almost everything are now more reliant on cash and individual opportunities.

Then there’s the so-called “Black Tax,” a strange legacy of the old communal system: if you’ve got any money at all, you’re expected to share it with your parents, your siblings, your cousins, to pay school fees, medical bills, funerals, etc. I understand the instinct. In the ancestral way of doing things nobody made it thru life alone, and the people who fed and raised you just naturally expected you to take care of the whole community with whatever you got from life as you matured. That’s how the whole organism survived (it wasn’t charity).

But these days, the pressure to give back can be soul destroying. People have a lot less of the communal life that held the obligation up (the shared land, work, childcare, food and daily belonging), but they still carry it. So if one of them makes it into the cash economy, it’s really hard to build any independence or long-term stability, because they may be expected to carry everybody. And the relatives stay dependent too, since the payments aren’t in something that builds on itself, like compost for soil. Injecting cash into non-cash economies might feel good, but like candy, it can also undermine the health of the local relationships and sustainability.

Maybe some of you will build something useful from this. Maybe that community will teach someone else, who’ll build another. Passing it on doesn’t need one institution or one founder. And there doesn’t have to be one official version of it, either.

I am not currently recruiting anyone or founding a community, which makes it easier for me to write an article like this, since I’m not trying to get you onto my land. I do plan to find some land, and people may naturally end up living around me. Based on the folks who’ve so far expressed interest, I’m planning to call my commune, “Uncle Joe’s Crazy Farm.” 🤪 Hopefully not gonna be another Trungpa Rinpoche cult.

section: The Four Parts That Have to Pl/ork Together
text: ![Diagram of a house. The roof is Community. Three pillars hold it up: inner pl/ork (reparenting, somatic regulation, contemplative practice), relational pl/ork (peer counseling, jealousy processing, honesty practices, conflict handling) and medicine pl/ork (peer-guided, no shamans, gated behind the other work). They stand on the container: membership, land, money, governance, children and exit. If one of the four gets skipped, it will need to be dealt with eventually, at high stress.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!QNQe!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F8957e830-477b-4df4-bc9b-c1babc022045_718x499.png)

section: The Four Parts That Have to Pl/ork Together
text: Communities tend to focus on the aspect of their project that was most interesting to the original founders, for example political types getting super into writing by-laws, or spiritual types just meditating all the time, or therapists processing each other, or people who like psychedelics discovering they’re all God together and never getting to the point of deciding who will put their name on the deed.

section: The Four Parts That Have to Pl/ork Together
text: I’ve broken the model I propose down into the 4 parts shown in the above diagram. Note, Pl/ork means play + work. Calling therapy “inner work” forgets the inner child, who also wants to play. (Forgive the neologism. I hope pl/ork isn’t too corny. 🌽): 1) inner pl/ork (reparenting), 2) relational pl/ork (peer counseling especially), 3) medicine pl/ork (like loveyhuasca or iboga), and 4) the practical logistical foundation which is most of this article, since I have guides separately on the other parts. Obviously the details are complicated, and jealousy, children, money, land, God, and iboga don’t fit neatly into four boxes, but let’s go with it.
Probably the most obvious type of pl/ork is reparenting. Here’s an example: you teach your inner child geography, while s/he teaches you the world is a cat!

Inner-child reparenting means learning to identify as the best holistic inner adult, which is comprised of the three inner adult roles: Nurturer, Protector, and Guide. The newly developed adult reparents their newly recognized inner child. The child receives all that love, protection, and guidance that you give it, and as a result, your little one gains more freedom to remain alive inside you, which brings back the joy of life that many adults have forgotten about.

And this reparenting journey is built on somatic regulation first. I.e., listening to the body’s feelings before making a decision with the mind. And that actually symbolizes the adult/child relationship to me in some way as well.

The idea is that the capacity to be there for people when they need help isn’t located in one professional or guru, or the founder of the group that everyone emotionally depends on, but in the community as a whole.

But since we’re merging peer therapy with community, we also need to make sure that the person caring about you and listening to you doesn’t turn what you tell them into administration over your life, the way a professional therapist might diagnose you as this or that and then suddenly you’re ineligible for certain careers. Although obviously that information can come out regardless when people are in close quarters.

Community can reach new heights by carefully incorporating serious plant medicines with peer guidance rather than exalting any one person as a special shaman. I’ll go more in detail on this in “The Medicine Part” section below. Just because taking part in the ceremonies is optional doesn’t mean people don’t have to work with the other parts.

The first three parts are the inside of the container, and this container is what gives those a stable place to manifest. It’s the practical logistical foundation that gets built once the architects can work well together.

section: The Medicine Part - Yes, I’m Naming It
text: Most of the writing on communities hasn’t caught up with psychedelics. They’ve gone, or are going, from taboo toward regulated use for physical and mental health indications really fast as their benefits become more studied. And most intentional communities using psychedelics are still not public about it, due to possible trouble (even where the law allows some use) from parents worried about children, from neighbors imagining chaos, from insurance providers who might drop them, and from local officials who may not understand any of the distinctions.

section: The Medicine Part - Yes, I’m Naming It
text: I’m talking about psychedelics here because not to talk about it would be to falsify my model. Many of the people who read this article are already familiar with my writing about psychedelics, including my loveyhuasca/Haoma material.

section: The Medicine Part - Yes, I’m Naming It
text: And I believe there are real reasons to take psychedelics communally too - e.g. they can lower defensive barriers which otherwise dominate every serious conversation, and create strong bonds between members of the community who have been through the harder nights together.

Using medicine is secondary to all of the other pl/ork that comes first: reparenting, developing somatic capacity, and learning to do peer counseling. The medicine can deepen the well you already learned how to dig, or it can show you a window into the future you want to see, but it’s not a simple shortcut.

This prerequisite also takes care of another issue in one shot: it weeds out the experience collectors. If someone is unwilling to put in 6 months learning to listen without imposing their solution, it is unlikely they will come out of a ceremony more relationally mature, regardless of how many self-transforming fractalized machine elves told them they are the reincarnation of King David & Elvis.😂

Integration is a term thrown around so much that I’m not sure if it still has meaning. But basically, post-ceremony integration is your everyday life. The ceremony is supposed to open something up in you. Look at your life in the weeks after the ceremony and see how things have changed. That includes your relationships, behaviors, sleeping habits, your decision-making, and perhaps most importantly, how well you can deal with frustration without declaring a new spiritual emergency. 😂
As a community, you need to write down what is and isn’t allowed, and which activities are private (to the individual, to a group in the community, or to the community vs the outside).

section: Community Is What Makes Psychedelics Pl/ork Best!
text:
Part of it is integration: an insight needs somewhere to land. What happens when you come back from an amazing experience which gave you insight and clarity about your life, into the same old environment where nobody knows what you’ve been through and you’re faced with the same old cues? It can be super helpful to have gone through the experience in a community, where the people who held you through it can also notice what happens to you over the following months.
The deeper you go, the more alienated you can feel. After my original ayahuasca ego deaths at age 25, I had trouble finding anyone in the physical world who seemed to have experienced anything similar. I couldn’t even find them at Buddhist monasteries despite all the preaching about enlightenment. That helped give me a God complex, a Savior complex, or both, which then attracted exactly the right people to show me my limits. 😂 I often feel like if I’d gone thru that in a community with others, it would have been much more of a healthy and durable transformation, although without the challenges I guess we don’t learn as much also…
Do you trust the people you’re relying on for support? Support from people you trust is different from paid support, which is often paying people you don’t know to look after you for a night. To me it seems way too much of a gamble if I have a better alternative.

section: Community Is What Makes Psychedelics Pl/ork Best!
text: In a community, your sober sitter could ideally be someone who’s known you for years. Someone who not only watches you based on a safety protocol, but someone you know cares about you. They not only want the best for you altruistically, but because they have to live with the version of you that emerges 😊. This is especially important when doing iboga or other long and medically risky experiences. For those you need to be properly screened beforehand and monitored continuously.

section: Community Is What Makes Psychedelics Pl/ork Best!
text: Your peers can also reality check any downloads you may have had. Psychedelics can give you insight and they can give you convincing nonsense, all in the same bright shining light. A few friends who know your history may notice the difference between new understanding and… mom.

section: Community Is What Makes Psychedelics Pl/ork Best!
text:
One of the benefits of community is rhythm, and many traditional medicinal practices occur within ceremonies that have a communal schedule. The shared schedule of ceremonies, rather than each person doing ceremonies when they want, can serve to limit compulsive use and provide for integration time.
There are the practical benefits: logistics are easier when it comes to things like having childcare arranged by the group that parents are comfortable leaving their kid(s) with, not needing to drive away from the ceremony, having someone bring water to someone or just sit quietly with them while they come back to normal consciousness, etc. And if you scream in release, the neighbors and landlord don’t call 911.
And then there will be people to play with! Raves often let strangers fast-track intimacy (getting to a level of intimacy that usually comes after building trust), but imagine doing ecstatic music & dance in a community that already knows each other (and each other’s inconvenient habits). 💃🕺

Physical and psychological negative effects of ayahuasca were common in the Global Ayahuasca Survey, although severe effects were far less common and context mattered. And these medicines can open things up faster than a person (or their group) can deal with. One of the best resources on this topic is the Challenging Psychedelic Experiences project.

Some people and communities should avoid them. Where access is ahead of competence, people will become casualties of enthusiasm. Is your community humble enough to say no? To pause? Using the medicine takes that. It also takes humility to refer people out, and admit when an experience did harm.

They do also attract people who are all for revelation and hate the follow-through, people who can collect 12 ceremonies and 6 origin stories and still can’t say sorry to their housemate. Any community based mainly around the peak experience is going to find out sooner or later that the insight doesn’t do the practical work for it. Sometimes the dishes need doing and a scared kid needs comforting.

Traditional lineages usually disagree with me on this, and many ayahuasca tribes and Bwiti iboga communities believe the medicine should stay under trained lineage authority. I respect what those traditions have preserved, and I’ve learned some “dos & don’t dos” from their sensible practices and less sensible practices. For example, although I do highly value loving kindness meditation, inner child reparenting, and nibbana meditation before ceremony, during, and at all times, I notice a lot of people want their ceremony to look and feel like some kind of abstract mix of indigenous rituals & props to make it feel more authentic and sacred than their everyday life. I understand the benefit of setting aside one time and place for sacred experiences (the book, “God is Red” comes to mind), although the shadow side to that is making the spiritual seem like another world apart from your regular life, which is sort of opposite to integration.

And while I do think it’s valuable to have someone highly experienced in navigating the spirit worlds who is able to sense where you are in those and guide you, I also wouldn’t trust many of these shamans to guide me, considering it’s common to find that even the ones who can heal people very well may still be happy to send evil spirits to kill someone, if that hit job is lucrative. I also don’t trust their medical intuition in general, considering the Huni Kuin shamans are famous for claiming that all other ayahuasca shamans are giving people cancer by using the knotted B. caapi vine (since the knots remind them of tumors). The lineages are right, though, that modern folk do very often decide they’re ready to lead ceremonies long before they’re really trained and prepared. I’m sure I could still learn a lot from those traditions, and they will continue to develop their understandings as well.

My basic issue is with placing one charismatic person above everyone else’s direct experience. The facilitator on the retreat circuit may be wise. Or they may be someone who hasn’t been vetted by anybody, who isn’t accountable to anyone, maybe even a sexual predator, or financially dependent on people coming back to them for more feather-waving. And the more deeply someone is opening up, the more it costs not to personally know who’s running their ceremony.

Even in a culture of peer medicine, there could still be an informal “shaman”, someone everyone trusts and gradually stops questioning, even though nobody gave them the title. I don’t know yet how to avoid this. Things that might help would be to have rotation of roles, and public accountability. The four questions in “Founderism” below apply to these roles too.
Just because it’s a peer-led ceremony doesn’t mean it’s ok to be casually irresponsible. In fact, since the authority is spread around, there needs to be more competence.

All of the “supports” are important: preparation, nutrition, screening for drug interactions, being disciplined about the dose, having the right kind of sober sitter present, and having a plan for dealing with emergencies. Those matter more than ceremony aesthetics. My current safety material is at Altered States Triage.
While there may be some pure learning that could come from having several altered members figure out what rules and boundaries are needed on the spot, it’s not something I recommend.

Also, I am especially cautious about medicines and protocols that I see as more destabilizing and/or presenting more of a medical burden. This includes some uses of ketamine and MDMA and bufo. My reasons are given in those articles, respectively, since they need more space.

![A traveler in a cloak stands in a carved stone doorway, with a glowing world of giant mushrooms and sacred geometry behind them, looking out over a village at sunset where people share a meal and walk the paths.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!5y74!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F0844bbea-ba0a-4ff0-8b62-4e46426dae51_1672x941.png)

A lot of people feel the urge to form a village after going through some serious psychedelic and/or mystical experiences. Finding their people and helping others get to whatever just opened up is part of the same urge. That call may be real, but forming a community based on omnipotence is a terrible idea.

I’ve felt that urge myself. The problem is that it can come with grandiosity, and I’ve felt that too. You come back believing love can heal anyone, and then you meet people who don’t want to change, people who have some part of them that sincerely wants to change yet they keep choosing the opposite, and people in such a crisis that their need for help is more than your enthusiasm can hold.

Once the euphoria wears off and people have a more sober view of the call they feel, it can become useful. A community can be a place for people to train up in the practices, and sometimes go off and start another experiment. That answers the reasonable objection that communes are just privileged escape pods, which gets double dipped with the objection that psychedelics are also privileged escape pods (or, alternatively, as some say, “a vacation for the poor”).

section: Which Connections to the Technosphere Do You Keep?
text: How accurate are the fears about the future? I don’t know exactly. Maybe AI will improve the lot of humanity enormously. Maybe millions of people will lose their jobs to AI. Maybe AI will become the administrative layer between us and nearly everything. Maybe all of these things will happen before Chantress Seba finishes going through all the applications to her commune. 😂

section: Which Connections to the Technosphere Do You Keep?
text: Ok, so on a personal level, it makes more sense to me to focus on cultivating more human independence from the technosphere, all the machines and systems modern life runs on, than to wait for certainty. It’s better to have community and find out I didn’t need a way out of the technosphere than to need one after spending ten years optimizing my social media feed, right?

section: Which Connections to the Technosphere Do You Keep?
text: What connections to the technosphere do you keep, and which do you limit, when you’re designing a community? This is also one area where many modern folk will balk. Let the community decide if I can use my social media, or ChatGPT? Are you kidding? I get it. I really do. You’re not a child anymore. But on the other hand, these technologies don’t just affect you, they affect how you relate to the community as well.

section: Which Connections to the Technosphere Do You Keep?
text: Medical care, banking, phones, vehicles, schools, supply chains, government ID, internet and energy are each a separate interlink with the wider world that folks must consider. If you opt out of them completely, it can feel like the ideology of independence is more important than life itself sometimes. If you depend on them too much, though, the outside system can remain too essential to truly evolve past.

section: Which Connections to the Technosphere Do You Keep?
text: The Amish, over generations, have made community decisions about where and if they want to use a piece of technology based on how it affects their community. Different Amish communities make different decisions. Sometimes they use it at work but restrict it at home. Sometimes they share it instead of everyone owning a device. Sometimes they hold off on using it until they know more about its social effects.

section: Which Connections to the Technosphere Do You Keep?
text: Medical care is one of the toughest dependencies to work out. A community may prefer natural care, but what happens when someone in the community needs trauma surgery, antibiotics, dentistry, emergency obstetric care, or any number of specialist services? What kind of care is going to be guaranteed to community members by the community using common resources? What things might require outside dollars or some form of insurance?

section: Which Connections to the Technosphere Do You Keep?
text: No member should have to prove their ideological loyalty when they’re scared or sick. There should be pre-existing agreements in place so that their choices will be protected, both for catastrophic illness and end of life care. Medical privacy should be discussed, but may not be guaranteed, since some medical conditions are contagious, and a common purse requires common decision-making for things that take from it.

section: Which Connections to the Technosphere Do You Keep?
text: On the other hand, while medical care is a big tripping point for communes, having social connections is measurably good for a person’s health. The Surgeon General’s advisory notes an increased risk for a range of health outcomes among people who are socially isolated. Community can make a difference, day to day, in the conditions people get sick, heal, age, and die in.

section: Jealousy Can Capture Monogamy or Free Love
text: Any community that lasts will eventually be reorganized by attraction and pair-bonding. When two exes live in the same city, they can move to different sides of the city. When they’re part of a thirty-person commune, they may still be in the same barn the next morning, working in the same team, attending the same meetings, sharing childcare and the same friends. A couple’s jealousy or breakup becomes a problem for the entire community, because it will change the loyalties, the sleeping arrangements, the labor, the kids, the alliances, and sometimes who’s leaving.

section: Jealousy Can Capture Monogamy or Free Love
text: The discussion on this topic generally goes straight to “should people be monogamous or poly?” But as I discuss in my Romance Guide, this is one level too late in the conversation. The community problem is that, in close quarters, jealousy gets magnified, and jealousy can capture either system.

section: Jealousy Can Capture Monogamy or Free Love
text: Rigid monogamy can turn fear and possession into a moral law. If people are doing free love, but aren’t doing the inner pl/ork, they can just end up with a larger spreadsheet to distribute their fear over. It’s not like calling something by a certain name dissolves the childhood panic, the comparison, the terror of abandonment, or the desire to control another person.

section: Jealousy Can Capture Monogamy or Free Love
text: I don’t think it should be up to the community to decide for everyone what form relationships will take. People can make different agreements with each other, in pairs, threes, fours, whatever. They can change those agreements as they wish. And they can ask for support when those agreements bring up old material.

section: Jealousy Can Capture Monogamy or Free Love
text: Whatever forms people choose, I do think that housing, security for kids, membership and access to common necessities should not be contingent on a person staying in some agreement with the people they’re romantically involved with.

section: Jealousy Can Capture Monogamy or Free Love
text: ZEGG, a community near Berlin, and Tamera, a ZEGG offshoot in Portugal, have spent decades experimenting with relationships inside community. They are an example of how a community can acknowledge the erotic aspects of life.

section: Jealousy Can Capture Monogamy or Free Love
text: The non-negotiable for me is that jealousy not be allowed to become the hidden governor. It needs to be able to be talked about and felt in the body. It needs to be explored without humiliation. And it needs to be let go of gradually, and not allowed to turn into punishment, or into community rules.

section: The Grown Children Get the Final Review
text: Couples who live together, share the same culture and even the same bed, still disagree about screens, vaccines, beans (vs meat), schooling, religion, discipline and medical care. And I mean, that’s just two people... Now think of twenty adults, all with different childhoods and value systems.

section: The Grown Children Get the Final Review
text: The community has to share enough principles about raising kids to offer them coherence, and yet still leave parents enough room to contribute their individual humanity, insights, gifts, and so on.

section: The Grown Children Get the Final Review
text: My own childhood broke many mainstream rules about what children should see and do. There’s no space to get into all of it here, but I’m grateful that my mother nursed me until I was five and let me sleep in their bed until 11. I’m grateful my parents didn’t vaccinate me, and grateful for nearly all of the unusual world they gave me, which has given me endless stories to tell.

section: The Grown Children Get the Final Review
text: I mention vaccination specifically because it’s a super divisive issue for people in the more medicalized countries. I’ve personally seen a lot of folks injured by vaccines, even injured by spike protein shedding from others who took the Covid vaccines, and I don’t trust Big Pharma or the government. I’m not sure actually if there even are many communities that believe in vaccination, but if there are, I’d stay away. I’m fine being friends at a distance with the pro-vaxxers, but I’m not trying to design a village for everyone. Echo chambers aren’t ideal either, but we need enough agreement to make life together work.

section: The Grown Children Get the Final Review
text: And regardless of what the adults think, all of the community’s design and practical unfoldment will ultimately be reviewed by the kids, once they’re grown and even while still young. That’s the review I’d say counts, like the results of a longitudinal study count more than the initial hypothesis.

section: The Grown Children Get the Final Review
text: And a friend who reviewed this draft grew up in a Christian commune in Colorado where her father was a pastor. She calls her childhood “a treasure and a burden.” A treasure because she belonged, and everybody cared for everybody. A burden because of the strict religious life she never chose. What she said is more useful than the usual promo video showing kids smiling and carrying vegetables.

One of the biggest reasons I think community matters for kids is Jean Liedloff’s The Continuum Concept. Liedloff was writing about what she learned while living with the Ye’kuana tribe in the Venezuelan rainforest. Some say she idealized what she saw, but I still find it powerful: the babies are carried by the adults (and not just by one exhausted parent) all the time, so they participate in everything adults do from the start. Instead of age-matched cohorts like we have in our schools, kids are with others of all ages. Some modern parents try to adopt some of the Ye’kuana child-rearing practices, but the full stack requires the actual communal support they had.

Experiments where kids sleep and live apart from their parents deserve special caution. Research on Israeli kibbutzim found that the practice of kids sleeping communally eventually ended due to developmental findings, parents’ preferences and social change.

!A summary card, “What happens to adults raised with different caregiving practices?”: in a 1994 study of 48 infants on Israeli kibbutzim, 48% were securely attached with communal sleeping and 80% with sleeping at home, a 32-point difference in favor of family sleeping; the families weren’t randomly assigned, and the sample was small.

Tamera’s Children’s Place has semi-repeated some of this old Kibbutz philosophy, taking children away from biological parents, because their founders’ ideology said that children are traumatized by the nuclear family and its unstable romantic underpinnings. On the other hand, their actual practice did allow parents (including fathers) to sometimes stay with their children in Children’s Place, so they weren’t as dogmatic as I originally thought.

section: Children Need Freedom Inside Real Protection
text: My own bias is still toward a system where kids are not solely taken care of by their parents, while still honoring the parent-child bond. If the father is unknown, the whole community can do the fathering, but the biological mom’s role should always be honored, since that attachment is formed already from years of nursing. Kids do need their own territory, places where they can create their own society, invent games and work out ordinary disputes, without always being under the management of adults.

section: Children Need Freedom Inside Real Protection
text: The adults still have to pay attention to what goes on in the children’s territory. Older kids can’t be allowed to boss the younger ones around there. And keeping secrets shouldn’t be part of how independence manifests.

section: Children Need Freedom Inside Real Protection
text: I feel very much saddened by the way that adults are seen as (and actually often are) so dangerous for children in the West, especially when an adult and a child are fond of each other. It’s good for kids to have a whole bunch of grownups who know them and enjoy them, who would notice when something changes, and who would act when something’s wrong. When adults panic like that, kids can lose all those grownups without the panic actually preventing abuse. It’s amazing when you travel the world and you see how sick US culture is especially… all over Africa and parts of Asia, I’ve seen parents let their kids run around naked in public with no qualms or concerns. That’s real freedom!

section: Children Need Freedom Inside Real Protection
text:
Give children real agency. When kids say no to an adult who wants to be alone with them or touch them, that’s a hard line that can’t be crossed. Apart from that, obedience should not be demanded from kids outside of legitimate safety needs.
Create a no-secrets rule. No grownup has a right to ask a kid to keep a secret from their mom or another trusted adult, whether it’s about a gift, a game, a touch, a conversation or a relationship. (A surprise has an end date. But secrets meant to isolate a kid aren’t allowed.)
Teach Honesty. Protecting children is the duty of adults, but it requires children to help also. “The Boy Who Cried Wolf” is a didactic children’s story which continues to be useful generation after generation. The Buddha even taught his son Rahula honesty as the most important first lesson. I agree. We must teach children truthfulness before there’s a crisis. “Make believe” must be labeled as such.\

section: Children Need Freedom Inside Real Protection
text: When adults lie to children (like “Santa is real!” etc), that teaches them to misunderstand the difference between reality and make-believe. Make sure kids understand what they say will be taken seriously if they are known to be honest. Those who are known to lie a lot are especially targeted by abusers who know their accusations won’t be believed. Don’t let the teaching turn into interrogation or punishment when they’re not sure. A scared or confused kid may get mixed up telling what happened and still need protection.

section: Children Need Freedom Inside Real Protection
text:
Hear the child even when the accused is someone people love. Communities fail here, because the adult may be charismatic, useful, rich, spiritually important, or everybody’s friend. Decide on the response process ahead of time, before anyone’s face is attached to it. Keep everyone at risk safe first, right away, then make sure the accusation is investigated competently and fairly.
Make sure kids have relationships and a reporting route outside the community. Grandparents, cousins, local friends, teachers and other trusted adults give them perspective on their life, and someone to talk to. State intervention can fail spectacularly, and enclosing kids completely in a community can fail too. Kids need more than one world. In 1984, Vermont authorities raided a religious community in Island Pond and took 112 kids into custody over suspected abuse. A judge turned down the state’s blanket request to hold them, because it couldn’t name any specific case, and the kids went home that same day. There was apparently some physical abuse going on there as a disciplinary practice, but what counts as acceptable physical discipline varies a lot from one society to another, and it happens to some degree in every society, communes included.

Sometimes we also need to protect people from the rare, but real threat posed by dangerous children. I looked through the research corpus for a well-documented case of a child in an intentional community who remained seriously dangerous to others. I was looking to find the reported conduct, the assessment, the intervention, the review, and what happened later. I couldn’t find one. I can’t claim communities already know how to handle the hardest cases on their own. In those cases, the child, the family, and the people at risk all need access to competent help and review, hopefully including non-intrusive help from outside the home community.

section: The Door Must Open Outward at Adulthood
text: If a community’s kids never leave, it has no way of knowing whether they’d come back freely. So let them study, travel and make friends, encounter other ways of living, and disagree with the founders without being treated as traitors. And kids coming back isn’t necessarily the best thing for the communal movement either. If they then start their own communities, we may see more evolution than if they simply return and continue what their parents started.

section: The Door Must Open Outward at Adulthood
text: Amish young people, from about age 16, go through an indefinite period of freedom from parental control called Rumspringa. During this time they might travel outside, although they normally choose to stay in the community and begin acting as adults, including courtship. At the end of this period, they decide as adults whether to join the church, and roughly 85 percent or more of them end up joining. Pop culture makes Rumspringa seem like a wilder, more universal teenage free-for-all than it is, but the main point is that they’re baptized as adults, which means belonging is a commitment they make.

Most ordinary parents aren’t going to give their kid a bunch of money at 18 and say, “Go see the world!” They’ll try to get them ready for some next step that can actually work, so they can become self-sufficient, and eventually take care of their aging parents. A poor or money-free community may have even less cash to offer.

Unlimited freedom isn’t realistic, but it doesn’t need to be artificially impossible for grown kids to leave. Kids in or outside of intentional communities all need to learn enough about how the money world outside operates that they aren’t helpless in it. Like how to get a job, pay rent, read contracts, handle banks, get IDs, avoid getting scammed, and how to ask for help when they’re unsure about any of that. And all that sounds amorphous if it’s not structured into plausible next steps outside the community (school, an apprenticeship, work, family, another community).

Kids also need transferable skills and education. It helps if they have relationships with people outside the community. They should be able to access their own records and documents. It would be great if the community could also provide resources to smooth the transition, like temporary housing, help with travel, etc. If it can’t, it can still avoid punishing departure.

What kind of legal or illegal entity (cooperative, trust, association, company, or tribal squatting?) will hold the land? This needs to be decided before it’s bought or occupied. Then you’ll need to decide who has what voting rights, who has what access and use rights to common resources, how you will account for people’s contributions (if at all), how inheritance works, outside debts… oh my! Read the founderism questions next, and agree on the exit terms in “Leaving, Removal, and Dissolution” before anyone commits.

Like my father, I’m aiming for communities with less and less money involved, since money is antagonistic to the spirit of community. If I have money, I can get whatever I want, regardless of whether anyone cares about my wellbeing. That’s the hegemonic philosophy of life we are trying to overturn. I think the path there has three stages.

First there will be no money exchanged between members for basic community functions like food, housing, care, tools, education, transport etc. Members might have outside jobs, and they bring an agreed share of that income in. This is probably a good place to start if someone wants to create a community now and have it be realistic.

Later all wages and other income earned by the members from work outside the community, or from business inside the community, will be paid into the common purse of the community. No member accumulates private wealth while a member of the community. Some version of this is how things have been done in the Bruderhof community for generations, and my father lived there for 17 years. It is also done, in a somewhat different way, at Twin Oaks, and a number of other income-sharing communities.

Eventually, the community would also stop using money outside. People would meet their needs directly, or through exchange (be it trade, gift, work, obligation, or whatever). I couldn’t find a well-documented modern community that has gone this far, and in fact, it may be impractical in some locations because of government requirements like taxes on land. So perhaps the practical end point here is a community that is nearly entirely moneyless, but has a small collective cash boundary on the outside.

None of this does away with scarcity or economic power. There are lots of areas where such power can be wielded: access to food storage, housing, tools, land, medicine, transportation, and the outside world’s currency, to name a few. Even in a moneyless community, someone can control what’s scarce. Who decides how these things are budgeted and distributed?

In every community there was somebody (or some founding group) who took the initiative to get it started. They found the land, wrote the first documents, taught the method, recruited the first members, or kept things going when everybody else lost interest. Like the U.S. Founding Fathers.

The founder(s) end(s) up with real influence, and pretending they don’t just makes that influence harder to look at. When that power fails to get distributed as the conditions ripen for that, it’s called founderism, which is a fledgling form of what can become a subtle dictatorship.

I’ve seen founderism in many communes that I’ve visited, and I can see it playing out if I were to be a founder as well. I’ve got all these proposals and visions here in my guides, and so it would be very easy for me to become the person who decides whether or not everyone else “understood” them correctly, even while I wish to remain humble and open to the input of all involved.

There are some things we can do to keep founders in check. For one, we can judge the lofty methodology by results people can actually see. Will insiders and outsiders see the members safely flourishing without being trapped? Able to leave without it being stigmatized? Can folks resolve conflicts in healthy ways? Are the kids doing well once they grow up? And if the community is meant to spread, do we see daughter projects actually start up and last? Those questions seem more revealing to me than how big or old the commune gets, or how many decisions are made by some form of consensus.

Can the community respectfully override the founder(s)?
Can the community replace the role of the founder(s)?
Can the community alter the vision of the founder(s)?
Can the community exist without the founder(s)?

Then follow the practical power. Whose name is on the deed? Who’s in charge of the resources? Who keeps the records? Who decides who gets admitted, and who picks the people who review the founder? Who controls access to the kids, or to medicine, and who can make a complaint go away? The org chart might look flat and horizontal, while the keys, passwords, titles and even just general reputation all point to one person or clique.

If several of these point to one person or clique, they are worth paying attention to before the founder(s) can explain how the situation is uniquely different in a spiritual way. Ask these questions about any community, teacher or method, including me.

While founderism is a problem in every community, it’s especially so in communities which form naturally over time, as I’ve said may happen in my case. In such cases, there’s no formal community and no formal rules until people decide to come together to make them. It doesn’t make sense to do that at first, if, say, I’m the only one there and I don’t know who else will be there that I could trust. If there’s one other person who comes to visit, it also doesn’t make sense, so there’s a critical mass point at which people decide “we were just living together like friends, but now we want to formalize the community.”

If I could find a suitable commune to join, that would basically reverse this problem. I would then be the one on probation. And if we are all starting together from scratch, then we would all be at an equal probationary level with each other.

section: How My Own Model Could Become a Cult
text: As if a founderism-type subtle dictatorship isn’t bad enough, we often find groups that are even proudly and overtly controlled by some Pharaoh at the top of the pyramid, especially when the organization of the group is as advanced as what it took to build the Great Pyramids.

section: How My Own Model Could Become a Cult
text: “Nothing suppressed, everything processed” can become a situation where someone in the group must tell all, even if they don’t want to. I have seen that risk in groups that use the ZEGG Forum practice. But privacy also can be resistance to the communal spirit, so there has to be a living, always re-assessed balance between what you and the community owe each other, and what remains your own domain. But some private practices go too far against the communal spirit. If someone starts worshipping Satan, say, they get booted.

section: How My Own Model Could Become a Cult
text: Dissent is important for growth. Sometimes it really is the dissenter’s wounded ego projecting, and that should be acknowledged. But again, balance, because if complaints are too often or too broadly painted as projection, that’s as much a failure, if not more so.

section: How My Own Model Could Become a Cult
text: There are some basic human rights that can’t be voted away from you by the majority in a community, unless it’s a question of resource availability as a whole. If safety and the conditions for health can be provided, they should be provided. People should be able to maintain relationships with others outside the community, as long as those relationships don’t interfere with the community as a whole (for example, you can’t bring your boyfriend from outside to live with you if he’s antagonistic towards the commune).

section: How My Own Model Could Become a Cult
text: Let’s say a grandmother is demonizing the commune. Cutting off contact with her could make things way worse. When it’s tricky and dangerous for everyone like that, I think the commune needs to step in and help people decide how to communicate with outsiders.

section: From One Community to a Movement
text: The problem of how these communities stay connected does eventually need to be solved somehow, if the idea is for them to spread without building another state. It should be solved in a way that allows help between communities and the movement of people and knowledge, and also keeps the differences alive, so communities can keep learning from one another. And communities already do have federations which provide some degrees of assistance in training people, seeding new projects, logging experiences and lessons, and so forth.

section: From One Community to a Movement
text: The Federation of Egalitarian Communities (FEC) says it’s rebuilding, and that’s a good warning. It takes work to run a federation. Delegates. Records. Compliance. Coordinating resources. Holding meetings. Succession. Whatever dispute function it actually takes on. These things all take up labor and material capacity before any local crisis has eaten into both. But the work of federation doesn’t have to be done by a single entity. There can also be local clusters, or single-function institutions like the FEC’s PEACH health pool, which isn’t currently governed by the FEC delegates.

section: From One Community to a Movement
text: Cooperation also shouldn’t slide into assimilation. The FEC has full members and communities working toward full membership, and Friends who may just want to stay friends. Fortunately, the interface between communities can often be thin, saying who’s responsible for what while somebody crosses between them, and communities don’t have to have the same internal systems for it to work.

section: From One Community to a Movement
text: Solidarity doesn’t mean every community is liable for whatever the others owe, and it doesn’t mean anyone has an unlimited claim on another community’s labor and stores, or its land and tools. Even if nobody uses money internally, communities still need the same honesty about exchanges and obligations. Decide in advance which offers of help are purely goodwill and which go on a ledger of mutual aid. The federation can keep track of these for each purpose, without having to put a value on them or require every exchange to be “even”.

section: From One Community to a Movement
text: Whenever a community or a federation creates or applies a rule, it’s best practice to store the full case history (with private details protected) so it can be re-evaluated in future: what happened, the principles that actually conflicted, your first judgments, and your final decision and rationale. Any dissenting opinions should go in there as well, along with the consequences in the case. When the rule changes because of a new case, run the old case through again to see how it would turn out. That saves each generation from having to rediscover the same constitutional fight from scratch.

Experimenting with a different rule doesn’t have to mean everybody goes out and buys new land right away. Try it inside the parent group first, then as a semi-autonomous project, and then, if it needs more independence, as a seed group nearby that still shares some tools, childcare, business or friendships.

Some experiments (like a different land system, or a different population size, or any number of rules that work together) can’t be tried in a way that’s cheap. They may look bad when they’re starved of the assets they actually need. “We tried it in one room for three months” isn’t always a fair test.

Good people leave for good reasons -- dying parent, love, work, health, exhaustion, change of mind, etc. You don’t want them to lose everything they’ve put in. Whether or not you use money, you’ll need to have a way of providing people with resources when they leave (cash, if you use it, but also tools, transportation, temporary housing, stored up goods, the right to keep using something, or whatever). Otherwise their “right” to leave is only on paper -- it only works when the community happens to have spare money. Write up the exit terms while leaving is still only theoretical -- like a pre-nup when you’re planning the wedding. Not romantic, but protective. Much easier than doing it once anybody’s furious.

A safe community can’t promise to keep everyone. There may be times when someone has to go. If someone is a serious or generalized danger to others, or keeps violating essential boundaries, or for whatever reason just makes everyday life together impossible for everyone else, it can be the right call to eject them. If restorative work can help in a reasonable amount of time, all the better. But it’s not the community’s job to be a treatment program for someone who’s endangering everyone else.

This power to remove people is so easily abused, though. So work out the process before it’s about anyone in particular. What counts as cause for immediate protective action? Who has to step aside because they’re too close to it? Who decides to put temporary restrictions on someone? Who will make sure all the evidence is preserved? How will the person be able to reply to the concerns? What review or appeal is possible without endangering others? What protections will there be for the person’s interests (housing, records, family contact, access to common resources, outside funds if any) during the separation? When is it time to bring in outside help?

Note that “outside” doesn’t have to mean the nation-state. My research initially leaned too far that way. The basic need here is for a competent level of authority that is not reviewing its own conduct. That could mean another community, a federation of communities, professionals, autonomous regional institutions, courts, regulatory agencies, emergency services, etc. The key is that it’s not the same people.

Also decide on a mediator or ombudsperson in advance. Why bother? People often won’t trust someone they haven’t already met, who comes in during a crisis as a “neutral stranger.” A mediator doesn’t obviate the need for evidence, safeguarding, rulings, etc. Mediation is an attempt to restore good relations between people. When people can’t or won’t consent to being in community any more, they still need a final separation.

![A wedding with a coffin in front of the altar: the bride and groom look startled, a guest in sunglasses throws rose petals, and a sign reads “Till Death Do Us Party”.](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!9Q3c!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fsubstack-post-media.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fddd2a051-9ac5-4630-868b-5a37226707f9_1536x1024.png)

Dissolution is something founders rarely want to talk about while they’re picking a name for their community and looking forward to its first harvest. Who would? But that’s exactly when it needs to be talked about.

If the community dissolves, what happens to the land and any outside debts? What about its buildings, equipment, common stores or funds? What happens to each member’s agreed rights? More immediately, who is responsible for ensuring that everyone has a place to live and food to eat? Who takes responsibility for making sure people get their medications and the other care they need? Who keeps childcare going, and makes sure the kids’ schooling carries on? Who takes responsibility for transportation, for the records, for family contact, for the animals, for making sure land obligations are met, and for any unresolved claims? That’s a lot of loose ends!

Think of it like a living will, and assign a bridge or successor for each critical function in advance, so basic life doesn’t depend on reviving the commune. The institution may not be salvageable, but who’s making breakfast tomorrow?

Dissolution terms are also a way for a group to end without turning every friendship into evidence. Who wants that? People may leave hurt, but they keep the transition support they agreed on, and their dignity. And they can tell a coherent story of what happened.

Institutions and relationships don’t die at the same time, and some of what people learned to give one another may go on too. What a relief! The film American Commune follows two sisters who grew up on The Farm. When one of them later became ill, former members who hadn’t seen her in years reached out with support. The Farm’s communal economy had changed dramatically, but the bonds hadn’t vanished.

Where’s Utopia? (1988) is a documentary by my father, made with Jerry Mintz.
A Place Called Chiapas (1998) is about the early days of the Zapatistas.
American Commune (2013) is about The Farm, seen through the eyes of two sisters who grew up there. Why this one? For this article, the view of the grown children is essential.
Commune (2005) is about Black Bear Ranch, and what radical freedom did to the relationships there.
A New We takes you on a tour of a bunch of ecovillages in Europe. How many different arrangements can hide under that one label? A lot, it turns out!
Within Reach follows a couple as they bike 6,500 miles, visiting a hundred or so communities.
Seeking the Good Life in America compares Twin Oaks, Acorn and Light Morning.
Voices of Cohousing shows the partial-community option, where you get high neighborliness and more private autonomy.
Inside the Bruderhof is about a high-commitment religious community, including the autonomy it requires members to give up. Oh, and the Bruderhof has a pretty extensive YouTube channel too.
Living in the Future: Lammas is about what happens when community-building meets land use and planning law.

The Continuum Concept by Jean Liedloff (1975) is a foundational natural-child-rearing book, based on her time with the Ye’kuana. Is it settled anthropology? No, it’s provocative observation.
Hunt, Gather, Parent by Michaeleen Doucleff (2021) is a practical, accessible book about kids taking part in family life. It’s also about autonomy, and spreading out the work of caring for them.

Where do you start with the nuts and bolts? Creating a Life Together by Diana Leafe Christian, for membership, money, land and agreements.
Want a guide to intentional community that covers the whole system? There’s Building Belonging by Yana Ludwig.

Many Voices One Song by Rau and Koch-Gonzalez is a practical manual for doing sociocracy.
Building United Judgment by Schaub and colleagues is about consensus decision-making.
Ludwig and Gimnig’s The Cooperative Culture Handbook has a bunch of exercises for being more cooperative, dealing with conflict and building group culture.

section: What Helps Communities Last—and Whether Longevity Is Enough
text: Communities That Abide by Dmitry Orlov makes an uncomfortable argument: the communities that last a long time often rely on a religious ideology which makes members feel alienated from the wider society. Basically, the more cultish, the more durable, since cults are designed to capture people.

section: What Helps Communities Last—and Whether Longevity Is Enough
text: It makes one wonder, is longevity alone a meaningful measure, when a community may keep going without its members flourishing? That’s the question in “Measuring Success in Intentional Communities”, a paper by Rubin, Willis and Ludwig.

section: What Helps Communities Last—and Whether Longevity Is Enough
text:
Commitment and Community by Rosabeth Moss Kanter is a classic. It compares a bunch of nineteenth-century communes, and the practices that built commitment in them.
Alienation and Charisma by Benjamin Zablocki is field research on communes, and on the role charisma plays in them.
Jo Freeman’s “The Tyranny of Structurelessness” (1970) is the classic essay on hidden hierarchy. Can it be harder to challenge than explicit authority? She argues it can.

The Fire and the Word by Gloria Muñoz Ramírez and Subcomandante Marcos is about how the Zapatista movement came about.
Want it straight from the Zapatistas? Their own archive is Enlace Zapatista, and look especially for their 2023 explanations of the new autonomy.

If you’re curious about the research behind this, it was a much bigger source audit than would comfortably fit in an article. It’s all in the public research report: the evidence base and its limits, the counterexamples, what I still couldn’t verify, etc. So you can check it yourself, and this article doesn’t have to be a 200-row ledger. Can you imagine? 😂

When people tell me they have trauma, I generally recommend they follow my inner child therapy guide, which includes somatic therapy & breathwork. To help people engage more deeply with the practices, I have advised the use of my Ultimate Psychedelic protocol. But recently, I realized that there’s some more basic physiological interventions we need to implement before getting to those levels. The very first step is fixing your physical health and neuro-inflammation. I suggest starting with my detox guide. After addressing overall health and neuro-inflammation, this de-armoring guide gets more specific to address the hardened neural pathways that have developed over a lifetime.

This protocol is partly theoretical and partly based on experience reports. There’s no peer-reviewed study that says all this, although there are studies supporting various parts of it. As with any guide, see what makes sense for you, your genetics, your situation, and your experience. People are all quite different, and you never know until you try.
